In effect, you might say that I’m taking the computer science concept of lazy evaluation — not evaluating results until they are requested — and trying to kick it up a notch to hyper lazy evaluation by just saying, “Nah, you don’t need those; I just won’t compute them” — and trying to figure out when I can get away with it. (The eagle-eyed might view both of my previous optimizations and the current one as different forms of “Make N smaller.” The previous two optimizations did that through finding alternative ways to compute or approximate some of the renames, while the current one is literally about deciding to just not compute some of the renames.) Why do we need renames anyway? The merge machinery uses renames for two purposes: Three-way content merging : in order to do three-way content merging of files, we need three different file versions. If one side of history renamed a file, then some of the content for the file is found under a different path than in the merge base. Directory rename detection : when one side of history renames a directory, and the other side of history adds new files to that directory, we want to be able to warn the user about the need to choose whether those new files stay in the old directory or move to the new one. If we don’t do rename detection, renamed files are likely to appear as modify/delete conflicts for the old filename and as a new file for the new filename. Both will be present in the working copy, both will have edits, the original version of the file from the merge base won’t be obvious, and users will be left attempting to reconcile the two. Also, if we don’t do rename detection, new files placed into old directories could be “left behind” when all the other files in those directories have moved elsewhere. Ok, we need renames; but do we need all of them? If a rename is needed for the purposes of three-way content merging or for the purposes of directory rename detection, then we need it. Let’s dig into those two cases to see if either of them need renames in all cases, or if they have cases where rename detection can be skipped: Three-way content merges Three-way content merges are about reconciling differences made on both sides of history. If only one side of history modified the content of a file, then we don’t need to do a three-way content merge. Let’s look at each of the two possibilities to see why this is the case. The brief version is: If the file content wasn’t modified on the renamed side ⇒ we get to do exact rename detection, which is cheap If the file content wasn’t modified on the unrenamed side ⇒ detection of a rename for that source file is irrelevant Let’s walk through both in more detail. Let’s use two filenames, old.c & new.c, with the following abbreviated object ids (and where the value ‘000000’ is used to denote that the file is missing in that commit). The first case corresponds to something like this: old.c new.c MERGE_BASE: 01d01d 000000 MERGE_SIDE1: 000000 01d01d MERGE_SIDE2: 5e1ec7 000000 Here, exact rename detection will determine that old.c in MERGE_BASE and new.c in MERGE_SIDE1 are related (identical, in fact). That would suggest we should do a threeway content merge between MERGE_BASE:old.c, MERGE_SIDE1:new.c, and MERGE_SIDE2:old.c. However, two of those three files have the same content (noted by having the same hash), so the three-way content merge isn’t even needed; we already know the result will be a file whose hash is 5e1ec7 — which we already have stored in our repository. And the knowledge about the rename lets us know that 5e1ec7 is the hash for file named new.c in the result of the merge, while old.c should be removed from the result. The second case is a bit more involved, and perhaps the claim that the rename is irrelevant is surprising. Let’s walk through what that case looks like: old.c new.c MERGE_BASE: 01d01d 000000 MERGE_SIDE1: 01d01d 000000 MERGE_SIDE2: 000000 5e1ec7 Since I claimed that detection of the rename was irrelevant for this case, let’s compare what happens both with and without the rename being detected: Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in If the rename IS NOT detected ⇒ then old.c looks like it was unmodified on one side and deleted on the other and should thus be removed. new.c looks like a new file we should keep as-is. If the rename IS detected ⇒ the code sets up a three-way content merge between MERGE_BASE:old.c, MERGE_SIDE1:old.c, and MERGE_SIDE2:new.c. This runs as follows… Since the version of the file in MERGE_BASE and MERGE_SIDE1 are identical (both are files with hash 01d01d), the three-way content merge would produce exactly the version of the file whose abbreviated object id is 5e1ec7. In fact, the code looks at the hashes and returns the answer without even looking at the file contents since it knows the answer and knows the repository already has a file with the necessary hash stored in it. Since the file was renamed from old.c to new.c, it will record the file contents whose hash is 5e1ec7 at new.c (which means keeping it as-is), and remove old.c. If you compare the two results above, you’ll note that they have an identical conclusion, even if they used different logic to arrive there. Thus we have the same result regardless of whether we detect a rename for old.c. There is no way for us to know a priori what file new.c would be paired with and whether that file has been modified, so new.c will have to be left in our big matrix of comparisons when searching for renames. The fact that old.c is unmodified on one side of history, though, is enough for us to know that it doesn’t need to be included — at least not for the purpose of three-way content merging. Directory rename detection We only need renames for source files as part of directory rename detection if: The directory containing the file no longer appears on the side of history for which we are detecting renames (if the directory still appears, it hasn’t been renamed, at least not on that side of history). The containing directory had new files added to it on the other side of history from which we are detecting renames (if there were no new files added to that directory, then there will be nothing for directory rename detection to warn about or move into a new location). Further, even in these cases, we don’t need renames for all the source files in a renamed directory, we only need enough renames to satisfy the “majority wins” rule, so if we get enough renames from exact rename detection or basename-guided rename detection (see the last two blog posts in this series) then we don’t need to detect any more — at least not for the purposes of directory rename detection. Much like three-way content merges, the needs for directory rename detection has focused on rename sources and gives us a way to mark certain source files as irrelevant for rename detection. We do not have a way to reduce the number of potential rename destinations. Abstraction layers It has been said that every problem in computer science can be solved with another layer of abstraction, except for the problem of having too many layers of abstraction. As software engineers, we love abstracting things; it allows us to create reusable components. However, sometimes the abstraction creates an artificial wall between different components of our programs, and we later find we want to create a building that spans both sides of the wall. Other times our reusable components were designed to solve one problem, but when we go to re-use them for a different problem, we find they provide enough information for us to solve what we need, but they provide more than what we actually need. In git, there is a specific component responsible for rename (and copy) detection. It’s a sub-component of the diff machinery, which takes two trees (a start and end state) and computes the differences. This is very handy for things like git diff OLD_COMMIT NEW_COMMIT or git log -p as they’ll want to know all the differences between two commits; the diff machinery solves such a problem well. Merges need two sets of renames — from the MERGE_BASE to MERGE_SIDE1 and from MERGE_BASE to MERGE_SIDE2. So, it seems quite obvious to just reuse our nice component twice to do rename detection for each side. That gives us the answers we need...but I think this abstraction obscured the optimization opportunities for a long time. Note that all of our work above about when renames can be skipped involved information about the other side of history. The diff component doesn’t have knowledge about three commits; only two, so it has no notion of another side of history. Implementing these optimizations basically means we’ve got to pass a bunch of extra information from the merge component to the rename detection component so that it can make decisions based on this extra information. It also means moving all the directory rename detection logic from the merge component into the rename detection component (despite the name similarity, directory rename detection had always been merge specific and since it was a post-processing step it lived outside of the rename detection umbrella). This all sounds really complicated and special case; is it worth it? At this point you may be noting some things that make you question the advisability of this optimization: This optimization will only help the merge machinery (so git commands like merge, revert, cherry-pick, or rebase); it won’t help commands in the plain diff family (so it won’t help git commands like diff, log, or status). This optimization is going to involve an awful lot of code and checking of special cases, as well as passing a lot of information across our old abstraction boundary. This is all for special cases where the unrenamed side of a file isn’t modified AND the file isn’t potentially part of a directory rename. The second of those conditions may be common, but the first sounds like a special case. So, is it worth it? In my opinion, this is the best of all the optimizations I did. To see why it can be so powerful, let’s say we need to cherry-pick an old commit of ours, but upstream in the meantime has renamed 5K files. Let’s ignore the previous optimizations (exact rename detection and basename-guided rename detection) for a moment, or assume that we have 5K files left after those optimizations. Inexact rename detection in git will need to do 5K * 5K file comparisons to match up the rename pairs. However, if the commit we need to cherry-pick is typical, then it modifies ~10 files, and likely doesn’t even add any new files. For a case like that, our 5K * 5K comparison drops to ~10 * 5K — a reduction factor of ~200. For our testcase of interest, the basename-guided rename detection happened to be very effective, meaning that there wasn’t that much remaining optimization potential. But despite that, using this additional optimization still yields some pretty impressive results: Before After mega-renames: 130.465 s ± 0.259 s 11.435 s ± 0.158 s Interestingly, if we turned off the basename-guided optimization from the last blog post, then this optimization by itself would have given us the following speedup for our testcase of interest: Before After mega-renames: 1799.937 s ± 0.493 s 16.148 s ± 0.169 s So it’s much more powerful than the basename-guided optimization, at least for typical rebases and cherry-picks. But the great thing is that some paths can only benefit from one of the optimizations, and we get to use whichever one is better for any given path. For more details about this optimization, see the two upstream threads where my patches were reviewed, namely the thread on avoiding detecting irrelevant renames and on avoiding detecting even more irrelevant renames . This optimization will appear in git-2.32, which is scheduled to be released in June 2021. Author Elijah Newren

title: Palantir: Fragen und Antworten
description: Hier antworten wir auf einige Mythen und Missverständnisse rund um unser Unternehmen
author: Palantir
body: Palantir: Fragen und Antworten Hier antworten wir auf einige Mythen und Missverständnisse rund um unser Unternehmen (Scroll down for English translation below) Oft wird Palantir als geheimnisvolles Unternehmen beschrieben. Ganz falsch ist das nicht. Tatsächlich haben wir viele Jahre vor allem für Organisationen im Bereich der Sicherheitsdienste und der Landes- und Bündnisverteidigung gearbeitet. Auf diesem Gebiet ist Vertraulichkeit entscheidend. Wir konnten uns also oft nicht öffentlich zu unserer Arbeit äußern, sogar wenn missverständlich oder gar falsch über uns berichtet wurde. Mittlerweile sind wir jedoch an der Börse notiert und arbeiten für Kunden aus einem wesentlich breiteren Spektrum. Das gibt uns die Möglichkeit, unsere Tätigkeit offener und transparenter darzustellen. Die nun folgende Sammlung von Fragen und Antworten thematisiert die gebräuchlichsten Fragen und Missverständnisse über die Arbeit von Palantir. Dabei ist uns bewusst, dass wir hier nicht alle Mythen aufführen und erschöpfend entkräften können. Wir wissen auch, dass manche Antworten Anlass für neue Fragen sind. Das begrüßen wir ausdrücklich: Jede Frage ist für uns eine Gelegenheit, mit einer interessierten Öffentlichkeit in Kontakt und ins Gespräch zu kommen. Wir wollen an dieser Stelle also nicht nur eine wahrheitsgetreue Darstellung unseres Unternehmens und unserer Arbeitsweise anbieten. Wir wollen auch in den Dialog mit Ihnen treten. Falls Sie weitere Fragen haben oder an einem vertieften Austausch interessiert sind, schreiben Sie uns doch einfach unter media@palantir.com. Was macht Palantir überhaupt? Wir entwickeln und lizenzieren Software für datengetriebene Entscheidungen und Arbeitsprozesse. Unsere Plattformen Palantir Gotham und Palantir Foundry verbinden die Datenanalyse mit konkreten Geschäftsprozessen: Die richtigen Daten gelangen zum richtigen Zeitpunkt an die richtigen Nutzer und Entscheidungsträger. Das ermöglicht anspruchsvolle Analysen, reibungslose Kooperation und kontinuierliche Verbesserungen. Für weitere Informationen über Palantir Foundry und Palantir Gotham besuchen Sie bitte unsere Homepage. Ist Palantir ein Datenunternehmen oder sogar eine Datenkrake? Nein, Palantir ist eine Softwarefirma. Im Gegensatz zu vielen Technologieunternehmen basiert unser Geschäftsmodell nicht auf der Monetarisierung personenbezogener Daten. Stattdessen entwickeln und lizenzieren wir Softwareplattformen, mit denen unsere Kunden ihre eigenen Datenbestände integrieren und analysieren können, um so zu besseren Entscheidungen zu gelangen. Datenschutz und Datensicherheit sind fundamental für Palantir und wurden von Anfang an in die Architektur der Software integriert. Aber Palantir wird doch immer wieder als Datenhändler oder Datenaggregator beschrieben. Sicherlich profitiert das Unternehmen doch vom Zugang zu Kundendaten? Nein. Wir sammeln, speichern oder verkaufen keine Kundendaten. Wir ermöglichen keinen Datenaustausch zwischen unseren Kunden, es sei denn, ein solcher Austausch ist ausdrücklich von unseren Kunden gewünscht. Jede Partnerschaft mit einem Kunden ist vollständig — also vertraglich, operational und technologisch — von allen weiteren Kundenpartnerschaften abgetrennt. Wir agieren als Auftragsverarbeiter, nicht als Verantwortliche der Datenverarbeitung. Der Einsatz unserer Software und Services erfolgt ausschließlich auf Anweisung unserer Kunden: Diese, und nur diese, legen fest, wie mit den Daten gearbeitet wird. Unsere Kunden kontrollieren die Accounts, in denen Analysen durchgeführt werden. Wir wollen und können die Daten unserer Kunden nicht für unsere eigenen Zwecke wiederverwenden oder übertragen. Der Versuch, so möglicherweise von Kundendaten zu profitieren, wäre illegal und würde darüber hinaus auch das notwendige Vertrauen unserer Kunden untergraben. Verwendet Palantir Kundendaten für eigene Zwecke? Nein. Wie andere SaaS-Anbieter verbessern wir unsere Software kontinuierlich, oft in Zusammenarbeit mit unseren Kunden. Wenn wir einen Softwarefehler beheben oder die Nutzerfreundlichkeit verbessern, stellen wir dies selbstverständlich allen Kunden zu Verfügung. Unter keinen Umständen verwenden wir KI-Modelle, die mit den Daten eines Kunden trainiert wurden, weder für eigene Zwecke noch für den Weiterverkauf an Dritte. Hat Palantir die COVID-19-Krise genutzt, um sich Zugang zu vertraulichen Gesundheitsdaten zu verschaffen? Nein. Palantir nutzt prinzipiell keine Kundendaten und tut dies selbstverständlich auch nicht im Rahmen unserer Partnerschaften im Kampf gegen COVID-19. Stattdessen sind es unsere Kunden, die unsere Software nutzen, um ihre eigenen Datenbestände rechtmäßig auszuwerten. Wenn es nicht um den Zugang zu Gesundheitsdaten ging, wieso hat Palantir dann seine Dienste während der COVID-19-Krise umsonst angeboten? Palantir hat seine Software im Kampf gegen COVID-19 in einigen Fällen pro bono angeboten, weil wir mit unserer Erfahrung, Expertise und Software schnell Hilfe bei einer der größten globalen Herausforderungen der vergangenen Jahrzehnte leisten wollen. Dabei bestand Palantirs Aufgabe darin, eine integrierte und umfassende Reaktion des Gesundheitssystem auf die Pandemie zu unterstützen. So konnten wir sicherstellen, dass die Entscheidungsträger unserer Partner nahezu in Echtzeit über alle relevanten Informationen im Kampf gegen COVID-19 verfügen. Um ein Beispiel zu geben: Unsere Software-Plattform wird derzeit vom U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) in seinem Programm HHS Protect sowie vom National Health Service (NHS) in Großbritannien eingesetzt. Mit HHS Protect werden mehr als 150 unterschiedliche Datenquellen in einem Ökosystem zusammengeführt. Dieses integriert Daten von Bundes-, Landes- und Kommunalbehörden sowie der Gesundheitsbranche, um einen ganzheitlichen Blick auf das gesamte Gesundheitssystem zu ermöglichen. Es gibt viele Softwarefirmen, die in irgendeiner Form Data Analytics bieten. Was unterscheidet Palantir von diesen Unternehmen? Zahlreiche Faktoren machen Palantir einzigartig und unterscheiden uns von anderen Softwareunternehmen. Erstens sehen wir unsere Software als Betriebssystem für die moderne Organisation. Wir bieten also nicht nur eine Datenplattform. Wir bieten nicht nur Analysefunktionen. Diese ermöglichen Erkenntnisse über Betriebsprozesse. Uns geht es aber hauptsächlich um die Frage, wie man es den Anwendern ermöglicht, basierend auf umfassenden und verifizierbaren Daten bessere Entscheidungen zu treffen, ob am Fließband oder in der Chefetage. Dem liegt, zweitens, eine einfache Überlegung zugrunde: Wir stellen uns eine Organisation als die Summe aller Entscheidungen vor, die diese Organisation trifft. Diese Entscheidungen sind auf komplexe Art voneinander abhängig. Organisationen werden dieser Komplexität aber selten gerecht, da Entscheidungen in voneinander unabhängigen Abteilungen basierend auf unverbundenen Datensilos getroffen werden. Die Plattformen von Palantir bringen Ordnung ins Datenchaos, indem sie es Kunden ermöglichen, einen umfassenden Überblick über alle relevanten Daten zu bekommen. Im Ergebnis entsteht das vernetzte Unternehmen und die vernetzte Verwaltung, auf deren Basis bessere und nachhaltigere Entscheidungen getroffen werden können. Drittens profitieren wir von unserer langjährigen Arbeit für einige der bedeutendsten Institutionen der Welt: Unsere Plattformen lassen sich schnell und effektiv beim Kunden implementieren und bieten sofortige Geschäftsergebnisse. Auf Basis unserer Erfahrung und Technologie konnten wir Implementierungszyklen, die häufig Monate in Anspruch nehmen, auf wenige Tage reduzieren. Schließlich sind Datenschutz und Datensicherheit fundamental für Palantir und wurden von Anfang an in die Architektur der Software integriert. Unser Anspruch ist dabei stets, dass unsere Plattformen nicht nur dem heutigen Stand gängiger Datenschutzanforderungen gerecht werden, sondern sich auch im Einklang mit rechtlichen und gesellschaftlichen Vorgaben kontinuierlich weiterentwickeln. Wie unterstützt Palantir seine Kunden beim Thema Datenschutz? Zu unseren langjährigen Kunden gehören Strafverfolgungsbehörden und Nachrichtendienste, aber auch Unternehmen aus der Finanz- und Gesundheitsbranche. Das alles sind Institutionen, die in hochsensiblen und komplexen Datenumgebungen arbeiten. Um diesen Organisationen zu helfen, ihren ethischen und rechtlichen Anforderungen gerecht zu werden, hat Palantir von Anfang an datenschutzrelevante Plattformfunktionalitäten in die Architektur der Software integriert und seither kontinuierlich weiterentwickelt. So erlaubt es zum Beispiel die Software von Palantir, exakt zu bestimmen, wer zu welchem Zweck welche Daten sieht. Gleichzeitig wird exakt geregelt, wie lange Daten überhaupt gespeichert werden. Weil für jeden Datensatz eine detaillierte Historie der Integration und Transformation erstellt wird, ist immer nachvollziehbar, wie die Daten verändert wurden. Außerdem vereinfacht die Software die Berichte an die zuständigen Aufsichtsstellen. Ein Beispiel dafür, wie unsere Produkte einen strengen Datenschutz und einen verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit sensiblen Informationen ermöglichen, ist unsere Zusammenarbeit mit der dänischen Nationalpolizei. Diese hat sich nicht zuletzt für eine Zusammenarbeit mit Palantir entschieden, weil wir der einzige Softwareanbieter waren, der die strengen gesetzlichen Datenschutzanforderungen erfüllen konnte. Die dänische Nationalpolizei nutzt untern anderem die in unserer Software integrierte Audit-Analysefunktion, die es auch nicht-technischen Nutzern innerhalb der Behörde ermöglicht, Audit-Protokolle zu analysieren und potenzielles Fehlverhalten zu untersuchen. Die dänische Nationalpolizei hat die Implementierung von Palantir gegenüber der Wochenzeitung Die Zeit als die wichtigste Anschaffung in der Geschichte der dänischen Polizei in Sachen Datenschutz bezeichnet. Palantir arbeitet seit langer Zeit für Polizeibehörden und Nachrichtendienste. Ist Palantir eine Überwachungsfirma? Nein. Palantir entwickelt Software, die es unseren Kunden ermöglicht, ihre eigenen Daten rechtmäßig und effektiv zu verarbeiten. Wir sind keine Überwachungs- oder Spionagefirma und verkaufen unsere Software auch nicht zu dem Zweck, Überwachung, zum Beispiel Kommunikationsüberwachung, zu ermöglichen. Haben Strafverfolgungsbehörden, die Palantir-Software verwenden, etwa über einen richterlichen Durchsuchungsbeschluss Zugriff auf personenbezogene Daten von Verdächtigen, können sie diese rechtmäßig erhaltenen Daten mithilfe unserer Software analysieren. Was ist mit Berichten, wonach Palantir Predictive Policing ermöglicht — stimmt das? Nein. Palantir ist kein Predictive Policing-Unternehmen und wir bieten auch kein Predictive Policing-Tool an. Vielmehr stellt Palantir den Polizeidienststellen Software-Plattformen zur Verfügung, die es ihnen ermöglichen, ihre reguläre Ermittlungsarbeit effektiver und in Übereinstimmung mit geltenden Richtlinien und Verfahren durchzuführen. Warum unterstützt Palantir die GAIA-X-Initiative, die die digitale Souveränität Europas stärken soll? Palantirs Mitgründer und CEO, Alex Karp, hat schon oft eine Bewunderung für die soziale Marktwirtschaft in Europa sowie die Tradition und immense Expertise der europäischen Industrie zum Ausdruck gebracht, etwa in einem Podcast mit Mathias Döpfner. In diesem Gespräch erklärt er auch den großen Einfluss, den sein Aufenthalt in Deutschland, seine Auseinandersetzung mit Jürgen Habermas und den Denkern der Frankfurter Schule und seine Promotion in Frankfurt am Main auf seine Unternehmerkarriere und die Gründung von Palantir hatten. Im Gegensatz zu vielen US-Tech-Firmen will Palantir nicht mit bestehenden Geschäftsmodellen etablierter europäischer Unternehmen konkurrieren, schon gar nicht diese aushebeln. Vielmehr sehen wir uns als Partner dieser Firmen und wollen sie auf ihrem Weg der digitalen Transformation begleiten. Hier wird eine vernetzte, offene Dateninfrastruktur, wie sie GAIA-X anstrebt, ein großer Schritt nach vorne sein. Seit unserer Gründung in den frühen 2000er Jahren beschäftigen wir uns mit Fragen, die auch für GAIA-X relevant sind: Wie können Institutionen des öffentlichen und privaten Sektors verteilte, heterogene Informationsbestände auswerten, die sie über Jahrzehnte angesammelt haben? Wie können Organisationen Daten effektiv nutzen und auch über Organisationsgrenzen hinaus kooperieren, ohne Datensicherheit und Datenschutz zu gefährden? In fast 20 Jahren Jahren Arbeit in hochkomplexen, hochregulierten Datenumgebungen haben wir ein Verständnis dafür entwickelt, wie technologische Lösungen mit Data-Governance-Richtlinien, rechtlichen Bestimmungen und weiteren normativen Rahmenbedingungen in Einklang gebracht werden können. Genau diese Erfahrung und Expertise wollen wir auch in das GAIA-X-Projekt einbringen. Wie ermöglicht Palantir sichere Zusammenarbeit zwischen Organisationen? Ein Beispiel dafür, wie unsere Produkte eine sichere und kontrollierte Zusammenarbeit innerhalb von Organisationen und über Organisationsgrenzen hinweg ermöglichen, ist Skywise: das digitale Ökosystem für die gesamte Luftfahrtindustrie, das von Airbus bereitgestellt wird und das auf der Software von Palantir basiert. Fluggesellschaften auf der ganzen Welt nutzen Skywise, um die betriebliche Effizienz und Sicherheit zu verbessern und Verspätungen zu vermeiden. Zulieferer können beispielsweise ihre Bestände optimieren und verspätete Lieferungen reduzieren. Airbus kann die Produktion beschleunigen und neue Geschäftsmodelle entwickeln. Skywise bringt verschiedene, sogar konkurrierende Organisationen in einem einzigen Ökosystem zusammen. Die sichere Zusammenarbeit wird mittels einer föderierten Datenintegrationsarchitektur ermöglicht, in der die Teilnehmer ihren eigenen föderierten Bereich verwalten und zweckgebunden kooperieren und Daten austauschen können. Würde Palantir jemals die Nutzung seiner Software aus ethischen Gründen einschränken? Ja. Das hat Palantir schon viele Male getan. In seinem Gastbeitrag in der Washington Post im September 2019 sowie in vielen weiteren Interviews hat sich unser CEO Dr. Alexander Karp zu der ethischen Verantwortung bekannt, die das Unternehmen trägt, um den Missbrauch seiner Technologie zu verhindern. Aus diesem Grund hat sich Palantir beispielsweise entschieden, unter der Trump-Administration keine Aufträge der U.S. Customs & Border Protection (CBP) anzunehmen, da diese Behörde für die Durchführung von Familientrennungen an der Grenze zwischen den USA und Mexiko verantwortlich war. Gleiches gilt für die Einheit Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) der United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), die für die Durchführung von Abschiebungen zuständig ist. Darüber hinaus war Palantir eines der ersten Tech-Unternehmen, das öffentlich erklärte, dass seine Software nicht zur Unterstützung irgendeiner Art von “Muslim Register” verwendet werden darf. Palantir arbeitet nur mit westlichen liberalen Demokratien und deren strategischen Verbündeten zusammen. In allen Fällen prüfen wir potenzielle Kunden und mögliche Anwendungsfälle sorgfältig auf Übereinstimmung mit unseren Werten und Prinzipien. Wie wir in unserem S-1-Filing bei der Börsenaufsicht SEC im Jahr 2020 deutlich gemacht haben, macht Palantir zum Beispiel keine Geschäfte mit der Kommunistischen Partei Chinas, hostet seine Plattformen nicht in China und verhängt Beschränkungen für den Zugang zu unseren Plattformen in China. Wir würden unsere Software auch nicht der russischen Regierung zur Verfügung stellen. Palantir hat die Zusammenarbeit mit vielen weiteren internationalen Regierungsbehörden aufgrund von Bedenken wegen Menschenrechtsverletzungen abgelehnt. Palantir hat seit vielen Jahren ein dezidiertes Team, das sich mit Fragen des Datenschutzes und der Datenethik auseinandersetzt. Weitere Informationen zu Palantirs Ansatz zum Thema Privacy and Civil Liberties Engineering finden Sie hier. Palantir: Questions & Answers Here we address some common myths and misconceptions about our company. Palantir is often described as a mysterious company. This is not entirely wrong. In fact, for many years we have worked primarily for organizations in the field of security services and national and allied defense. In this area, confidentiality is crucial. So we were often unable to comment publicly on our work, even when misleading or even false reports were made about us. However, we are now listed on the stock exchange and work for clients across a much broader spectrum. This gives us the opportunity to present our activities more openly and transparently. The following collection of questions and answers addresses the most common questions and misconceptions about Palantir’s work. We are aware that we cannot list and exhaustively debunk all myths here. We also know that some answers give rise to new questions. We welcome this: every question is an opportunity for us to get in touch with an interested public. So our aim here is not just to provide a truthful presentation of our company and the way we work. We also want to enter into a dialog with you. If you have any further questions or are interested in a more in-depth exchange, just contact us at media@palantir.com. What does Palantir actually do? We develop and license software for data-driven decisions and operational processes. Our platforms Palantir Gotham and Palantir Foundry connect data analysis with concrete business processes: The right data gets to the right users and decision makers at the right time. This enables sophisticated analytics, seamless collaboration, and continuous improvement. For more information about Palantir Foundry and Palantir Gotham, please visit our homepage. Is Palantir a data company? No, Palantir is a software company. Unlike many technology companies, our business model is not based on monetizing personal data. Instead, we develop and license software platforms that enable our customers to integrate and analyze their own data assets to make better decisions. Privacy and data security are fundamental to Palantir and have been built into the software’s architecture from the start. But Palantir is often described as a data broker or aggregator. Surely the company benefits from access to customer data? No. We do not collect, store, or sell customer data. We do not facilitate data sharing between our customers unless such sharing is specifically requested by our customers. Each partnership with a customer is completely separate — contractually, operationally and technologically — from all other customer partnerships. We act as a data processor, not as a data controller. Our software and services are used exclusively on the instructions of our customers: They, and only they, determine how their data is used. Our customers control the accounts in which analyses are performed. We do not and cannot reuse or transfer our customers’ data for our own purposes. Attempting to potentially profit from customer data in this way would be illegal and would also undermine the necessary trust of our customers. Does Palantir use customer data for its own purposes? No. Like other SaaS vendors, we continuously improve our software, often in collaboration with our customers. When we fix a software bug or improve the user experience, we naturally make this available to all customers. Under no circumstances do we use AI models trained with a customer’s data, either for our own purposes or for resale to third parties. Did Palantir use the COVID-19 crisis to gain access to confidential health data? No. As a matter of principle, Palantir does not use customer data and, of course, does not do so as part of our partnerships in the fight against COVID-19. Instead, it is our customers who use our software to lawfully analyze their own data. If access to health data wasn’t the issue, why did Palantir offer its services for free during the COVID-19 crisis? Palantir offered its software pro bono in some cases in the fight against COVID-19 because we wanted to offer our experience, expertise, and software to quickly provide help with one of the biggest global challenges of recent decades. In doing so, Palantir’s role was to support an integrated and comprehensive health system response to the pandemic. This allowed us to ensure that our partners’ decision-makers had near real-time access to all relevant information in the fight against COVID-19. To give an example: Our software platform is currently being used by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) in its HHS Protect program and by the National Health Service (NHS) in the United Kingdom. HHS Protect brings together more than 150 different data sources into one ecosystem. This integrates data from federal, state, and local agencies as well as the healthcare industry to provide a holistic view of the entire healthcare system. There are many software companies that offer data analytics in some form. What sets Palantir apart from these companies? Numerous factors make Palantir unique and set us apart from other software companies. First, we view our software as an operating system for the modern organization. So we don’t just provide a data platform. We don’t just provide analytics. These enable insights into operational processes. But our main concern is how to enable users to make better decisions based on comprehensive and verifiable data, whether on the assembly line or in the executive suite. This is based, secondly, on a simple consideration: we think of an organization as the sum of all the decisions that organization makes. These decisions are interdependent in complex ways. However, organizations rarely do justice to this complexity because decisions are made in independent departments based on disconnected silos of data. Palantir platforms bring order to the data chaos by enabling customers to gain a comprehensive view of all relevant data. The result is the networked enterprise and administration, on the basis of which better and more sustainable decisions can be made. Third, we benefit from our years of working for some of the world’s most prominent institutions: our platforms can be implemented quickly and effectively at the customer site and provide immediate business results. Based on our experience and technology, we have been able to reduce implementation cycles that often take months to just a few days. Finally, data protection and data security are fundamental to Palantir and have been built into the architecture of the software from the beginning. Our aspiration is always to ensure that our platforms not only meet the current state of common data protection requirements, but also continue to evolve in line with legal and social requirements. How does Palantir support its customers in the area of data protection? Our long-standing customers include law enforcement and intelligence agencies, as well as companies in the financial and healthcare industries. These are all institutions that operate in highly sensitive and complex data environments. To help these organizations meet their ethical and legal requirements, Palantir has integrated privacy-related platform functionality into the architecture of its software from the outset and has continued to develop it ever since. For example, Palantir’s software allows users to determine exactly who sees what data and for what purpose. At the same time, it precisely regulates how long data is stored at all. Because a detailed history of integration and transformation is created for each data set, it is always possible to see how the data was changed. The software also simplifies reports to the relevant supervisory bodies. One example of how our products enable strict data protection and responsible handling of sensitive information is our collaboration with the Danish National Police. They chose to work with Palantir not least because we were the only software provider that could meet the strict legal data protection requirements. Among other things, the Danish National Police uses the audit analysis function integrated in our software, which enables non-technical users within the agency to analyze audit logs and investigate potential misconduct. The Danish National Police has described the implementation of Palantir to the weekly newspaper Die Zeit as the most important purchase in the history of the Danish police in terms of data protection. Palantir has a long history of working for police departments and intelligence agencies. Is Palantir a surveillance company? No. Palantir develops software that enables our customers to process their own data lawfully and effectively. We are not a surveillance or spy company, nor do we sell our software for the purpose of enabling surveillance, for example, communications monitoring. If law enforcement agencies using Palantir software have access to personal data of suspects through a judicial search warrant, for example, they can analyze this lawfully obtained data using our software. What about reports that Palantir enables predictive policing — is that true? No. Palantir is not a predictive policing company, nor do we offer a predictive policing tool. Rather, Palantir provides software platforms to police departments that enable them to conduct their regular investigative work more effectively and in accordance with applicable policies and procedures. Why is Palantir supporting the GAIA-X initiative, which aims to strengthen Europe’s digital sovereignty? Palantir’s co-founder and CEO, Alex Karp, has often expressed an admiration for Europe’s social market economy and the tradition and immense expertise of European industry, such as in a podcast with Mathias Döpfner. In this conversation, he also explains the major influence that his stay in Germany, his exposure to Jürgen Habermas and the thinkers of the Frankfurt School, and his doctorate in Frankfurt am Main had on his entrepreneurial career and the founding of Palantir. Unlike many U.S. tech companies, Palantir does not want to compete with, much less undermine, existing business models of established European companies. Rather, we see ourselves as a partner to these companies and want to accompany them on their path to digital transformation. Here, a networked, open data infrastructure, such as the one GAIA-X is striving for, will be a major step forward. Since our founding in the early 2000s, we have been addressing questions that are also relevant to GAIA-X: How can public and private sector institutions exploit distributed, heterogeneous information assets that they have accumulated over decades? How can organizations use data effectively and cooperate across organizational boundaries without compromising data security and privacy? In nearly 20 years of working in highly complex, highly regulated data environments, we have developed an understanding of how technological solutions can be aligned with data governance policies, legal regulations and other normative frameworks. It is this experience and expertise that we intend to bring to the GAIA-X project. How does Palantir enable secure collaboration between organizations? One example of how our products enable secure and controlled collaboration within organizations and across organizational boundaries is Skywise: the digital ecosystem for the aviation industry provided by Airbus and based on Palantir’s software. Airlines around the world use Skywise to improve operational efficiency and safety and avoid delays. Suppliers, for example, can optimize inventory and reduce late deliveries. Airbus can speed up production and develop new business models. Skywise brings together disparate, even competing, organizations into a single ecosystem. Secure collaboration is enabled using a federated data integration architecture where participants manage their own federated space and can collaborate and share data for a specific purpose. Would Palantir ever restrict the use of its software for ethical reasons? Yes. Palantir has done so many times. In his guest editorial in the Washington Post in September 2019, as well as in many other interviews, our CEO Dr. Alexander Karp has acknowledged the ethical responsibility the company has to prevent the misuse of its technology. For this reason, for example, Palantir decided not to accept U.S. Customs & Border Protection (CBP) contracts under the Trump administration, as this agency was responsible for conducting family separations at the U.S.-Mexico border. The same is true for the Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) unit of United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which is responsible for conducting deportations. In addition, Palantir was one of the first tech companies to publicly state that its software may not be used to support any type of “Muslim Registry.” Palantir only works with Western liberal democracies and their strategic allies. In all cases, we carefully screen potential customers and potential use cases for consistency with our values and principles. For example, as we made clear in our S-1 filing with the SEC in 2020, Palantir does not do business with the Chinese Communist Party, does not host its platforms in China, and does not impose restrictions on access to our platforms in China. We also would not provide our software to the Russian government. Palantir has refused to cooperate with many other international government agencies due to concerns about human rights violations. Palantir has had a dedicated team working on privacy and data ethics issues for many years. For more information on Palantir’s approach to privacy and civil liberties engineering, click here.

title: Hardening Palantir’s Kubernetes Infrastructure with Cilium
description: Palantir’s InfoSec team shares their experience using Cilium to harden our Kubernetes Infrastructure
author: Palantir
body: Hardening Palantir’s Kubernetes Infrastructure with Cilium Containerized infrastructure has become an industry-wide trend as engineering teams lean on the likes of Docker or Kubernetes to manage, deploy, and scale their environments; here, Palantir is no exception. We built Rubix, Palantir’s Kubernetes infrastructure, with two primary goals in mind: streamlining and scaling the deployment of our software platforms and strengthening our security posture. In this blog post, Palantir’s Information Security (InfoSec) team will share our recent experience using Cilium: an open-source project by Isovalent dedicated to securing container-based infrastructure, enabling visibility & controls preferable to those of a traditional firewall. Using Cilium as a basis for network controls, Palantir’s engineers have made material improvements to the network rules regulating Rubix’s traffic. Likewise, Palantir’s Computer Incident Response Team (CIRT) has used Cilium’s logging as a valuable source of telemetry when authoring alerting & detection strategies that target theoretical attack primitives applicable to Rubix’s infrastructure. In this article, Palantir’s InfoSec team would like to: Walk through the Cilium functionality that allowed Palantir to further harden Rubix’s attack surface. Address the areas of Cilium’s logging telemetry that we’ve found valuable for alerting & detection. Shortcomings with traditional security tooling & controls Traditional “legacy” InfoSec controls & tooling (which were largely designed with static infrastructure in mind) can have shortcomings when working with a container attack surface, especially when that attack surface is largely ephemeral, or is part of a broader ecosystem of microservices in a SaaS environment. Network tooling & controls A common shortcoming seen in traditional network security tooling is a relative lack of support for granular networking controls covering the varying endpoints, microservices, and resources in an environment comprised of ephemeral containers. A traditional Layer 3/4 firewall can regulate ingress & egress on the basis of port & destination, but that rule is indiscriminate, and blocks (or allows) all traffic meeting the parameters of its ruleset. Some networking solutions build out their feature set with controls that go beyond basic port / IP ingress & egress (e.g., controls by domain, byte count, time of day, or IP reputation), but such controls still tend to operate based on identifiers such as a hostname, domain, or IP address. When working within a containerized ecosystem, in which most interaction occurs between ephemeral microservices and API resources, maintaining a concept of a given endpoint or resource’s identity can be challenging when approached in the context of traditional TCP/IP nomenclature. Endpoint tooling & controls Another common security tool shortcoming involves relying on telemetry from Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR) sources (See: osquery Across the Enterprise) that treat containerized infrastructure the same as any traditional static endpoint by solidifying its concept of identity based on an IP address, or a hostname. Each time an ephemeral resource is spun up, that resource must have an EDR agent installed, which in turn must check in to a central server, or must log its telemetry directly to a logging destination. Once an EDR agent is on an ephemeral host and successfully reporting telemetry, it’ll only continue doing so for as long as that resource exists (which could be a matter of seconds). Perhaps the service responsible for said endpoint spins up such a resource every minute or so; the result would be dozens of endpoints spinning up over the course of an hour, all pertaining to the same service, all doing the same job. However, for each endpoint spun up, EDR telemetry would treat it as a discrete entity (with its own ID, hostname, etc.). Containerized network security controls with Cilium Cilium’s concept of a resource within a given environment is based on a service, pod, or container identity, which allows for persistent visibility and controls around a given resource (or family of resources) in circumstances where such an object may only exist temporarily, or may have a sporadic lifecycle. Kubernetes labels are applied to each resource known to Cilium, which enrich a given resource’s title with further contextual data surrounding the resource’s role and function. Compared to operating based on a hostname or IP address, working with verbose labels and contextual metadata makes an analyst’s job infinitely easier when navigating the bespoke nuances of a containerized environment. To be compliant with Palantir’s security controls, Cilium must be deployed to each resource in our Rubix environment. Once deployed, Cilium operates based on rules established in its Network Policy. Cilium network policies are specified as rules that dictate the connections and flow permitted between resources in a given environment. Network Policy rules operate at Layer 3, Layer 4, or Layer 7, and each rule establishes controls based on the Kubernetes identifiers affiliated with a given resource. For example: Microservice A should only be able to make requests against API Resource X and API Resource Y, provided those requests match Z Criteria. Only pods with the label Purpose A can resolve Domain B. Policy examples Let’s look at two examples (sourced from Isovalent’s Network Policy documents) of typical Cilium rules for Kubernetes resources. First, the Layer 3/4 example demonstrates Cilium’s understanding of an endpoint’s “role” to control traffic. Labels-dependent Layer 4 rule [Source] In addition to Layer 3/4 controls, Cilium introduces the notion of Layer 7 rules, which lets an engineer regulate characteristics of network traffic at the application layer. With Layer 7 controls, engineers can take their knowledge of how endpoint & API resources should interact with one another in a containerized environment, and can then orient their network controls to prohibit deviations from that baseline. The following rule is one example of such controls, and restricts endpoints with a designated label from receiving traffic on any port other than the value provided, then further restricts the aforementioned activity to specific API traffic with the correct HTTP header: All GET /path1 and PUT /path2 when header set [Source] Using Cilium’s controls at Palantir At Palantir, our infrastructure and security engineers have used Cilium’s rules to establish network controls tailored to Rubix’s bespoke functionality. By ensuring that all of Rubix’s Kubernetes resources are appropriately labeled with an accurate representation of their role and function in our environment, we’ve equipped Cilium with the requisite identifiers needed to interpret Kubernetes’ identity-based concepts when regulating traffic within Rubix. With a robust set of rules in place, our InfoSec team’s attention turns to instances when Cilium’s rules succeed in their job by blocking non-compliant traffic in Rubix. The implication of such activity is that a possibly-malicious third party could be attempting actions in the environment. In such cases, our team pivots to the areas of alerting, detection, and response. Containerized Alerting and Detection with Cilium Hubble is the observability / logging platform built on top of Cilium; it uses eBPF to achieve visibility into the operations occurring on an endpoint, and in turn generates discrete log entries for a variety of events. Hubble log event types At the time of this publication, Hubble generates nine event types; such events can be split into two categories: 1) Network traffic events generated from Cilium’s networking visibility Cilium’s network-based logging includes telemetry from successful and unsuccessful netflow among Kubernetes resources. However, in the context of a network tool with Layer 7 controls such as Cilium, we receive block events for activity that we might not see if using a traditional network security solution. For example, if Endpoint A is a microservice whose only traffic should be a periodic GET request to HTTP 1, and Cilium blocks a POST to HTTP 1 we can assume a handful of conclusions. First, the same activity would likely have been allowed by security controls operating explicitly on IP & port restrictions, and second, an outside factor is responsible for generating the POST request. That’s not to necessarily say that every errant POST is due to a malicious actor, but having visibility into the traffic if an attacker were generating unsanctioned HTTP traffic in one’s environment would be a valuable resource in responding to such an incident. 2) Process events captured by Hubble’s on-endpoint eBPF visibility As noted, while some of Hubble’s events are derivative of Cilium-specific network visibility & activity, other logging events simply leverage Hubble’s on-endpoint eBPF visibility to record process activity. Palantir’s alerting & detection engineers have found that Hubble’s process-specific events can serve as an alternative to traditional enterprise EDR solutions (even if Cilium was originally deployed with a focus on network activity rather than process activity). Such telemetry includes process start events, socket connections, and process end events. There is broad overlap between Hubble’s process logging and that of traditional EDR solutions. We expect that an organization running Cilium & Hubble could tentatively reduce their agent footprint, SIEM ingestion, and enterprise EDR costs by relying on Hubble’s process logging in place of said environment’s prior EDR solution. Alerting & Detection at Palantir The aforementioned logging events could be used to surface a variety of attack scenarios. In the interest of providing an example as to how Palantir uses telemetry from Cilium / Hubble to surface potentially malicious behavior, our InfoSec team is publishing one of our internal alerting & detection strategies. This strategy was authored to alert on Hubble events generated when Cilium blocks a DNS request originating from pods in the Rubix environment. Alerting & Detection Strategy 006: Cilium Blocked DNS Resolution Ending notes Broadly, Palantir’s InfoSec team feels that our use of Cilium has hardened the network security posture of our Rubix environment, while also making material contributions to our alerting & detection repertoire. We’re delighted to have worked with Isovalent to support this open-source project for the benefit of the broader InfoSec community, and we’re looking forward to more developments in the security space that cater to container-based environments and infrastructure. Authors: Michael A. & Sean C.

title: Building the Digital Grid: The role of software in grid resilience
description: It has been a challenging decade for utilities. Palantir engineers examine the role of software in building grid resilience and stability
author: Palantir
body: Building the Digital Grid: The role of software in grid resilience A challenging decade for utilities Over the last ten years, changes in the power sector have challenged the stability and safety of the electrical grid. A few major changes include: The shifting mix of production technologies. A fall in the cost of renewables, pressure to meet the climate crisis, and political and investor decisions about coal and nuclear are all impacting grid stability and the cost of management. Changing patterns of demand. Trends including electric vehicle ownership, distributed generation, and smart meter enabled services (e.g., time-of-day pricing) are introducing new patterns of demand. An unpredictable climate. Volatile events like floods and hurricanes damage infrastructure, while hot and irregular weather increases the risk of grid-related wildfires and reduces the predictability of demand. These challenges are compounded by aging grid infrastructure that is becoming more and more expensive to maintain. Many of them also have a political aspect. As governments create policies to mitigate the physical risks of climate change, for example, or accelerate the rollout of renewable generation, they reveal pressures and costs in the grid. Grid operators urgently need new infrastructure, better maintenance regimes, and more efficient systems to satisfy customers and regulators and guarantee the resilience of the grid. Data-driven maintenance To maintain the grid with the resources they have, grid operators need to know which assets to replace, and schedule the work within the right timeframe. This should be informed by a complete picture of risk and a framework for prioritization decisions that ensures a good return on each new component. Grid operators have access to vast volumes of information about their assets. However, many lack the digital infrastructure to apply that information to complex prioritization decisions. Often operators are only able to access asset information in static reports that lack context and make it difficult to compare across asset types. As a result, rather than being driven by the data, decisions are made using heuristics like age or “first break first fix”. To meet the challenges facing the grid, operators need to move beyond static analysis and siloed information. They need a complete view of their data and a risk scoring system that links directly to investment prioritization decisions. This, in turn, should drive maintenance operations, with risk scores provided to decision-makers alongside relevant information from other systems, like finance and organizational constraints. Developing the digital grid Connecting data to grid operations is not easy. To deliver power safely to customers, operators have to track the real time status of all outages. They need to know the location of every element of their grid and the characteristics of each region — corrosion and snow loading zones for example. They must track all past inspections and repairs, know their customers, map vegetation around lines, predict the weather, and understand the status and location of planned work. On top of all of this, they have streams of sensor data flowing in that quickly reach massive scale and require advanced technology to process. Bringing these sources of information together to make informed decisions is a major challenge. It is often tackled via time-intensive manual processes. An engineer investigating asset failures, for example, might load up the relevant outages in one system, access information on past inspections in another system, and check against planned repairs in a third. Yet another system might hold information about budget and finances, making it hard to understand the cost of each intervention and the best way to allocate funds. All of this work to gather information only applies to a single point in time, so the result is quickly out of date. We’ve deployed Foundry, Palantir’s enterprise data platform, to provide a digital grid that helps cut back these time-intensive workflows. Foundry enables information from every part of the grid to be integrated securely in a central data operating system. This provides a picture of real-time grid state estimation, accelerating workflows like the one characterized above and unlocking uses of data that were previously too technically challenging. One partner, for example, was able to make use of an earlier investment in smart meters to improve customer service. Using Foundry, the company could integrate high frequency data streams from thousands of smart meters that contained information about the relationship between meters. This allowed them to algorithmically identify errors in the mapping between grid assets and customers, and to remedy mis-mapping where it might have led to customers being cut off from power without warning. Another workflow unlocked by Foundry is the use of smart meter data, paired with other sensors, to identify patterns that signal a high risk of asset failures. When such patterns are identified, alerts are surfaced to analysts who can evaluate them — again making use of multiple sources of information — and dispatch preventative maintenance crews as required. These are advanced use cases, but they illustrate just how quickly innovative approaches to maintenance can be developed once grid operators have centralized access to their data. Triaging a potential asset failure alert in the digital grid. The alert is based on sensor readings and incorporates contextual information from multiple systems. All data is notional. Risk-based maintenance: the gold standard Of course, technology is only one part of the solution. Investment decisions are a dynamic, human driven process and there are constraints that data won’t capture — political pressures, for example, and the dynamic market in which utilities operate. What Foundry has been able to offer partners in the utilities sector is a platform for teams to collaborate with all the relevant information. It’s not a magic bullet, but it allows decision-makers to work together with as much information as possible and link decisions to the evidence that informed them. As an example, in Foundry, the teams that collect data on assets and the teams that make maintenance decisions are able to work together. Team A can develop a risk model using all the relevant data about asset health, and Team B can use that model, combined with finance information, to prioritise investments. On the basis of this experience, we’ve formulated a gold standard for digital grid software with four key requirements: Integrate siloed systems. Bring all data and analytical assets into a centralized platform. Link data, analysis, and models together to unlock complex analytics like multi-model risk scoring. Ensure there is flexibility to integrate new information as things change. Offer cross-organizational collaboration and accountability. Allow teams to work together in one environment and configure access controls to enable collaboration in line with data governance requirements. Capture decisions in processes that are needed to align priorities: long term resilience doesn’t just mean understanding what work to prioritize. It involves breaking down team silos that incentivize local, rather than global optimizations. Establish a flexible framework for asset risk. Use integrated data and analytics to compile multiple measures of risk, for example by combining asset attributes, smart meter sensors and monitoring, outage analytics, failure and load data. Identify gaps in the data and put measures in place to remedy them — incomplete information gathering is one of the biggest barriers we encounter to data driven risk assessment. Set up models for flexibility in the future as new risk factors, such as greater EV use, evolve. Enable opportunity simulation. Priorities for grid operation will continue to change. Software needs to enable data and models to be combined to simulate the possible tradeoffs of different long term choices. When these requirements are met, operators can make informed decisions about investment based on all of the available information and the simulated outcomes of different decisions. By investing in gold standard software to drive spend on physical infrastructure, grid operators can make decisions that continuously bolster resilience and increase safety. In turn, by feeding these decisions back into their data, they build a digital asset that develops in tandem with the physical grid, informing a flexible and robust approach to maintenance for many years to come.

title: Testing in Depth. (Also, please don’t use undeclared dependencies.)
description: Testing in Depth. (Also, please don’t use undeclared dependencies.) I caught the following discussion (slightly paraphrased) in our internal chat this morning: Alice: We see a …
author: Robert Fink
body: Palantirtech Dependency Management Java Continuous Delivery Palantirengineering Testing in Depth. (Also, please don’t use undeclared dependencies.) Robert Fink 7 min read · May 27, 2021 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size I caught the following discussion (slightly paraphrased) in our internal chat this morning: Alice: We see a java.lang.ClassNotFoundException in our start-up logs; this happened after a dependencies upgrade of our database clients. Bob: The database folks need to update their RPC library dependency. The database client was using an OkHttp dependency coming transitively from the RPC library. The RPC library removed support for OkHttp, and so when you upgraded the database client can’t find the OkHttp class. Alice: Hmm, but our builds didn’t fail? Ah, I guess we use in-memory databases for our integration tests. They won’t hit the OkHttp path. Bob. Exactly. Fortunately, this won’t be a P0 for anyone, because Apollo has already automatically rolled back and recalled the affected release. Alice: True. But still, let’s fix the database dependency setup as soon as possible? How did this bug escape testing? Why didn’t it wake the engineers up in middle of the night? How exactly did our continuous delivery system, Apollo, help us? There’s a lot to unpack here, which the following blog post attempts to do. Don’t use undeclared dependencies: AKA, the bug. Press enter or click to view image in full size The product being discussed above has roughly the call shown here. The product uses an RPC library (we use Conjure for RPC) to make calls to several web services. It also has a dependency on a Database Client with two different implementations: For pre-release integration testing (“in vitro”, blue), we use an in-memory fake implementation (more on this below). The production implementation (“in vivo”, red) uses the RPC library to make calls to a remote database service. (This is AtlasDb / Cassandra ). You may already smell a diamond dependency problem; well, here it comes. The RPC library initially used OkHttp internally to make HTTP calls, yielding the following dependency setup: Product @1.0.0 → RPC @2.0.0 → OkHttp → DatabaseClient → RPC @2.0.0 → OkHttp The RPC library later migrated to the Apache HTTP client and removed the OkHttp dependency; when the product upgraded to the new RPC library with version 2.1. The dependency graph looked like this: Product @1.1.0 → RPC @2.1.0 → DatabaseClient → RPC @2.0.0 → OkHttp Note that the RPC dependency appears twice in the dependency graph — once as a direct dependency with version 2.1.0 (using the Apache HTTP Client) and once as a transitive dependency of DatabaseClient with version 2.0.0 (using OkHttp). Our build system ( Gradle ) uses lock files for dependencies (relatedly, check out our gradle-consistent-versions plugin, it’s pretty neat). Typically, the product developer would lock the RPC dependency to 2.1.0, effectively overriding and upgrading the DatabaseClient dependency on RPC@2.0.0. Get Robert Fink ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Thus far, we haven’t done anything wrong: RPC upgraded an internal library, none of its behavior or APIs changed (and so a minor version bump 2.0.0 → 2.1.0 is justified), and the build system picked up the new RPC dependency and applied it consistently. Note that OkHttp is no longer a dependency, but this is fine because RPC@2.1.0 no longer uses OkHttp. So, if we haven’t done anything wrong, how did this go sideways? It turns out that DatabaseClient was using OkHttp classes directly (i.e. outside of the RPC library). But, DatabaseClient did not declare a dependency on OkHttp . In other words, DatabaseClient used a transitive dependency without declaring it, effectively relying on private implementation details of the RPC library. This is a build system bug and is easily fixed by adding an explicit OkHttp dependency to the DatabaseClient library. Could we have prevented the bug? Well, it depends on the build system tooling. At Palantir, we use many Gradle plugins to help with dependency hygiene: gradle-consistent-versions lets developers declare dependency versions for projects. (It’s subtly different from nebula.dependency-recommender and vanilla Gradle 4.8+ lock files, take a look at the README for more detail.) checkClassUniqueness prevents duplicate classes on the class path. Note that deduplicating dependencies by Maven coordinate is not sufficient, for instance when internal or open-source dependencies get renamed. Duplicate classes are a nasty source of subtle bugs, because the runtime behavior (i.e. which class gets used) depends on hard-to-observe properties like the file system order of dependency JAR files. checkImplicitDependencies tries hard to prevent exactly what was causing the bug described above: dependencies that are used but not declared . At this point, determining exactly when a class is used but not declared is not a fully solved problem, in particular when libraries use reflection. Why didn’t checkImplicitDependencies catch the problem in this case? Unfortunately, the check was not enforced at CI time; we are of course fixing the root cause by adding the check . checkUnusedDependencies alerts developers when they declare dependencies that they don’t use. While this might look primarily like a hygiene problem, a minimal dependency footprint reduces the risk of shipping vulnerabilities and helps keep release sizes small. gradle-dependency-control (internal) manages central allowlists and denylists for dependencies The Java Jigsaw project as well as Maven’s dependency scopes (cleanly expressed using Gradle’s api vs implementation configurations ) target these problems in a more principled way by letting developers make explicit (and enforceable!) splits between public and private APIs and dependencies. I hope that Jigsaw module adoption will slowly percolate through open-source and Palantir code bases, helping to increase code quality and prevent dependency bugs. For more reading on the topic, check out the documentation to Google’s Bazel build system , describing exactly the same problem. Testing in Depth So far, we have discussed Alice and Bob’s bug and how certain build systems and plugins help with dependency hygiene. Now, let’s move on and talk about Alice’s “ Hmm, but our builds didn’t fail?“ and Bob’s “this won’t be a P0 for anyone“ statements . Why did this bug not lead to a widespread outage at Palantir? The answer is what I call Testing in Depth . By analogy with the concept of Defense in Depth in information security, Testing in Depth is the practice of layering different testing and monitoring techniques, each of them focusing on various aspects of overall software correctness. Standard testing layers are unit , integration , and end-to-end tests. The product discussed above has extensive unit test coverage and employs pre-merge integration tests to exercise product ↔ database interactions. With a focus on quick CI times, those tests are written against an in-memory test fake implementation of the database service. None of these tests failed, because they didn’t hit the RPC code path that depends on the (absent) OkHttp library. The obvious choice is to add end-to-end tests that exercise the RPC code path, for instance against a development database stack or against a Docker container. But is the obvious answer also the correct answer? It depends, and as always, there are trade-offs. End-to-end tests are slow and notoriously hard to maintain (see Software Engineering at Google for a second opinion). In other words, they are bad for development velocity and, thus, expensive in terms of developer time and ultimately dollars. If they only very occasionally catch problems, then the cost/benefit analysis doesn’t balance out. At Palantir, we prefer to layer in-vitro (i.e. pre-release) unit and integration tests with in-vivo (i.e. post-release) monitoring. I have previously written about Apollo , the continuous delivery system for our SaaS platforms. As alluded to in the conversation between Alice and Bob, a couple of Apollo features combined their powers to catch the dependency bug cheaply and effectively. First, all Apollo-managed applications produce health checks that Apollo, in turn, monitors. Health checks can alert on degraded performance, exception behavior, RPC issues, memory footprint, etc. Apollo continually monitors all health checks and uses them to take corrective action (see below). Second, new product releases are rolled out by Apollo in a controlled fashion. Apollo first upgrades development and canary stacks before moving to internal and finally customer-facing production stacks. Within a given stack, Apollo uses a variant of blue/green deployment to upgrade different nodes of the same application node-by-node. After each node upgrade, Apollo examines the health checks (we call this adjudication ). When health checks fail, two things happen: the upgrade immediately gets rolled back to the latest known-good version and the release gets recalled . A recalled release gets rolled back on all stacks (not just the one that reported the issue) and Apollo will never install it again. Affected development teams are automatically alerted of the rollback and recall so they can investigate and fix their product. This entire process is automatic, managed by Apollo across hundreds of stacks with hundreds of services, applications, and databases. In the case of Alice and Bob, Apollo prevented a fleet-wide outage and P0 by catching a small oversight in library dependency declaration. More generally, we have found that in-vivo monitoring produces better and cheaper error signaling than in-vitro end-to-end testing and as such is an integral component of Palantir’s Testing in Depth strategy. Authors Robert Fink is a Distinguished Software Engineer at Palantir and the founding engineer of Palantir Foundry . If you’d like to work on my team: I am hiring .

title: Transforming the Newsroom: Ringier and Palantir
description: Journalism is at an inflection point. Palantir and Ringier are partnering to bring data into the newsroom
author: Palantir
body: Transforming the Newsroom: Ringier and Palantir In this post, Chief Product Officer of Blick-Group and former Editor-in-Chief of Blick.ch, Katia Murmann, and Palantir Deployment Strategist Romain de Ganay discuss the foundations of Ringier AG’s partnership with Palantir and how they’re leveraging the platform to better inform readers. For more information, watch Palantir and Ringier’s recent partnership video. Katia Murmann Journalism is at an inflection point. On one hand, globalization, digitization and social media proliferation have shortened the ‘news cycle’ to seconds; readers are looking for the latest news — in the moment it happens. On the other hand, these same forces have driven an increased appetite for highly localized, targeted information; readers are looking for stories relevant to their immediate surroundings, communities and daily lives. As a media company, our principal challenge is to bridge this gap — to empower local newsrooms to connect high-quality, timely content to dedicated readers. While this may sound challenging enough, there’s another hurdle. An increasingly large share of advertising revenue, traditionally a principal source of funding for media companies, is being captured by Tech Giants. So, simply spending more is not an option. We must find ways of working smarter, staying agile and making informed decisions. That’s where data comes in. Internally, we doubled-down on analytics to understand what articles and topics were driving traction, who we were reaching, where our audiences were concentrated, and so on. However, as we quickly found out, the data landscape around a website is highly complex and nuanced. We were generating more than 200 reports across a slew of dashboards and applications. The more reports we generated, the more data we had, the harder it became to manage. We did not know where to find the data we needed in this bunch of reports. But all of these reports, and all of this data, was in the hands of data analysts: not editors, not journalists. The newsroom lacked data — and we had to change this. We needed a collaborative platform that put this information directly into the hands of the content creators. That’s when we started working with Palantir. Romain de Ganay To get started, we sat down with journalists and editors to really understand the lifecycle of a story. Where do you find inspiration? How do you weave that idea into a story? How do you collaborate? What article features (number of images, videos, length, etc.) drive the success of an article? And, most importantly, where does the story go once you publish it? Who reads it? Why this article and not another? Using Palantir Foundry, we were able to integrate data from Ringier’s Content Management System and in-house NLP algorithms with Blick website traffic data to create a unified ontology — a web of intuitive, human-intelligible objects such as Articles, Publishers, Journalists or Videos. We gave journalists and newsroom analysts permissioned access to this dynamic, explorable data foundation, and enabled them to build custom reports, and analytics personalized to them using this ontology. We enabled editorial teams to leverage forecasting algorithms to set their own quarterly targets, which are then written back in the ontology to be monitored. On top of this, Palantir’s various of out-of-the-box, low code/no code workflows meant that there was no technical barrier to entry. Journalists could easily onboard to the platform and start iterating — either on their own, or with selected collaborators. This journalist-driven exploration and optimization meant we could drive enhanced performance without an algorithm dictating what reporters should write about. Katia Murmann Today, data is everywhere in our newsroom, in the dashboards for every journalist, in every meeting that takes place. The results are stunning. 85% of our newsroom uses Foundry on a daily basis. Since we deployed Palantir Foundry, traffic has increased — and we’ve been able to convert the additional revenue to fund independent, quality journalism. We are still at the beginning of this data driven journey. We look forward to continuing to support journalists as they produce high quality content and meet readers where they are.

title: Optimizing Git’s Merge Machinery, #4
description: Palantir engineer Elijah continues exploring optimizations for the Git merge machinery.
author: Palantir
body: Optimizing Git’s Merge Machinery, #4 Editor’s note: This is the fourth post in a series by a Palantir Software Engineer on scaling Git’s merge and rename detection machinery. Click to read the first, second and third blog posts. The first post in this series included some background information on how the merge machinery works and why I have worked on optimizing and rewriting it. That background will be critical to understanding this post. So, if you’re unaware that Git stores hashes for files in addition to having hashes for commits, or you’re unaware that merging involves three-way content merges, or you don’t know that rebasing and cherry-picking involves a sequence of special merges, then you may want to go back and read that post first. If you know all that already, let’s keep going. In this post, I’ll consider another optimization, one that I summarized in my first post simply as: “don’t repeatedly detect the same renames done by the upstream branch when rebasing (or cherry-picking) a series of commits.” However, in reality, it’s a bit more complicated. Abstraction layers, again In the previous post, we discussed abstraction layers. In particular, since each merge involved doing two separate sets of rename detection (from the merge base to each of the two commits being merged), and since rename detection is designed to only work on two endpoints (for merges, that’d be the merge base and the side of history we are detecting renames for), rename detection was inherently unaware of what was happening to files on the other side of history. However, in order to implement a “skip irrelevant renames” optimization, we needed both sets of rename detection operations to know information about all three endpoints (the merge base and the commit at the tip of each branch being merged). To implement that optimization, we had to breach the rename detection abstraction layer and pass in some kind of information from an additional side of history. This idea of breaching abstraction layers is relevant to this optimization as well. As discussed in more detail in the first post in this series, rebases and cherry-picks of a series of commits involve a series of three-way merges. Each of those involves two sets of rename detection — from the “merge base” to side 1 (which happens to be the upstream side) of history, and from the “merge base” to side 2 (which happens to be the commit we are trying to transplant). So, for transplanting N commits in a rebase or cherry-pick operation, there would be 2*N calls to the rename detection machinery, and N of those calls for rename detection are for detecting renames done on the upstream side of history. Does that mean we are detecting the same renames N times? Repeatedly re-detecting the same renames? Let’s dive a little deeper to see how the repeated detection of the same renames on the upstream side of history comes up. Let’s revisit what it looks like to rebase or cherry-pick a series of commits. Consider the following setup: A---B---C topic / D---E---F---G main After rebasing or cherry-picking topic onto main, this will appear as: A'---B'---C' topic / D---E---F---G main The way the commits A’, B’, and C’ are created is through a series of merges, where rebase or cherry-pick sequentially uses each of the three A-B-C commits in a special merge operation.
