Use cases include: Opening data in an Integrative Genome Viewer Further investigating the phylogenetic tree Performing variant calling Foundry also enables conversion of FASTQ data into FASTA data by assembling the genome, whether assembled from scratch or with a reference. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Further, our robust security and data governance tooling allow institutions to facilitate secure and timely collaboration between their researchers and other legitimate parties for whom this information is essential. Press enter or click to view image in full size Palantir Foundry displaying notional genomic data Foundry and the De Novo Assembly Approach A genome can be assembled without knowing the likely sequence of DNA fragments from a ‘reference’ genome. Known as the ‘de novo assembly’ approach, it is performed in an HPC environment requiring significant compute power to execute. Traditionally, sequencers generate FASTQ format files, which are then transferred to HPC environments, where workflow languages are used to coordinate de novo assembly. This well established approach, on its own, has limitations; it doesn’t foster transparency, accountability, or automation. Such limitations, which are disadvantageous when looking for a fast and scalable solution during a pandemic, can be remedied with Foundry. Foundry has demonstrated its value to scientists and bioinformaticians who use this approach by easing automation while encouraging collaboration, transparency, and accountability in biomedical data handling. Foundry’s external compute module connector leverages the popular workload management system Slurm and other open-source tools to connect with high-performance computing nodes. By managing all the data and code versioning, while taking care of pipeline schedules validation and health checks, Foundry frees scientists and bioinformaticians from managing those processes. Instead, it focuses them on core genomic data analysis, research, and outcomes. Press enter or click to view image in full size Foundry and Map-based Reference Genome Sequencing In other cases, genomic sequences can be mapped to a reference strain when an organism’s fully sequenced genome in FASTA format is known. Typically accomplished in an HPC environment, scientists who run map-based reference genome sequencing using Foundry’s Genome Alignment Module have the added benefits of cloud elasticity to scale their pipeline in a fully automated way. This capability means that genomes can be aligned in a cluster of computing resources that can grow and shrink in size depending on demand without requiring additional pipeline changes. Palantir partners engaged in the COVID-19 response have highlighted the usefulness of such elasticity, particularly when there was a surge in need for viral genomic alignment to distinguish and track COVID-19 variants. Press enter or click to view image in full size A schematic of the Genome Alignment Module that is available in Foundry, which runs leveraging spark distributed computing capabilities Conclusion With Foundry, our partners are able to optimize their current HPC environments using the external compute module connector and leverage the flexibility of cloud elasticity as needed. Partners also benefit from Foundry’s standard capabilities (Data Integration, Code Versioning, Data Versioning , Data Health, Schedules, etc.) that emphasize automation, collaboration, transparency, and accountability. By leveraging Data Integration capabilities, researchers are able to link genomic data to clinical outcomes. Foundry enablement frees scientists to focus on what is truly important to them: research and development. Ultimately, Foundry is well positioned to lead more agile and informed outbreak response, advancing scientific understanding of virus evolution and epidemiology. (2012). Evolutionary Dynamics of Local Pandemic H1N1/2009 Influenza Virus Lineages Revealed by Whole-genome Analysis. Journal of Virology , 86 (1), 11–18. [2] Lauring, A.S., & Hodcroft, E.B. (2021). Genetic Variants of SARS-CoV-2 — What Do They Mean? JAMA , 325 (6), 529–531.

title: How Palantir Foundry Helps Customers Build and Deploy AI-Powered Decision-Making Applications
description: Today, organizations are looking to AI solutions as a way to accelerate decision-making. Learn about Palantir's integration with AWS to power effective AI.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech AWS Machine Learning Business Partnerships How Palantir Foundry Helps Customers Build and Deploy AI-Powered Decision-Making Applications Palantir 9 min read · Sep 16, 2021 -- 2 Listen Share Editor’s note: The following is a joint article with the AWS Partner Network (APN) Blog. See this post and explore related content on their page . Leveraging data to make better decisions is critical for driving optimal business outcomes. Palantir empowers organizations to rapidly extract maximum value from one of their most valuable assets — their data. Today more than ever, organizations across industries are looking to artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) solutions as a way to further accelerate and improve their decision making. The reality of operationalizing AI can be complex and costly, however. In fact, Gartner still predicts that 85% of traditional AI and ML projects developed within organizations will deliver erroneous outcomes. Even after a model is successfully developed, it often remains an experiment rather than an operational tool that generates consistent, long-term business value. This could be for any of number of reasons: The end-to-end model development process exists in a silo — far removed from subject matter experts. Models backed by static one-time data pulls quickly become stale and inaccurate. Model hand-off happens between teams without documentation, process, and structure. Models are deployed in a piecemeal fashion onto legacy systems and user interfaces. Developing a model was largely a one-time process to gain insight or an experiment, unaccountable to real business outcomes. Palantir Foundry solves for the real-world application of AI — not how it works in the lab. Effective AI is impossible without a trustworthy data foundation, a representation of an institution’s decisions, and the infrastructure to learn from every decision made. Foundry provides an end-to-end, modular and interoperable platform that meets these demands. It’s this modular and interoperable approach that’s at the heart of Foundry’s latest integrations with Amazon Web Services (AWS) AI and ML tools. In this post, we explain the process for making better AI-powered decisions with Palantir Foundry and Amazon SageMaker . Press enter or click to view image in full size About Palantir Foundry Foundry deployed on AWS utilizes many services under the hood — such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), and AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS). The collaboration between Palantir and AWS is helping to power critical operations at the world’s leading organizations — from accelerating clinical research and powering vaccine supply chains to improving the safety and reliability of the electric grid . Here are some examples of the innovative work that Palantir Foundry backed by AWS is powering: Sanofi , one of the world’s leading pharmaceutical companies, has used Foundry to provide core data infrastructure and an analytical platform as part of their platform for Real World Evidence (RWE) research, receiving a 2020 Gartner Healthcare and Life Sciences Eye on Innovation Award for this work. The U.S. National Institutes of Health utilize Foundry to combine public and internal research data in one secure interface. High-throughput screening, genomics, and other biological data are integrated into the platform to advance the research of teams at the National Cancer Institute and the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences. bp and Palantir have extended their partnership to support bp as it works towards its ambition to become a net zero company by 2050 or sooner, and to help the world get to net zero. bp’s digital twin applications , powered by Palantir, have already delivered significant value. Now, there are opportunities to apply these applications to accelerate bp’s new ambition, optimizing wind farms, electric charging networks, solar generation, and supporting the achievement of other aspects of bp’s net zero aims. As Foundry evolves, the team continues to learn how customers leverage services within each platform and have found many opportunities for tighter integrations moving up the technology stack. Over recent months, Palantir’s software development teams have worked closely with AWS to bring these tighter integrations to market, enabling deep integration with AWS data science tools across all layers of the application lifecycle. The focus has been on integrating the Amazon SageMaker suite of AI and ML services together with Foundry’s data integration and decision-making modules. Solution Overview Let’s explore the latest integrations between Foundry and AWS, and show how they can be used by organizations to overcome common data and AI challenges at every stage of the AI lifecycle — from data preparation to model operationalization. Data preparation: Rapidly prepare data with Foundry’s data connection, extract, transform, load (ETL), and data branching capabilities, and then leverage this data in Amazon SageMaker Studio Notebooks via Amazon Athena to analyze data and develop models. Model development: Empower technical and non-technical users alike to develop meaningful ML models with Amazon SageMaker Studio Notebooks and Amazon SageMaker Autopilot for no-code model development. Model integration: Integrate models from Amazon SageMaker Endpoints , Amazon SageMaker Autopilot, and AWS AI services into the Foundry machine learning environment. This benefits from Foundry’s rich deployment infrastructure, monitoring, health checks, and ontology integration. Model operationalization: Use Amazon SageMaker models in Foundry Application Builder and Foundry Simulation Engine to power operational applications and workflows that benefit from feedback loops and model retraining and generate long-term organizational value. The following diagram illustrates the various integration points of the solution. Figure 1 — Integration architecture. Data Preparation Before you can train a new model, you must connect to the relevant underlying data sources and prepare the data for use. Data collection and preparation accounts for a large proportion of a data scientist’s time, leaving little bandwidth for high-value activities like algorithm design, algorithm testing, and machine learning. Foundry’s technology and bidirectional off-the-shelf data connectors (which include AWS services such as Amazon S3, Amazon SQS , and Amazon RDS ) radically reduce the amount of time spent on preparing a high quality data foundation from which to start building models. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Foundry’s data integration capabilities help organizations transform source data into a digital twin of their enterprise, represented by Palantir’s unique semantic model, the “ontology.” The ontology presents all underlying data as objects that reflect the real-world components of your business — such as factories, products, and customers. Acting as a curated, validated, connected and reusable framework for models, this drastically accelerates the AI lifecycle for new models. The ontology will be used to back the operational applications, and the integrated tables backing these data objects will be used to train our ML model. Model Development Foundry has an open and interoperable approach to model development, allowing users to implement their models natively in Foundry’s Code Workbooks, or any third-party application of their choice. One of the core principles of Foundry is enabling both data scientists and business users (or other non-data science experts) to collaboratively utilize data and models to make better decisions. Less technical users — who are often the subject matter experts — are empowered by ML toolkits, no-code model development applications, and out-of-the-box AI services that complement and accelerate Foundry’s full suite of end-to-end AI modeling tools for data scientists. With AWS, users wishing to use data from Foundry in Amazon SageMaker Studio Notebooks can do so through a new integration between Foundry and Amazon Athena that leverages Amazon Athena Federated Query . Using the native Amazon SageMaker Athena SQL integration , users have an efficient way of querying the curated data asset from Foundry directly into their notebooks where it can be subsequently transformed and used for model development. Amazon Athena provides federated connectivity to a number of additional AWS applications and services . This architecture is particularly beneficial for datasets that are used for data science workflows with ad hoc or interactive queries, as the connection can be rapidly configured and does not require any additional synchronization or management. Press enter or click to view image in full size Figure 2 — Accessing Foundry data from Amazon SageMaker. For users looking for a more automated approach, Amazon SageMaker Autopilot eliminates the heavy lifting of building ML models, and helps you automatically build, train, and tune the best ML model based on your data. The integration between Foundry and Autopilot allows users to launch Autopilot jobs via a user interface in Foundry directly off of data in the ontology. This gives users a way to train, evaluate, and deploy a model into production in a matter of clicks, without the need for code. Model Integration Models deployed through Amazon SageMaker Endpoints (plus pre-trained AWS AI services such as Amazon Textract , Amazon Translate , and Amazon Lookout for Equipment ) can now be connected to Foundry ML and bound to Palantir ontology objects in the same way as native Foundry models. Users simply browse the in-service Amazon SageMaker Endpoints and select their model. This will create a new model in Foundry that represents the connection to that Amazon SageMaker Endpoint. Press enter or click to view image in full size Figure 3 — Palantir Foundry’s Modeling Objective Library. Your Amazon SageMaker models and AWS AI services are now first-class citizens in Foundry, and they can benefit from the same deployment infrastructure, monitoring, health checks, as native Foundry models. The final step before making this model operational is to integrate it into the ontology. The input and output parameters of the model are simply bound to data properties in the ontology. This generates a connected web of models that are chained together through these property relations. Native ontology integration ensures your Amazon SageMaker models can be leveraged, collaboratively, for broader organizational workflows, simulations, or end-user facing applications, amplifying their usability and organizational impact. Press enter or click to view image in full size Figure 4 — Palantir Foundry’s ML tooling. Model Operationalization From here, Amazon SageMaker models can be integrated into Palantir operational applications and used to power end-user workflows in Foundry. This is the point where many AI and ML projects can fail for the reasons we outlined in the beginning of this post. However, in Foundry, once models are integrated into the ontology, any user can incorporate them into operational applications and workflows by simply consuming the model outputs. These users are likely intimately familiar with the subject matter in which the model operates but don’t need to be experts in how the model was developed. Nor do they need to be experts in how to invoke the model. Foundry Simulation Engine handles all of the data loading and model orchestration. The integration with Amazon SageMaker transparently manages the hand-off of data between the two platforms and model invocation. Foundry Simulation Engine allows users to run “what-if” simulations over these models with hypothesized inputs and outputs to inform the correct course of action. Any decision, and the context in which it was taken, will be written back to the ontology and, if applicable, the original data source. This feedback loop enables model retraining and allows the platform to continuously improve decisions and recommendations over time. For example, bp uses Foundry’s advanced simulation engines to automatically identify opportunities to increase production. Engineers pose “what-if” questions such as what configuration of wells, facilities, and routing will allow for maximal oil production. This generates hundreds of millions (USD) of additional revenues per year via 30,000 barrels of additional production per day. Press enter or click to view image in full size Figure 5 — Palantir Foundry’s Vertex Simulation Engine. Conclusion The new integration points between Palantir Foundry and Amazon SageMaker allow users to develop, integrate, and operationalize AI that can power the decision making of a modern connected enterprise. To help your organization build and deploy AI-powered decision-making applications, please contact Palantir . If you’re interested in learning about other Palantir and AWS projects, check out how the Foundry ERP Suite is delivering cost savings for AWS customers. Authors Andrew Higgins, Forward Deployed Engineer — Palantir Thomas Powell, Forward Deployed Engineer — Palantir Mehmet Bakkaloglu, Sr. Solutions Architect — AWS Zach Green, Solutions Architect — AWS

title: Optimizing Git’s Merge Machinery, #6
description: In the series finale, Palantir engineer Elijah reviews the impact of his micro and macro-optimizations to the Git merge machinery.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech Github Git Software Development SaaS Optimizing Git’s Merge Machinery, #6 Palantir 11 min read · Sep 20, 2021 -- 1 Listen Share Editor’s note: This is the sixth and final post in a series by a Palantir Software Engineer on scaling Git’s merge and rename detection machinery. Click to read the first , second , third , fourth , and fifth blog posts. Press enter or click to view image in full size The first post in this series included some background information on how the Git merge machinery works and why I have worked on optimizing and rewriting it. That background may be helpful in understanding some parts of this post. However, unlike the previous posts, this one doesn’t delve into the intricacies of merges. While the earlier posts used clever ideas that exploited various properties of merges to reduce the work required, this post instead looks at more traditional, straightforward optimizations. Also, unlike the previous posts centered around specific themes that each took a fair amount of effort to explain, this post will include optimizations that are pretty easy to explain and group them into a single post. Large optimizations First, let’s take a look at the optimizations, grouped into two categories: Fundamental changes in merge-ort design Fundamental to Git is an in-memory data structure mirroring the index (i.e., the .git/index file). It’s just an array of entries for each path tracked in the repository, sorted by pathname. This data structure was at the heart of merge-recursive and most of the rest of the Git codebase. In the fifth blog post, I discussed how the in-memory index data structure would have prevented trivial directory resolutions; here, I discuss how it also caused some performance problems for merges. The fact that the in-memory index is an array makes for fast iteration and relatively fast searching (O(log N)) but is somewhat slow for insertion/removal since O(N) items will have to shift. Usually, that isn’t much of a problem because it’s an array of pointers, and shifting lots of pointers can be done relatively cheaply (using the memmove() function, which is likely optimized for the system). Also, the initial iteration traverses all three trees simultaneously, adding multiple entries for each path when there is a conflict. The initial traversal takes care to only insert entries at the end of the array. The combination of these characteristics mean that most merges will only have a small number of insertions and removals to handle. However, if there are lots of three-way content merges needed (and they resolve cleanly, so the three conflicting entries will be removed and a new entry put in their place), or if there are a lot of renames (causing paths to need to be removed and added elsewhere in the array), then we may have O(N) insertions and/or removals that we need to make. Since each of those is O(N), we spend O(N^2) time shifting elements in the array. The second problem with the old algorithm came from a low-level function named unpack_trees() . This function would walk one or more trees simultaneously to create or update an in-memory index and invoke various callbacks. This design was very useful for commands such as checkout or reset. In simple cases, it also provided what looked like a solid foundation for merging (because it would only need a “few simple fix-ups for special cases”). In reality, the information provided in this scheme was insufficient for the needs of a merging algorithm. Merges need more data and the ability to change traversal orders with deferring and skipping of subtrees entirely, mainly to handle renames well. My early attempts to tweak all the tricky logic in unpack_trees() to address the extra requirements eventually made me realize that we just needed a different abstraction entirely for merge-ort. Since merge-recursive was built on top of unpack_trees(), it did have functions that would re-iterate trees either entirely (to search for specific information, e.g., directory/file conflicts) or re-traverse from the top-level tree down to individual paths (e.g., as done for every rename), to collect more information. That was expensive and we wanted to avoid that expense in merge-ort. merge-ort avoided both the above problems by side-stepping the in-memory index and any use of unpack_trees(). merge-ort was written to create a new merge result as a tree (which possibly included files with conflict markers if the merge had conflicts) without touching the working tree or index. Only after the merge result will merge-ort use the checkout logic to move from the current tree to the merge result. This design avoided the quadratic behavior from the insertions and removals of index entries and the numerous expensive mini-tree traversals done by merge-recursive. I believe these two improvements were responsible for the lion’s share of the speedup seen between the starting point for merge-recursive and the starting point for merge-ort: merge-recursive merge-ort mega-renames: 5964.031 s ± 10.459 s 5504.231 s ± 5.150 s As a reminder, the “mega-renames” test case involved rebasing 35 commits across a branch with about 26,000 renames. This speedup technically also includes numerous “micro-optimizations” listed in the section below. However, they are subsecond optimizations, so nearly all of the speedup above came from the two big optimizations of skipping quadratic array entry shifts and avoiding additional tree re-traversals. From the above results, these two optimizations provide a savings of nearly 459.8 seconds or 7.66 minutes. See commit 557ac0350d (merge-ort: begin performance work; instrument with trace2_region_* calls, 2021–01–23) if you want to read about other test cases and how far ahead of merge-recursive merge-ort started on those other test cases too. Prefetching missing objects in batches for partial clones The next optimization will only benefit folks using partial clones, but it’s a pretty substantial optimization for them. Partial clones operate by only downloading a partial or incomplete set of objects. Typically, it skips all the files and downloads the trees, commits, and tags with the associated branch names and the commits they point to. Then, when any operation needs to access certain files, it will download them on the fly from the original repository. The fallback code to ensure partial clones works will download any given object the first time it is accessed by any Git command, which can result in many objects being downloaded in separate connections to the server, one at a time. Using separate sequential connections for each needed object can be slow. It is helpful if operations that will need many objects can first do some computation to determine which objects it will need and then call a function to prefetch all those objects. A few years ago, Jonathan Tan from Google added such prefetch functionality to the rename detection logic . However, after the optimizations in my first , second , third , and fourth blog posts, we often need far fewer objects to complete rename detection. That provided an opportunity to modify the prefetch logic in rename detection first to do a more limited set of prefetching and then fall back to the more thorough prefetching only in cases that needed it. This modification could potentially increase download operations but often significantly reduce the number of objects downloaded. While at it, I also added some prefetching to merge-ort for the three-way content merges to further reduce the number of download operations. The combination yielded some pretty impressive results in a partial clone: Number of `git fetch` ops during rebase Before Series After Series merge-recursive: 62 63 merge-ort: 30 20 Number of objects fetched during rebase Before Series After Series merge-recursive: 11423 11423 merge-ort: 11391 63 See the upstream thread discussing this optimization if you want to see more details. In particular, these results got Microsoft talking about potentially enabling rename detection for their big monorepos. Their monorepos have more than 25 times as many files as the Linux kernel, forcing them to need partial clones, sparse checkouts, and a pile of special configurations to make things function well. One of those things was turning off rename detection because it was too costly for them. Being able to show somebody that far fewer files would be needed with these new algorithms has them talking about enabling it again. Micro-optimizations There was a long list of micro-optimizations, which include all the sub-second optimizations I made. These ranged in magnitude from hundreds to tens of milliseconds to even just a few milliseconds. There were also some for which I didn’t even have measurements (e.g., because it was part of the basic rewrite and I didn’t have a way to test just that item in isolation). I won’t discuss all these micro-optimizations in detail but will provide links in many cases if you want to dive deeper. Small stuff baked into the merge-ort design Avoid unconditional dropping and re-reading of the index Avoid re-comparing hashes (cached in match_masks) Reduce the size of the (heavily used) merged_info struct by eight bytes, identified by pahole diffcore-rename optimizations b970b4ef62 (diffcore-rename: simplify and accelerate register_rename_src()) 9db2ac5616 (diffcore-rename: accelerate rename_dst setup) 350410f6b1 (diffcore-rename: remove unnecessary duplicate entry checks) hashmap/strmap optimizations 33f20d8217 (hashmap: introduce a new hashmap_partial_clear()) 6ccdfc2a20 (strmap: enable faster clearing and reusing of strmaps) 23a276a9c4 (strmap: take advantage of FLEXPTR_ALLOC_STR when relevant) a208ec1f0b (strmap: enable allocations to come from a mem_pool) Using memory pools f239fff4c1 (merge-ort: store filepairs and filespecs in our mem_pool, 2021–02–04) 6697ee01b5 (merge-ort: switch our strmaps over to using memory pools, 2021–02–04) fa0e936fbb (diffcore-rename: use a mem_pool for exact rename detection’s hashmap, 2021–02–04) Miscellaneous minor optimizations 092e5115d1 (merge-ort: reuse path strings in pool_alloc_filespec, 2021–02–04) 5a3743da32 (merge-ort: replace string_list_df_name_compare with faster alternative, 2021–06–08) The combined effect of micro-optimizations As noted above, several of these optimizations were in the initial timings. For several of them, clicking on the links will provide some details about performance improvements. However, for those closely following all six blog posts in this series, there are two sets of micro-optimizations that I’d like to call out. First, the replacement of string_list_df_name_compare was submitted in the middle of the other optimizations from the other blog posts and made the following difference: Before Series After Series mega-renames: 10.127 s ± 0.073 s 9.419 s ± 0.107 s The four optimizations before it (the use of memory pools and reusing path strings) were submitted at the end of all other optimizations and made the following difference: Before Series After Series mega-renames: 1.076 s ± 0.015 s 661.8 ms ± 5.9 ms Preview-only optimizations (not merge or rename detection related) Some optimizations will not yet be available in released versions of Git but foreshadow future work. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in The machinery for applying a sequence of patches (for either rebasing, cherry-picking, or reverting) is in sequencer.c. Since no merge backend could operate without updating the working tree as it went, sequencer was built with that as a hard assumption — in a way that permeates the code. Further, since all the sequencer logic originally existed as shell scripts that were migrated over time to C, it also had assumptions about re-reading and verifying the state with each patch and still has a design that forks several subprocesses. The rebasing machinery also has a multitude of checks which could be viewed as part feature, part attempt to workaround slowness in the former merge machinery. Even though these checks originally had performance as their goal, they can be particularly slow and painful in very large repositories and/or when using partial clones. Trying to change all this was a significant undertaking that was out of scope for my initial work. As a result, I created a simple fast-rebase tool with very limited applicability (and in particular would error out if it hit conflicts) but was designed to operate very quickly and show the possibilities for Git’s rebase and cherry-pick. In particular, fast-rebase would: avoid updating working-tree/index with every intermediate patch avoid reading/writing rebase metadata until conflict or other stopping points avoid checking index matches HEAD with every patch being rebased; do it at the start only avoid unnecessary process forking (a side-effect of the original shell-script design) avoid per-commit hooks that were only triggered due to a design accident of history avoid unnecessary history traversals (from various can-fast-forward and is-linear-history checks) and patch inspections of commits not being rebased (due to --no-reapply-cherry-picks being the historical default) These changes add up to about six seconds of execution time, which may not sound like a lot, but is when you compare it to the final optimization results we achieved on the “mega-renames” test case, as shown below. Overall Results Here I’d like to look at the overall improvements achieved across all optimizations, from where the old merge algorithm started (using Git version 2.30.0). I’ll include a few more test cases as well (note that “no-renames” was a misnomer; it should have been “few-renames”), which are explained in more detail here . For each of the three test cases, I’ll provide the original timings using the old merge algorithm (merge-recursive), how much merge-recursive improved (as a side effect of optimizing the new merge algorithm, merge-ort), what kind of timings we would have gotten with a theoretical implementation that replaced the rename detection code with an infinitely parallelized version (i.e., an implementation where rename detection was instantaneous), and what timings I achieved with the new merge algorithm. In each case, you can see that I did far better than the infinitely parallelized rename detection version because I optimized things other than rename detection. I also include the relative speedup factors achieved for each of the three cases: Timings Infinite merge- merge- Parallelism recursive recursive of rename merge-ort v2.30.0 current detection current ---------- --------- ----------- --------- no-renames: 18.912 s 18.030 s 11.699 s 198.3 ms mega-renames: 5964.031 s 361.281 s 203.886 s 661.8 ms just-one-mega: 149.583 s 11.009 s 7.553 s 264.6 ms Speedup factors Infinite merge- merge- Parallelism recursive recursive of rename v2.30.0 current detection merge-ort ---------- --------- ----------- --------- no-renames: 1 1.05 1.6 95 mega-renames: 1 16.5 29 9012 just-one-mega: 1 13.6 20 565 However, note that without the “preview only” optimizations, the mega-renames test case would have been ~10x slower, still faster than the infinitely parallelized rename detection case, but not quite as quick as shown above. So there’s still work to do, but outside of the rename detection logic and merge machinery. Many of the optimizations in this post already appear in released versions of Git, accessible via passing the --strategy ort option to merge/rebase/cherry-pick or by setting git config --global pull.twohead ort (lame configuration option name due to backward compatibility). Other than the “Preview only” ones, the remaining optimizations will appear in Git 2.34 in late 2021. Special Thanks — Reviewers Based on my experience, the Git project has more thorough code reviews than other projects. I think it’s a wonderful thing, but it does mean that landing code changes in Git upstream require an awful lot of work by people who are not the original code authors. (For context, after I got the new merge backend fully working and optimized, it took me a whole year to get it all submitted upstream…despite having sent numerous preparatory patches and cleanups upstream before that time.) These reviewers often manage to make the code much better than how it started. That is certainly true here; the code is cleaner, more portable, more future-proof, faster (the reviewers did manage to find and suggest a couple additional minor optimizations , and ask the right questions to help me catch where an optimization wasn’t quite fully active but should have been), and just all around better. And so, I’d like to thank the many folks who put time into reviewing the hundreds of patches involved in all the work from these six blog posts. I’m certain I’ll miss a few folks (sorry!), because there were so many spread over the years behind these efforts. In alphabetical order, except for one I want to call out at the end, the folks who helped review patches (none of whom share an employer with me) include: Eric Sunshine Jeff King Johannes Schindelin Jonathan Tan Junio Hamano René Scharfe Taylor Blau Ævar Arnfjörð Bjarmason And I want to give a huge thanks to Derrick Stolee . Derrick single-handedly reviewed nearly all merge-ort and diffcore-rename patches. Most folks will pick and choose some patches here and there to review (I certainly do that), but Derrick reviewed nearly everything once I was past the cleanup of merge-recursive and test-suite preparation stages. He jumped in when I started submitting patches for the new merge algorithm and kept with it the whole way through. Author Elijah Newren

title: Gotham Online Migration Framework
description: Palantir Gotham informs mission-critical work in some of the most remote environments. So how do we manage upgrades and data migrations with no downtime?
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech Software Development SaaS Edge Computing Palantirengineering Gotham Online Migration Framework Palantir 12 min read · Sep 23, 2021 -- 1 Listen Share There’s one concern that unites software engineers across the globe, regardless of project, industry or tenure: how do I best deploy and manage updates to my software? From new features to bug fixes to performance improvements, we want to make sure our products are running optimally. This question is particularly pertinent at Palantir , where we deploy software to some of the most remote locales on Earth to solve some of the world’s hardest problems. Apollo , the platform that powers both Foundry and Gotham , manages the complexity of all our environments and safely and consistently delivers product updates to our customers live without disrupting users on the system; our Online Migration Framework complements Apollo by ensuring that services can safely manage schema and data migrations through Apollo’s upgrades. In the days before I wrote this post, I wrote, tested, and shipped a data migration using the Online Migration Framework. It only took me about two hours. Without the framework, it likely would have taken days and required much more careful thought and planning — and possibly caused bugs in the field, as even a fairly simple data migration is still a complex problem to solve without the framework. In this blog post, I’ll talk about: Why Palantir uses online upgrades over offline ones The challenges of and common strategies for online upgrades How Palantir uses the Online Migration Framework to streamline online upgrades across data scale, deployment and execution scale, and development scale. Press enter or click to view image in full size Why Palantir Uses Online vs. Offline Upgrades There are two common strategies in the industry for changing the structure of stored data: offline upgrades and online upgrades. You’re probably familiar with offline upgrades. The device you’re reading this on likely upgrades this way. When a new version of the device’s software becomes available, the device prompts you to save your work and shut down to perform upgrades. Once the upgrade is complete, you start your device back up again and are using the latest and greatest software version. From a software development standpoint, offline upgrades are fantastic. They are relatively simple to implement and easy to understand. For this reason, offline upgrades are often the preferred strategy if you have the luxury of doing so. Palantir does not have this luxury. Our software supports 24/7 mission-critical work around the world, often in life-and-death situations. The system must be available at all times, so we need to perform online data migrations. The Challenge of Online Upgrades Online data migrations are much trickier than offline ones. If your software needs to upgrade live, you need the new version to be up and available before taking down the old version (Apollo supports rolling blue-green upgrades). The old code wants to use data in the old format, and the new code wants to use data in the new format. For a less technical example, imagine trying to raise the height of a table. An offline migration would be reasonably straightforward. Take the legs off, replace them with longer legs, and stand the table back up again. But what if the table needs to be used while you’re doing this? You’d need to carefully replace the legs one at a time. But how exactly will you fit the new longer legs under the table while the shorter legs are still supporting it? Of course, Palantir is not the only company whose software has high uptime demands; many companies need to perform online data migrations on large-scale data. The standard strategy for doing so is nicely described in the Stripe tech blog . We used a very similar strategy when upgrading Gotham with AtlasDB to serve as the transactional layer for data. In summary, the strategy is as follows: Create the destination for the data to be migrated (e.g., a new column or table in a relational database). Migrate the data from the old format to the new format. While the migration is in progress, code should read from the old format and write to both the old and new formats. Once the migration is done, code can read and write the new format only, and the old format can be deleted (e.g., drop no-longer-used columns or tables). This approach is pretty straightforward at a high level. However, like the analogous solution in the table metaphor (i.e., building extendable table legs that you extend only after replacing each leg one by one), getting the details right poses a much more significant technical challenge than offline migrations. Engineers can spend weeks or even months planning, developing, and carefully executing such a migration for their production stack. If you have one or just a few production stacks where this migration needs to run and your engineers have access to them, this is usually a manageable project. Once again, Palantir does not have this luxury. Our software is deployed to hundreds of environments, including on and under the water, in the air, and in remote outposts far from home. Even if we could somehow manage to upgrade these stacks using the standard strategy, the approach would not scale. We need to automate the execution of our migrations. Furthermore, Palantir moves quickly. We’re constantly improving our software and developing new capabilities, necessitating frequent data migrations. Some of our fastest-moving projects require significant data migrations almost monthly. Spending a month every month developing a data migration is devastating to forward progress. Benefits of the Online Migration Framework The Online Migration Framework is our solution to the challenge of live data migration. This framework is effective because it scales across data, deployment and execution, and development. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in To help make this framework concrete, I’ll be using a running example of a classic migration: changing the storage of a name from a single last, first column to two separate last_name and first_name columns, as shown below. I’ll be writing in pseudo-code to give an idea of what the development of this migration might look like. Press enter or click to view image in full size Writing Migrations The first thing the Online Migration Framework provides is a way for developers to write migrations. This is broken into three parts that should look familiar: Pre-migration schema additions : Developers create tables, columns, and any other schema elements necessary to support the new format of the data. CREATE TABLE Users_2 ( user_id VARCHAR2(128), last_name VARCHAR2(128), first_name VARCHAR2(128), CONSTRAINT pk_users_2 PRIMARY KEY (user_id) ); Migration batches : Developers write code to migrate data from the old format to the new format in batches. The framework also provides a data store for migrations to store their progress during this phase, since it’s possible at any point for the process running the migration to fail. We don’t want to have to start a long migration from scratch. ... List<Users2Record> userBatch = sql.select(Users.USER_ID, Users.FULL_NAME) .from(Users) .where(Users.USER_ID.greaterThan(getLastProcessedId())) .orderBy(Users.USER_ID.asc()) .limit(batchSize) .fetch(row -> createUsers2Record(row.get(Users.USER_ID), row.get(Users.FULL_NAME))); if (userBatch.size() > 0) { List<Query> inserts = userBatch.stream() .map(record -> sql.insertInto(Users_2).set(record).onDuplicateKeyIgnore()) .collect(Collectors.toList(); sql.batch(inserts).execute(); updateLastProcessedId(userBatch.get(userBatch.size() - 1).getUserId()); } else { markMigrationCompleted(); } ... Post-migration schema drops : Developers drop any no-longer-needed schema elements and the data they contain. DROP TABLE Users; Because, as mentioned, the process running these migrations could fail at any time, each of these sections must be idempotent, meaning that running them multiple times is safe and has the same effect as running them once (for the DDL statements, it suffices to catch any exception returned by the data store and check if it is the expected type; e.g., the table already exists). Supporting Rollback These migrations also need to support rollback. The fastest way to mitigate an issue is to return to the last known working state. This often means downgrading the software to an earlier version. But what if a migration was in progress? The old version of the code may not know how to handle this state, so we need to roll the migration back. Because the only reason to roll back a migration is to mitigate an issue, we require rollback to be fast. In fact, the only place to implement it is as part of step one above, hinting that rollback code should be as fast as dropping the new columns or tables you created. Updating Code to handle In-Progress Migrations Developers also need to update the code that accesses this data in order for the code to work correctly before, during, and after the migration. To support this, we’ve built a Migration Proxy. Developers can put their data access code behind an interface and annotate the interface’s methods with @Read or @Write. They can then implement this interface once for the new state of the data and once for the old state. Along with the Write annotation, developers can also specify what the behavior should be while the migration is in progress: Writing to both implementations (default). Writing to only the new implementation — -for example, when adding a column to a table where the new write is a superset of the old write. Writing only to the old implementation — for example, when the migration just drops a column where the old write is a superset of the new write. (Rare) Writing to a “middle” implementation that provides custom handling when a migration is in-progress. In the example: public interface UserStore { @Read User loadUser(String userId); @Write void storeUser(User); } This sounds like it could be a lot of work, but we’ve developed a process where developers keep a primary implementation up to date with the latest data format and subclass this implementation, overriding only the methods that need to be overridden for each migration going backward. As this suggests, this process can be repeated for multiple migrations affecting the same data, and the Migration Proxy will accept a list of implementations and the migrations that go between them. From this list, it will choose the correct implementation(s) to use based on the state of each migration. In our example, a Migration Proxy for the UserStore would be created like so: UserStore proxiedUserStore = SimpleMigrationAwareProxy.wrap( UserStore.class, new LegacyUserStoreImpl(dbSession), new UserStoreImpl(dbSession), USER_STORE_MIGRATION_TASK_ID, dbSession); Coordinating Migrations through the Migration Runner Each of these migrations, at commit time, get a monotonically increasing ID (e.g USER_STORE_MIGRATION_TASK_ID ) and will be run by our Migration Runner in order. By having migrations run in the same order in every environment, we’re able to keep the number of possible states of the data store to a manageable level and also look at the migration state of any service and immediately know what the state of the data store is even without inspecting it. As it runs migrations, the Runner coordinates with Migration Proxies by grabbing a write lock on a migration’s status whenever it changes it. Meanwhile, the Proxy grabs a read lock on the status for the duration of the operation it’s performing. Critically, this allows large-scale migrations to run safely with minimal impact on the rest of the code because multiple threads can hold the read lock while doing data access operations. The Runner only needs to hold the write lock for the brief moments where it is changing the migration status in the data store, not during any actual migration execution. When the Runner starts up, it executes a consensus protocol with the other nodes of the service to determine what migrations are known by all nodes. This is important because as we continually deliver new software in ever-shorter development cycles, we will more and more frequently be in situations where a service may have multiple nodes with heterogeneous versions of software deployed. The Runner needs to determine what migrations are supported by all nodes so it can continue to make progress through the series of migrations even when a service is receiving frequent rolling upgrades via Apollo. Employing Soak Time and Migrating in Stages In order to expedite rollbacks, we employ a configurable “soak time” (default of four days) after a migration becomes available before we start running it. The Migration Runner tracks each individual migration when it first becomes available. After soaking, the Runner begins its work. Running a migration proceeds in several stages, more numerous than the three parts mentioned above, to handle the Runner failing at any point in execution. Uninitialized : The migration has not yet begun, and all Proxies read and write the old data format. Rolling Back : The migration is in the process of rolling back to the Uninitialized state but may have yet to finish this. Initializing : The Runner is executing pre-migration schema additions but may not have completed them. Rollback will need to run if we need to downgrade. Proxies still read and write the old format. Running : Pre-migration schema additions are complete, and the migration has (maybe) started running its batches. Proxies read the old format and write both formats (or just old or new based on developer-specified behavior). Awaiting Additional Action (optional) : The migration has completed, but there is action outside of the framework’s control that needs to be taken. For example, new data may need to be indexed into Elasticsearch or some other secondary index before the migration can be considered fully complete. Proxies now begin reading the new format but still write to both to support rollback. Awaiting Finalization : The migration is complete. Proxies read the new format but still write to both to support rollback. Finishing : The Runner is executing post-migration schema drops but may not have finished. The migration can no longer be rolled back. Proxies read and write only the new format. Finished : The migration is complete and all old schemas and data have been dropped. Developers must write idempotent migration behavior, so if the Runner fails at any point, we can restart that stage and keep moving along without issue. We also employ an additional soak time between Awaiting Finalization and Finishing. This allows us to identify issues that only become apparent once the new data format is available and address those issues before we are no longer able to roll back to the original state. Managing the Migration Lifecycle After a migration has been completed, we generally want to remove the migration code. But when exactly is a migration complete? It has to run on potentially hundreds of separate environments. Some migrations take less than a second, while others can take weeks. To have a clear point at which migration code can be removed, we designate specific releases as “checkpoints.” To install upgrades beyond a checkpoint, a service must complete all the migrations up to that checkpoint. Apollo notes (1) which schema versions each release supports and (2) the current schema version of the live service based on what migrations have run. For the releases beyond a checkpoint, we change the minimum schema version to the version of the last migration in the checkpoint so that Apollo can enforce this requirement. Apollo can also require that migrations are rolled back before downgrades, since the old binary will report a maximum schema version that is only as high as the migrations it knows about. This post-checkpoint cleanup is often relatively trivial because of the above-mentioned multiple implementations supporting both old and new data formats. Because we already have the complete implementation of the data access code for all completed migrations, we can delete the old subclasses that supported old versions and in-line the latest implementation rather than having it wrapped in a Proxy. This allows us to scale our development efforts while keeping our codebase neat and tidy. Developers need only minutes to clean up after a checkpoint. Testing Migrations Across the Platform We’ve also built a comprehensive testing framework for our online migrations. Migration developers can leverage a simple JUnit test extension that provides a custom Migration Runner for the migration they are testing and allows easy roll-forward and roll-back testing. We use this same extension framework for more comprehensive testing across the entire product. When a new migration is committed, our build system will generate tests for every combination of data store we support. It will also generate tests for the four migration states (Uninitialized, Running, Awaiting Finalization, and Finished) and run our tests across all those combinations to ensure our products work throughout all phases of the migration. Finally, the Online Migration Framework is service- and datastore-agnostic and has been implemented across a number of our services and several different data stores. We’ve developed a suite of abstract test classes that can be implemented with a service’s implementation of the framework to quickly test that the implementation is working properly. This allows us to quickly scale our ability to safely and sustainably migrate data across our product ecosystem. The Online Migration Framework at Scale The Online Migration Framework has greatly improved our ability to continually deliver improvements and new features to our customers. Over the last couple years, dozens of developers have written several hundred migrations. Overall, we’ve run approximately 15,000 online data migrations across the fleet without disruption to users. The Online Migration Framework has even been extended to uses beyond data migration and has had several common migration types built into it so developers may only need to write ten lines of code to complete a migration, allowing them to focus on delivering the best technology to our customers. Author Michael Harris, Software Engineer, Gotham Delivery Interested in working on technical challenges like scalable online data migration? We’re hiring. Reach out to us at palantir.com/careers .

title: Products with Purpose: Foundry — Archetypes
description: Palantir Software Engineer Julien shares how Foundry Archetypes is driving successful outcomes for customers when timelines matter most.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech Software Engineer Palantir Palantir Culture Teams Products with Purpose: Foundry — Archetypes Palantir 6 min read · Oct 5, 2021 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Julien is a Software Engineer at Palantir , currently working on one of the products within our Foundry platform. We sat down with Julien to learn more about the product and his own journey at Palantir. Hi Julien, thanks for joining us today. Could you tell us a little bit about who you are and what you do at Palantir? Sure! I’m Julien, my pronouns are he/him, and I am currently a Software Engineer working on Foundry in our London office. I joined Palantir in 2017, and during these last four years, I have worked as a developer on different products across the Foundry platform, in product management, and as a Forward Deployed Software Engineer embedded with customers. (Editor’s note: You can learn more about the difference between our Software Engineer, or Dev, roles and our Forward Deployed Software Engineer roles in this prior blog post .) What brought you to Palantir? Before Palantir, I had varied experiences both as a software engineer and as a strategy consultant. As a software engineer, I enjoyed the technical and productized approach to solving problems, and as a consultant, I valued seeing the impact I could have on broad real-world problems. Palantir was the best of what had excited me in both, providing me the ability to work on problems that have a real-world impact, while creating scalable technical solutions that could help our products profoundly improve operations for multiple customers. You work on one of our flagship platforms, Foundry. Can you tell us a little bit about the platform? At a high level, Foundry is a platform that allows our customers to manage their own data, create models that represent their organization, and operationalize data to actually help drive decisions. The goal is not to have a shiny analysis that remains on a shelf in a deck; Foundry actually changes how our customers operate and helps them make decisions in the real world, where the situation may be constantly evolving. Foundry can be adapted for a wide variety of customers and use cases, because the widgets, modules, UI, and configurations can all be customized. Foundry provides the infrastructure to easily build the logic, models, and apps that power operational outcomes at different levels of an organization. This infrastructure includes: Data syncing : How do you read data from the customer’s system? Data transformation : How do you clean up and transform that data to a useful format? Ontology : How do you make that data understandable, so you’re not just talking in terms of tables and rows, but in terms of real-world objects that those tables and rows actually represent? Modeling : How do you manage the models that represent the cause and effect relationship between those entities? Enablement : How do you build apps so that people can actually interact with those objects and drive real-world outcomes? This is a high-level overview of what Foundry does right now, but Foundry is constantly evolving to provide more value for our customers. Because of our operating model, our Forward Deployed Software Engineers are able to give the Product Development team direction about insights and trends they’re seeing first-hand in the field. This direction drives a lot of our product work within Foundry, and it’s actually how the product I’m currently working on came into existence. Can you tell us more about the product you’re currently working on? In early 2020, we noticed that many of our customers, government and commercial alike, were experiencing similar problems — namely, how to track the impact of COVID-19 on their facilities, people, or supply chains. Our customers needed to be able to understand and measure the impact the pandemic was having on their business in real time. So we created a product called Archetypes, which provides workflow templates that can be deployed from a configuration wizard in minutes and drive real-world outcomes for these organizations. Press enter or click to view image in full size Foundry Archetypes Homepage As one example, manufacturers can use Archetypes to view, understand, and resolve disruptions to their supply chains. Whether you’re manufacturing chemicals or cars, managing supply-chain disruptions share certain commonalities. At the same time, every industry and every organization has its own unique constraints and context, whether that’s the nature of a disruption or the means to resolve it. So the goal of Archetypes is not to write a cookie-cutter solution, but to harness high-level patterns to provide tools that allow our customers to get to value faster. Press enter or click to view image in full size Foundry Archetypes for Supply Chain Use What are some of the challenges you’ve faced engineering products like Archetypes? Some of the technical complexity relates to what I just mentioned: figuring out how organizations can harness both the benefits of an out-of-the-box offering and the customization they need to represent their own unique organization. Defining the APIs that allow the right level of flexibility and reusability is a hard technical problem. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in We also have to figure out how to make Archetypes play nicely with other Foundry products, from an app builder to an analysis tool to a map. That means we need to add a layer of templatization to our frontend products, so they can work across chemicals or cars (to return to our prior supply-chain example). And all backend services need to integrate with a framework to allow out-of-the-box offerings, without reinventing a new solution for each service. And even once you’ve figured out how to build an Archetype that addresses all these challenges, you need to improve that offering over time. We need to release upgrades, recall releases, upgrade customers, aggregate usage statistics in a privacy-protective way, and more. What is it like to work on the Foundry team? In order for us to build and deploy quickly and efficiently, the Foundry product organization is structured as a flat organization composed of small dev teams, typically around three to six people. This means each team member gets to play a significant role in defining the team’s strategic direction and technical architecture. To streamline internal collaboration, these teams are then organized into groups that work on closely related components of the Foundry platform. Another thing I appreciate about working on the Foundry team is that we get to work closely with our users, whether that’s our internal users like Forward Deployed Software Engineers or external users like customers. This means our engineers are able to identify, advocate for, and implement the necessary innovations to tackle the evolving problems our customers face. Personally, I’ve found this element of our work very energizing — it ensures our work is always anchored in real-world value and impact. You’ve done a variety of things during your time at Palantir. How have you thought about your growth? Growth at Palantir is often non-linear, and we tend to think about growth not in terms of climbing rungs on a ladder but in terms of impact. Maximizing your impact could involve taking on additional responsibility within your team, transferring to a new project, or even taking on an entirely different role. Right now, for example, I am a Dev Lead for my team, but also hold some responsibilities that would traditionally fall on a Product Manager. That means I spend my time writing code, but also organizing the team, mentoring other engineers, holding the engineering bar, and exploring what we should build next from the needs of our business — and how we can build it. What would you tell someone considering whether to join Palantir today? Ultimately, the reason I’m still at Palantir is because our culture optimizes for the best outcome while being cognizant of what expertise each engineer brings to the table. Every employee is given immense responsibility and opportunity to make an impact on our products and our customers. Early in my career at Palantir, it felt scary to be making decisions that would have such an impact so recently after I had joined, or to voice opinions that might significantly influence product direction. But at the end of the day, it’s incredibly rewarding to have direct access to such critical problems, and you have access to a lot of support structures to help you grow and make the best decisions, like mentors (in or outside of your team), engineering reviews with senior engineers from across the org, and more. And it’s exciting to see that Foundry and Archetypes are driving successful outcomes for our customers, whether that’s empowering them to make better decisions in minutes during the height of the pandemic last year, or getting anti-money laundering workflows up and running in days. To learn more about open roles at Palantir and apply, visit our website .

title: Driving Social Change: SOMPO and Palantir
description: In 2019, SOMPO and Palantir established Palantir Technologies Japan K.K. to drive social change through digital transformation
author: Palantir
body: Driving Social Change: SOMPO and Palantir SOMPOと共に社会の変化とデジタルトランスフォーメーションを牽引 (Scroll down for Japanese translation below) In 2019, SOMPO and Palantir partnered to jointly establish Palantir Technologies Japan K.K., a technology company that provides Palantir’s data platforms and services in Japan. As part of this partnership, SOMPO has created the Real Data Platform (RDP), powered by Palantir Foundry. The platform seeks to drive impact across four key pillars: Wellbeing: Improving elderly care in Japan and abroad by customizing plans & streamlining the supply chain Resilience: Making Japan and other countries more resilient by integrating insurance with real-world operations Integrated Internet of Things (IoT): Incorporating and safely connecting data across devices, workflows, and industries National Healthcare Infrastructure: Creating a connected healthcare infrastructure that enables secure collaboration between research, government, and private industry in Japan and abroad The RDP addresses these four pillars by integrating the high volume of valuable data that SOMPO has already accumulated — from nursing care, to accidents and catastrophes, to risks and claims. The platform then makes this integrated data available to users of all technical ability, subject to the appropriate access controls. The ultimate vision of the RDP is to increase the security, health, and wellbeing of SOMPO’s customers — including those working and living in elder care. There are approximately 60,000 elder care facilities across Japan, which is one of the world’s oldest countries in terms of population longevity. In recent years, SOMPO has built out a nursing care service called SOMPO Care. Starting in 2020, SOMPO Care has been partnering with Palantir to use the RDP to drive more personalized nursing care services. SOMPO’s RDP is designed to serve as the operating system for elder care across the nation, and even globally. Social cost for elder care in Japan is estimated to be over $100 billion, and this number is projected to double by 2040. However, more than a third of that, approximately $35 billion, is thought to be lost to inefficiencies in the operations. The RDP is addressing these inefficiencies by improving data sharing and communication between the government and the private sector industries providing elder care services. As a result, the RDP reduces taxpayer waste, enables greater efficiency for SOMPO, and ultimately improves elderly care. “We had invested in various operational systems and sensor technologies, but the data was siloed in many different places and not fully utilized. That’s when we came across Foundry,” says Satoshi Kasai, CEO of Nursing Care and Seniors Business for SOMPO. “Foundry is able to connect these various systems together and bring structure to and analyze the data, which created tremendous value for us. With this technology, we connect not only SOMPO Care’s data but other care provider’s data to perform even more advanced data analysis and generate significant value.” In a new video, we show how SOMPO Care has used the RDP to securely integrate hundreds of different types of data previously stored in disparate systems, including 700 datasets covering nursing records, relevant customer data (such as sleep, diet, medication), care worker data, and facilities information. Beyond simply analyzing and visualizing this data, the employees within the care homes are able to use the data in actual nursing operations to improve both employee experience and, most importantly, the quality of care. If you’re interested using Palantir software at your organization, click here to request a demo. Key workflows include: Utilizing a single source of truth: Employees in SOMPO elderly care homes usually work in shifts. By having all the data related to tenant care in one place, on a mobile device, it is easy to log changes in real-time. Foundry allows all employees to make care decisions based on not only their experience, but also the most up-to-date information. They are able to surface care plans at a glance, rather than the 30 minutes it used to take. Harnessing the power of sensor data: In recent years, SOMPO has led the way in leveraging technology to improve quality of care. In elder care facilities, SOMPO has invested in sensors placed under beds to measure critical vital signs like sleep, breathing, and pulse rate. As explained in the video, this functionality allowed caregivers to identify an irregularity — some tenants were sleeping for much longer than usual. Using Foundry, the care facility manager was able to detect a correlation with a change in prescription and was able to adjust the medication accordingly. Moving from reactive to proactive with tailored alerts: Facility managers now receive alerts providing an overview of all tenants. This allows them to give personalized, data-driven instructions to caregivers. Driving social change in Japan and beyond: Through the use of Palantir Foundry, SOMPO is making cutting-edge technology available to hundreds of smaller care facilities across Japan and plans to expand this work into an ecosystem that will benefit care providers around the world. SOMPO’s RDP was designed with privacy and civil liberties in mind. Built-in data protection functionalities facilitate compliance with strict rules and regulations. These protection functionalities include granular access controls, along with additional tooling to facilitate transparency and accountability, that help ensure that sensitive patient and caregiving data will only be accessed for approved purposes. SOMPOと共に社会の変化とデジタルトランスフォーメーションを牽引 2019年にSOMPOとPalantirは、Palantirのデータプラットフォームとサービスを日本で提供するテクノロジー企業であるPalantir Technologies Japan株式会社を共同出資により設立しました。SOMPOはこのパートナーシップの一環として、Palantir Foundryを活用したリアルデータプラットフォーム（RDP）の構築を目指したプロジェクトを開始しました。このプラットフォームは、以下の4つの主要な柱を推進していきます。 ウェルビーイング：ケアプランのカスタマイズとサプライチェーンの合理化により、日本国内外における高齢者向け介護現場を改善していく レジリエンス（回復力）：保険事業と実社会のオペレーションを統合することで、日本およびその他の国のレジリエンスを高めていく 統合されたモノのインターネット（IoT）：機器、ワークフロー、産業全体のデータを取り込み、より安全に繋げていく ヘルスケアインフラストラクチャ：日本国内外において研究機関、政府、民間産業などとの連携によって、より良いヘルスケアインフラストラクチャを実現していく RDPは、介護事業、事故や大災害、またリスク情報から保険金請求の情報まで、SOMPOがこれまでに蓄積してきた大量の価値あるデータを統合することで、これら4つの柱に対応していきます。そして、幅広いユーザーが適切なアクセス制御に基づき、プラットフォーム上でこれらの統合データを利用できるようにしていきます。 高齢者介護の現場で働く人や在宅介護をしている人など、SOMPOのお客様の安心・安全・健康を向上させることが、RDPの最終的なビジョンです。平均寿命が世界一の長寿国に挙げられる日本には、約60,000の高齢者介護施設があります。SOMPOは近年、介護サービスを提供するSOMPOケアを設立しました。2020年以降、SOMPOケアはPalantirと提携し、一人ひとりのお客様に合わせた介護サービスの提供を推進するためにRDPを利用してきました。 SOMPOのRDPは、日本国内だけでなく世界各地において高齢者介護のオペレーティングシステムとして機能するように設計されています。日本における高齢者介護の社会保障費は1,000億ドルを超えると推定されており、2040年にはこれが2倍になると予測されています。しかし、この3分の1以上にあたる約350億ドルは、オペレーションの非効率性により失われていると考えられています。RDPは、パートナーとなる他の高齢者向け介護サービス事業者がデータに基づいたより良い意思決定を行い、ケアに関する知見が共有され、政府と介護事業者との間のコミュニケーションを改善することで、この非効率性に対処していきます。その結果、RDPは社会保障費の支出を削減し、SOMPOの業務効率性を大幅に改善するだけでなく、最終的には介護産業全体を改善していきます。 「SOMPOケアでは様々な業務システムや センシング技術を 導入してまいりましたが、データの活用という観点ではシステムごとにデータが分散しているという 課題に直面しました。その時にFoundryと出会っています。」とSOMPOホールディングスの笠井聡 介護シニア事業オーナー執行役は述べています。「様々な業務システムやデバイスを繋いでデータを構造化し、解析していくFoundryの技術は大きな価値を生みます。この技術があればSOMPOケアだけではなく、複数の介護事業者のデータを繋いで、さらに高度なデータ解析をし大きな付加価値を生み出して いくことが期待できます。」 新しい動画では、介護記録、関連する顧客データ（睡眠、食事、服薬など）、介護士のデータ、施設情報を網羅する700のデータセットなど、これまでまったく別のシステムに保存されていた異なる種類の数百ものデータを、SOMPOケアがRDPを活用して安全に統合した方法をご紹介します。このデータは単に分析したり視覚化したりできるだけでなく、介護施設の従業員が現場の介護オペレーションで利用するために、従業員の業務の変化と、最も重要な要素である介護サービスの質の向上につながっていきます。 あなたの組織でPalantirのソフトウェアを使用する事にご興味があれば、こちらをクリックしてデモをリクエストしてください。 主な内容は以下のとおりです。 信頼できる唯一の情報源を活用：SOMPOの高齢者介護施設の従業員は、通常、シフト制で勤務しています。入居者の介護に関連するすべてのデータをモバイル機器上の1箇所にまとめることで、簡単かつリアルタイムに変化を記録できます。Foundryによって、すべての従業員が自分自身の経験だけではなく、最新の情報に基づいて、介護に関する決定を下せるようになります。また、これまではケアプランの策定に必要な情報の確認に30分かかっていましたが、これを一目で分かるように表示できます。 センサーデータの力を活用：近年SOMPOは、テクノロジーを活用した介護の質の改善を主導しています。SOMPOは高齢者介護施設において、睡眠、呼吸、脈拍などの重要なバイタルサインを測定するために、ベッドにセンサーを配備してきました。動画で説明しているとおり、介護施設長はこの機能により、通常よりはるかに睡眠時間が長い入居者がいるなどの異常を特定できるようになりました。Foundryを利用することで、介護施設長は処方薬の変更との相関関係を認識し、それに従って服薬の調整を医師に相談できるようになりました。 状況に応じたアラートで受動的な介護から積極的な介護へ移行：介護施設長は、すべての入居者の状態に関するアラートを受信できるようになりました。これにより介護施設長は、一人ひとりに合わせたデータに基づく指示を介護士に出すことができます。 日本国内外において社会の変化を牽引：SOMPOはPalantir Foundryを利用して、日本全国の何百もの小規模な介護施設が最先端のテクノロジーを利用できる環境の実現を目指しています。また、将来的にSOMPOはこの事業を世界中の介護事業者の利益となるエコシステムに拡大していく予定です。 SOMPOのRDPはプライバシーと人々の自由を考慮して設計されています。組み込まれているデータ保護機能は厳格な規則と規制の遵守を促進するものです。これらの保護機能には詳細なアクセス制御のほか、透明性と説明責任を促進するその他のツールも含まれており、患者の機密データへのアクセスが承認済みの目的でのみ行われることを保証します。

title: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part I
description: Until recently, most data integration work remained ‘human-defined.’ We decided to change that.
author: Palantir
body: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part I Editor’s note: This is the first in a four-part series of posts exploring the origins, capabilities and impact of Palantir’s Software-Defined Data Integration. Stay tuned for parts two, three and four. At Palantir, we’ve spent the better part of two decades tackling some of the world’s most formidable data integration challenges alongside our customers — from digitizing the electrical grid to fighting child exploitation and pursuing information dominance. Time and again, we’ve experienced firsthand the frustration of business decision-makers and IT departments alike at trying to find, surface, and operationalize the right data to solve a pressing business problem. Questions that seem only logical and straightforward (i.e. “how much less does it cost to manufacture Product X vs. Product Y?” or “how long does it usually take for Product Z to arrive from our suppliers?”) prompt weeks, months or even years of technical road-blocks and data wrangling. Of course, we’ve evolved our software products to alleviate much of this pain and time drain. However, until recently, the bulk of data integration work remained ‘human-defined’. Whether written by a forward-deployed Palantir engineer or a resident data scientist at one of our partners, data was integrated based on code written by a human. This manual data integration was not only error-prone and time-consuming, but it presented a significant maintenance overhead, as the structure of the data inevitably changes over time. Instead of continuing to spend precious time and resources doing the same work over and over, we decided to take a new approach. “Necessity is the mother of invention.” We had already started working on a way of automating away the manual work of building data pipelines in 2019. Then, in early 2020, the pandemic hit and the world changed in an instant. Organizations needed to know, immediately, how COVID-19 impacted their workforce, their supply chain, their customers, and their finances. They didn’t have the luxury of weeks- or months-long data integration projects to find the answers. These questions were existential. We set to work, rapidly deploying our fledgling integration solution at customers, existing and new, observing what worked and what didn’t, and refining our approach in real time. We soon realized that our solution to automatically extract, transform and harmonize data from across existing systems could massively reduce the time and effort spent comprehending complex data landscapes. In some cases, we could do in hours what had previously taken months — a valuable upgrade even outside of the crisis we were helping to combat. In the midst of it all, the term “software-defined data integration” took hold for our solution and a set of guiding philosophies crystallized. Guiding Philosophies Integrate data from first principles: the richest and most flexible downstream applications of data integration rely on starting from the most granular source data. Using preprocessed data may feel like a shortcut, but doing so immediately narrows the scope of problems that could be addressed in the future. Automate as much as possible: metadata is as valuable as the data itself — it can power dynamic data pipeline generation, slashing the overheads of manual data integration now and in the future. A data pipeline, albeit one written by hand, is a form of automation; in dynamically generating that pipeline, you are automating your automation. Build a highly extensible knowledge framework: not everything can be automated, but learnings encoded as product will compound over time. Make it easy both to contribute knowledge and to review those contributions so as to maintain a high bar for quality. Close the operational loop: a first-class method for writing back to source systems ensures data-driven decisions result in concrete actions. So often, data only flows in one direction, but in a world that has moved from monolithic platforms to multi-system interoperability, bi-directionality is key. Over the course of this blog series, we will expand on what we have learnt on this journey and how it has empowered our customers to do more with their data. Looking to learn more about SDDI? Download the new whitepaper.

title: Break the Machine: Hack Week 2021
description: Since our earliest days, Hack Week has been a hallowed tradition. But, this year posed novel challenges. See how we met the moment.
author: Palantir
body: Break the Machine: Hack Week 2021 Since our earliest days as a company, Hack Week has been a hallowed tradition at Palantir. It’s a time to set aside day-to-day work to explore those novel and even heretical ideas that have the potential to totally change Palantir — and the world. As our COO Shyam Sankar said in our Q2 Earnings Call, many of our best and most profound ideas originated from past Hack Weeks (including the precursor to Apollo, Palantir’s continuous delivery software for SaaS platforms). But this year’s event posed novel challenges. In this post, we discuss how Palantir adapted Hack Week to meet the moment in 2021. The big ideas aren’t always on the roadmap. The big ideas come out of inspiration and perspiration. And I am keenly aware as management that the very best ideas — the most profound ideas — they start as heresy. — Shyam Sankar, Palantir COO New Year, New Challenges Over the past year, our teams have been working around the clock to help governments and organizations respond to the COVID-19 crisis. We’re so proud of the work we did (and are still doing!) to help our partners manage the pandemic. But the pace of the last 18 months also meant it was hard to create space for personal investigation and exploration. We also had over 500 new Palantirians start during that time, so we needed to find ways of engaging those people who might never have even met another Palantirian in person. Our DC office’s resident Chewbacca statue prepares for Hack Week 2021. With all this in mind, we knew we had to rethink the way we’d structured Hack Weeks in the past. In prior years, we’ve focused a lot on the competitive aspect, but that tended to incentivize flashier projects and disincentivize the kind of high-risk, high-reward projects that have made past Hack Weeks so valuable. This year, we wanted to instead incentivize widespread participation and get back to the real, almost heretical spirit of Hack Week. This spirit was encapsulated in our theme, which was “Break the Machine.” Building the Machine One thing we did was invest in tools and structures to make the event successful. That included socializing potential project ideas on a leaderboard hosted on Palantir servers. Any Palantirian could add their own ideas to recruit fellow hackers, or see existing ideas and join those groups.
