In addition to getting people excited to hack, this had the added benefit of fostering teams that cut across job functions and parts of the business — which is something that’s generally been harder to facilitate in a world where not everyone is coming into offices. To foster team-building, we also provided funds so that Hack Week participants could gather, eat, drink, and build together. Ultimately, these efforts resulted in the highest participation of any Hack Week in Palantir history, with almost 900 Palantirians (out of 2700 employees) hacking and over 100 projects submitted. (Other projects, like self-directed learning or paper drafting, also took place behind the scenes and so weren’t captured in these submission totals.) Palantirians share their Hack Week ideas in our DC office. While we focused a lot on participation, it was also important that the competition aspect of Hack Week remained fair and unbiased. This year, a Palantir intern built a robust voting portal using our Foundry platform. The voting portal ensured that every project was viewed by the same number of voters across Palantir, so that projects built by the newest employee (or intern!) were given the same chance to impress as those from our most tenured employees. Projects Of the more than 100 projects submitted, 12 advanced to the finals. The final judges selected three winners: Hack Fast BAS: This project helped rebuild the broad area search (BAS) imagery pipeline within Palantir Gotham, specifically focused on high-scale image processing and realtime reprioritization of a GPU cluster. Foundry Containers: For implementations of Palantir Foundry in the life sciences, this project enhanced the ability to securely run open-source software like Jupyter Notebook, ImageJ, and more. Garble: Foundry Data in Gaia: This project allows users to apply the full suite of Gaia’s geo-analysis tools against Foundry data, giving users the full power of Gaia and Foundry at their fingertips. The Foundry Augmented Reality team worked across in-person and virtual lines to add an AR component to our digital twin technology. What Didn’t Work While Hack Week 2021 was definitely a success, there are also plenty of things we didn’t get quite right — and that, in the spirit of breaking the machine, we plan on improving in future years. Those include: Team-building: While our project portal made it easy for people to submit and view projects, it wasn’t as useful for actually building out teams. We need to figure out a more intuitive, easy-to-use way for people to form and join teams — especially people who are newer to the company and don’t have existing networks. On the other end of the spectrum, some people dabbled in multiple projects but ultimately didn’t commit to any of them. We need to figure out the last-mile problem of getting dabblers to commit to a single project — because otherwise they often wind up dropping out of the event entirely. Voting: In previous years, we’ve separated the votes by category, awarding the highest-voted projects per category. The problem with that approach is that sometimes second-place projects in more competitive categories wind up feeling snubbed. So this year, we decided to do away with category-based voting and go with a “direct democracy” approach, advancing the highest-voted projects to finals, regardless of category. What we didn’t foresee was that this would wind up disadvantaging projects from less-populous parts of our business, which had smaller constituencies. Moving forward, we’re thinking about different voting schemes to try and more accurately reflect our goals, including quadratic voting, representative democracy, participation-based voting tokens, and a more complex multi-tiered “graph-based” system — we’ll continue experimenting and report back! Cross-pollination: One of the benefits of Hack Week, at least in theory, is that it’s an opportunity for people from different parts of the business to work together. However, we realized that there was an asymmetry in who knew people from other parts of the business well enough to feel comfortable working with them: More tenured and more senior employees tended to know more people across org lines, while newer or more junior employees knew fewer. This problem was especially acute this year, given those who joined during the pandemic haven’t had as many opportunities to meet coworkers in person as they normally would. In future years, we want to figure out how to incentivize different teams to work together, particularly across Product Development and Business Development. All in all, we’re proud of what we accomplished this year. But like any good hacker, we look forward to continuing to develop and iterate on what Hack Week looks like in the years to come. Authors Peter Wilczynski, Product Manager D.J. Angelini, Technical Program Manager

title: Our Comments to the National AI Research Resource Task Force
description: Our message was clear: the completeness, accuracy, and appropriateness of data is the greatest determinant of success for AI
author: Palantir
body: Our Comments to the National AI Research Resource Task Force Last week, Palantir responded to a request for information (RFI) from the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy regarding the establishment of a National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR). The RFI sought comments from industry, academia, and the public to inform the Congressionally-directed development of a shared artificial intelligence (AI) research infrastructure. This capability will provide access to computational resources, high-quality data, educational tools, and user support to AI researchers and students across scientific disciplines. We support efforts such as the NAIRR, which seek to establish thoughtful approaches to building the holistic computing ecosystems needed to responsibly empower AI researchers, practitioners and students. At its core, we see this effort as an opportunity to cultivate a network of people, data, expertise, and resources to advance state of the art AI research; hone U.S. competitiveness in AI; and to use the NAIRR to demonstrate the technical best practices, values, norms, and ethics the U.S. seeks to advance in developing effective and responsible AI. Our message to the NAIRR Task Force was clear: in our experience, the holistic situating of data — its completeness, its accuracy, and its appropriateness to the problem — is the greatest determinant of an AI effort’s outcomes and should be central to the NAIRR’s ultimate implementation. To that end, we encouraged the NAIRR to focus on collaboration as well as ensuring trustworthiness, security, and proper use of data used for AI research by prioritizing infrastructure, governance, and intentional resource allocation. Infrastructure and Data Foundation Trustworthy and secure AI models require a trustworthy and secure data foundation (as the saying goes, “garbage in, garbage out”). In considering the NAIRR implementation roadmap, we urge the Task Force to prioritize specific data infrastructure components that are most essential and practical to ensuring high quality and reliable AI outputs: intuitive data integration and pipeline transformations, audit logs, granular access controls, the ability to version and branch data, and collaboration features for annotating datasets and identifying addressable issues over time (e.g., statistical and other forms of unwanted data bias). With these key investments, the NAIRR effort has the potential to support, enrich, and grow the AI research community by providing a shared data environment, not just static datasets. The NAIRR data resource can enable tangible, trustworthy results through collaboration tools that allow for secure modifications, annotations, and improvements to datasets and the ability to share knowledge and performance metrics. These investments will enable the NAIRR infrastructure to scale and support cross-organization, cross-discipline research to springboard the U.S.’ AI capabilities. Technical, Governance, and Cultural Awareness in Responsible AI Not only should the NAIRR incorporate best practices around AI Privacy and Civil Liberties (PCL), Bias, and Ethics, but it can — and should — enforce these best practices (e.g., stringent security and access controls) through a combination of a) technical infrastructure that facilitates enforcement of key data protection and responsible AI principles; b) governance that incentivizes and rewards best practices; and c) cultural awareness and discipline-specific frameworks to contextualize AI research and guide determinations of when and how AI applications can best align with the interests of impacted communities. Through our decades-long work developing and implementing data integration and management platforms built on granular security and privacy-preserving capabilities, we have demonstrated that well-engineered data infrastructure must provide the technical implementation measures that attach to and reinforce critical institutional governance measures. The challenges that AI research will ultimately address are not exclusively technological in nature, rather, they are techno-social and require an understanding of the cultural contexts, innovative data science practices, and institutional controls. Problem Prioritization through Resource Allocation The Task Force is well-positioned to provide opinionated oversight that steers the NAIRR towards pressing, relevant problems and historically overlooked or underfunded initiatives. Similar to how the NSF approves grants, the Task Force can provide incentives and allocate resources (compute, data, etc.) based on problem evaluation. For example, the Task Force could identify AI safety research as a topic requiring more focused research and development. When industry alone researches this topic, it is likely to direct its attention to narrow, commercially-focused use cases. The NAIRR, in contrast, could expand the scope and insights produced by the AI research community. With the appropriate infrastructure and governance in place, the NAIRR has the potential to shed light on how AI resources are being used, discover whether the most important problems (as seen through a broader societal impact lens) are being researched, drive investment, and compound knowledge from across academic, government, and industry participants. Recommendations to the NAIRR Task Force Building off these three themes, we shared with the NAIRR Task Force several recommendations to proactively craft processes and policies that will sustain the NAIRR over the long-term. Prioritizing data quality and policies that incentivize and promote flexibility and a constantly improving technical infrastructure will empower the NAIRR with a sustainable program to harness the power of the U.S. technology sector to benefit the AI research community. We have summarized our key recommendations in the chart below: Read our full response to the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource Task Force RFI.

title: Who Wants to be a Delta?
description: Chinemerem E. reflects on her journey to becoming a Forward Deployed Software Engineer.
author: Palantir
body: Who Wants to be a Delta? Editor’s Note: In this blog post, Chinemerem E. reflects on her journey from Backend Engineer at a FinTech company to a Forward Deployed Software Engineer (FDSE) at Palantir. Finding Palantir I joined Palantir as a Forward Deployed Software Engineer (or FDSE, also internally referred to as a Delta) in September 2020, after almost two years working as a backend Engineer at a Nigerian FinTech company. My former role involved planning and building out Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) and infrastructure for various features on a payment gateway application. Though the technical work was exciting, I realized I wanted to solve challenging problems beyond finance and to do so, I needed to find a new opportunity. Around the time I started my job search, I heard about Palantir from a friend. Honestly, it couldn’t have been a better match. The company, itself impressive, was doing exciting work with real impact across various industries. But the icing on the cake for me was the Forward Deployed Software Engineer role. A position where I could build right next to the customer, build for more than one customer, and apply myself in areas outside core software development? Count me in. I’ll start tomorrow! Becoming a Palantirian I onboarded in the midst of a global pandemic. The onboarding team did a fantastic job easing my cohort into Palantir via a completely virtual environment. But as the excitement of joining the best software company in the world (yes, I said it) slowly faded, I started to see just how different the FDSE role is, and that I needed a new perspective in order to be successful. Initially, I tried to cling to how my past job and the FDSE role were similar but doing so was holding me back from realizing my full potential. I had a breakthrough when I finally accepted that the Delta role is simply different from what I’d known. I was now a Forward Deployed Software Engineer and didn’t need to bend my new reality to fit the traditional software engineering role. In fact, being an FDSE is its own unique role. In this blog, I share my observations and reflect on the changes I’ve made to fully embrace this new forward deployed life as a Delta. A Different Engineering Landscape The work that FDSEs do at Palantir can be wide ranging. For the most part, Deltas work within Foundry and Gotham, Palantir’s key platforms that offer a suite of services, applications, and application-builders that provide capabilities like data integration, privacy and security controls, interactive data analysis, dashboards and reporting, operational workflows, AI & ML infrastructure, high-frequency data streaming, and more. So far, I’ve worked primarily with Foundry, which drives the observations that follow. As a new Delta, one of the first major adjustments I had to make concerned my engineering toolkit. I went from having multiple applications/platforms that handled the different aspects of my software engineering role to working almost entirely in one web-based platform: Foundry. I felt like I had lost something important or maybe become less of an engineer. My perception changed as I got to experience the power the Foundry platform wields. Foundry became my primary tool for solving problems. Among other things, Foundry served as my integrated development environment (IDE), database client, and testing tool. It is no small feat for one platform to house both development environment and user-facing interface, all with a very intuitive user experience! Did I already mention I work at the best software company in the world? I also came to realize that in my new role, productivity and effectiveness are tied more to delivering business outcomes than knowing every single technical detail of the solutions I deliver. For example, if I want to set up an automatic data synchronization (sync) from a customer’s database to build an operational application, I don’t need to build out the entire data sync logic from scratch. I would simply configure the data sync application in Foundry to do the job. Having been abstracted from the technical details of the data synchronization tool, I am able to spend more time ensuring the end application truly solves the relevant business problem. Thinking About Data Differently “I have to think about data differently now.” I remember saying this repeatedly in my first few months as a Delta. In my previous roles, data was typically just a record of events that occurred in a system, the result of users creating or modifying an entity with the click of a button on the front-end or via an API. My primary responsibility to data had been to arrange it neatly into a relational database, making sure the database schema was as normalized as possible and that if business rules changed, the schema could easily be modified or extended. “Data is no longer a mere record of the past but the very foundation to build and shape a desired future. I now ask myself: ‘What can I build to turn this data into actionable intelligence?’” Over the course of my first year as a Delta, working across two regions and three industries, I began to see data differently. Data is no longer a mere record of the past but the very foundation to build and shape a desired future. I now ask myself: “What can I build to turn this data into actionable intelligence?” As a result, I am better positioned as a Delta to truly help our customers emancipate their data. Embracing Autonomy & Taking Ownership Prior to joining, I’d heard about Palantir’s flat, decentralized teams, each with decision-making authority, and that its people have the freedom to approach, own, and solve problems creatively. I found the prospect of that kind of autonomy at work exciting. I wasn’t sure what that freedom would look like in practice but I was hoping it would lead to a sense of fulfillment from succeeding at doing the most valuable kind of work. It turns out that autonomy at Palantir is a function of ownership; we take responsibility for the decisions we make. And since I’ve joined Palantir, this freedom has helped me find that sense of fulfillment I’d been seeking. Over the course of my first year at Palantir, I learned to be brave, to not shy away from unfamiliar situations, to embrace the dynamism of the Delta role that is both enticing and intimidating, and consequently to own more aspects of the work required to drive the outcomes I want for our customers. To illustrate how I’ve grown into being a Delta, it’s helpful to consider how the Forward Deployed Software Engineer role differs from a traditional Software Engineer role. At a typical software company, a software engineer’s scope of influence is just one leg in what I think of as a relay race. A handful of people (Company Executives, Product Managers, Engineering Leads, etc.) determine the product’s direction and decide which features should be built. Then, they pass the baton to the engineering team to plan, design, and build out the product features. Once built, the engineering team then passes the baton to the sales and customer support team to ensure end users are satisfied with the originally scoped product. When enough user feedback has been obtained to inform learning, this last team shares the feedback with the Product Managers, and the relay race starts again. As a Forward Deployed Software Engineer, I’m responsible for more than just application development on a project. Deltas engage in initial customer discussions to explore, identify, and scope out the customer’s business problems. We determine how best to deploy Palantir products to solve these problems and work with our Product Development teams when new capabilities are required. We are there with the users when the applications go live and we enable the client’s IT teams to build independently on Foundry (or Gotham). By design, the Delta role is high touch and requires taking ownership, which has widened my scope of influence as an engineer. I’ve come to realize that I have quite a bit of freedom to take my work to the next level and that typically I’m the only one who can hold myself back. At Palantir, it’s up to the individual to step up and decide to own more. I have also seen (from my experience and that of more tenured Palantirians) that growth — or a promotion, if you like — happens when a person demonstrates their increased capacity simply by owning more. Focusing on Customer Outcomes Deltas are first and foremost focused on customer outcomes, an aspect that appealed to me as a prospective employee as did Palantir’s wide array of customers and penchant for solving complex problems. Initially, I expected a ‘customer outcome focus’ would translate to building all kinds of cool solutions for all the cool companies in the world. While it’s true we do cool things, the real impact comes from putting the customer first, not the technology. Keeping that prioritization clear has helped me shift my focus from technical contributions to business outcomes. My mentor in the Palantir affinity group Palnoir remarked that “one of the best parts about being an FDSE is being able to point to a real life implication of your work.” This is so true. It’s not only the most rewarding part of being a Delta but also a core responsibility. Creating impactful outcomes for customers is front of mind for me each day. “Over the course of my first year at Palantir, I learned to be brave, to not shy away from unfamiliar situations, to embrace the dynamism of the Delta role that is both enticing and intimidating, and consequently to own more aspects of the work required to drive the outcomes I want for our customers.” When I engage with customers to help solve their business problems, my approach centers around paying attention to the problem and showing empathy. Paying attention to the problem is clearly important so that we don’t spend time and resources building solutions that are not useful. But there is also the risk that not paying attention could mean that we only build a good solution at the expense of a solution that markedly elevates the way the customer operates. Empathy is also very important. We work with real people who have real problems that our software can solve. I have found that it is not enough to understand the problem well but to also put the customer first in determining a solution. This is how I take responsibility for the outcomes I want to see, by making sure that I am in tune with what the customer really needs and building toward that. Let’s Change the World I joined Palantir as an FDSE because I wanted to do more as an engineer. I wanted to work in more industries than Finance. I wanted more autonomy and the chance to have a greater impact. And here I am! Life as a Delta feels different because it is different. It has taken some getting used to but it is amazing. I am no longer showing up to work just to build an app or a platform. I show up each day to change the world. Well, at least some part of it. So, now who wants to be a Delta? Join me.

title: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part II, Data Discovery
description: Data can quickly turn from commodity to avalanche. Software-Defined Data integration facilitates exploration across vast data landscapes.
author: Palantir
body: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part II, Data Discovery Editor’s note: This is the second in a four-part series of posts exploring the origins, capabilities and impact of Palantir’s Software-Defined Data Integration. Find part one here, and stay tuned for posts three and four. Over the past few years, much thought has been dedicated to the “commoditization of data.” For good reason, too; in the Information Age, data is the single most valuable resource available to any organization — whether public, private or non-profit. However, data can quickly turn from commodity to avalanche. Unlike any physical commodity, the volume of data worldwide is increasing at an almost exponential rate. It’s estimated that the amount of data created in the next 3 years will eclipse the amount created in the past 30 years combined. And with technologies like Edge AI, IoT and data streaming burgeoning, the pace is only increasing. The issue facing most modern enterprises is not necessarily producing, housing, or cataloguing this influx of data, but rather finding it and operationalizing it against critical issues. Time and again, we’ve seen partners work around the clock to pinpoint their most pressing business problems only to realize they don’t have a structure in place to surface the data needed to address those problems. They know they have it, somewhere, but they can’t find it when they need it most. The onus then falls on IT to manually search for and assemble the datasets needed into a cohesive report. But, by the time that’s done, the time to act has passed and there’s a new problem that needs addressing. For example, a partner’s IT organization was describing an end-to-end supply chain integration project they were undertaking. It took almost a full month just to gather the list of tables needed to construct the ‘golden table’ representing the semantics of sales orders. Over the course of countless similar projects, we saw that this experience was not exceptional; in fact, it was the norm. We needed a ‘Rosetta Stone’ of sorts to decipher and preview data sources, helping end-users rapidly surface insights across vast data landscapes. “Discovery is the journey; insight is the destination.” — Gary Hamel With this intent in mind, we set out to build Palantir Foundry’s software-defined data discovery tooling with an extensible knowledge framework, utilizing source system metadata to reveal content in an intuitive and interactive manner. This was the key to automation and scalability — use the metadata already residing within common source systems (such as ERP and CRM) to inform how to transform the data. This metadata contains important information about the data and how it’s structured, so users can quickly understand what they’re looking at and pull the information they need. But ‘seeing’ the data using metadata-defined transformation was only half of the battle; the other half was knowing what datasets and source systems to use in the first place. For instance, if I want to run an end-to-end cost-of-goods workflow for my supply chain, how do I know what sources I need? That’s why we encoded SDDI with workflow-specific, opinionated data exploration. If desired, SDDI can automatically surface and group (based on years of data integration expertise) the distributed datasets necessary for a specified workflow. Of course, groupings can be dynamically modified before any integration or analysis. With SDDI, business decision-makers and data teams alike have a common platform to explore source systems and locate the data they need to address urgent business problems. The platform is point-and-click, abstracting away technical barriers and empowering users to shift their attention from “where’s the data?” to “how can I use this insight to optimize my operations?” Not only does SDDI allow users to surface the right data easily, but it also encourages them to integrate from first principles, using the most granular sources and avoiding preprocessed or aggregated data. Starting with the most fundamental, granular data paves the way for the richest, most flexible application layer atop this data foundation. The third part of our series will explore just that: how does SDDI automate the existing automation of pipeline building to power downstream applications? Then, in part four, we’ll go through some impact studies to showcase how our partners are unlocking unprecedented value at pace with SDDI. Looking to learn more about SDDI? Download the new whitepaper.

title: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part III, Data Pipelines
description: Writing data pipelines is slow, messy and expensive. Palantir's SDDI automates this pain away by generating complete pipelines out-of-the-box.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech Erp Software SaaS Software Development Data Integration From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part III, Data Pipelines Palantir 4 min read · Nov 8, 2021 -- Listen Share Editor’s note: This is the third in a four-part series of posts exploring the origins, capabilities and impact of Palantir’s Software-Defined Data Integration . Explore part one and part two , and stay tuned for the series finale . The phrase “data pipelining” might conjure mental images of supreme efficiency and organization: a neat grid of interlacing infrastructure seamlessly transporting packages of zeros and ones. Far afield from the mudslinging mess of pipelining oil, you might think. Just the contrary, writing data pipelines (like building real pipelines) is slow, messy and expensive. Data engineers must be highly knowledgable not only in the practice of pipeline development, but also the intricacies of the source systems they are connecting. For the most complex data landscapes, this amounts to engineers needing to understand the relationships between tens (or hundreds) of source systems, design ways to harmonize distinct schemas and models, and constantly adapt their pipelines in response to changes in said schemas, or changing needs of end-users. In other words, a colossal undertaking; and one that too often results in a patchwork of unmanageable pipelines that are (a.) expensive in both time and money to upkeep, (b.) inaccessible to non-technical users, and (c.) maintained by tribal knowledge and continuous support from large teams, who could be better deployed elsewhere. At Palantir , we saw this problem stymie crucial business objectives at companies of all sizes, and across all industries. Even with the best-in-class data integration capabilities of Palantir Foundry , the work of assembling production-ready pipelines required a huge amount of manual effort, expert knowledge, and continued maintenance. Software-Defined Data Integration was the answer. Press enter or click to view image in full size The previous post in this series explored SDDI’s innovative approach for processing source metadata across systems and how this facilitates end-user exploration of data before integration. SDDI pairs this capability with a modularized pipeline generation product, a suite of data harmonization tools, and an intuitive user interface for easy deployment and maintenance. Together, these offerings enable users of Foundry SDDI to take advantage of intelligent automation that all but removes the need for data pipelining, unblocking projects in days that may have previously taken years and simplifying their maintenance to a control panel UI. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Let’s break it down: Pipeline Generation SDDI generates complete, efficient pipelines out-of-the-box. It intelligently reads the shape of data and change data capture artifacts to adapt pipeline generation to the specifications of the source systems, all while administering frequent data health and data accuracy checks. The finished pipelines ship with source-specific cleaning logic and honor the locale settings of the source system. Metadata Inference Using our approaches to source metadata inference across the entire data landscape connected to Foundry, SDDI learns from the shape of the source data and adapts the dynamic pipeline generation to that shape. Rather than being prescriptive, it seamlessly adapts to business-specific customizations to the data landscape, without expensive additional maintenance or intervention. Data Harmonization Using the same inference methods, SDDI can determine or recommend matches between datasets across different source systems, such as Oracle NetSuite, SAP S/4HANA, or Salesforce Sales Cloud. Users simply confirm or reject SDDI’s recommendations for resolving entities, enabling a simple, scalable way to combine hundreds of disparate sources into a single semantic layer. Business Knowledge SDDI is encoded with more than a decade of data integration expertise across industries, workflows, and end-users. We’ve codified these learnings into the platform itself, meaning users can select from a collection of common use cases such as Inventory Management or Value Chain Visibility to be automatically prepared and configured. These rules are source agnostic and SDDI provides intelligent mapping recommendations to make it easy to enable this business logic, no matter the underlying data. “E ach problem that I solved became a rule, which served afterwards to solve other problems.” — Rene Descartes Encoded Learning Not only does SDDI come with encoded knowledge, but it enables continuous customization and feedback by providing a framework for users to catalogue their own business logic. This allows users to solidify tribal organizational knowledge as product, compounding returns over time. SDDI intelligently leverages this to continuously improve and deliver pipelines tailored to the specific organization’s needs. Press enter or click to view image in full size In data lakes or warehouses, you often find tables in the form shown under ‘Raw data’; at best, they’re a cryptic puzzle; at worst, they make it impossible for teams to make data-driven decisions. User-Friendly Interface The entire offering is driven by a simple user interface, meaning users of all technical abilities can collaborate and co-develop. While specific plugin points are designed for more complex development as needed, the whole pipeline can be managed in a few clicks. Selecting what data to process, tuning performance and resource usage, adjusting parameters to modify the behavior of the pipeline, and much more can all be done using point-and-click dynamics. Conclusion The process to go from lakes or warehouses of raw, unprocessed data to data-informed decision-making can be extraordinarily complicated, and costly. However, with Palantir’s Software-Defined Data Integration, most of this overhead is automated away — empowering organizations to focus instead on modeling their data, testing scenarios and making informed decisions based on accurate, real-time data. In part four of this series, we’ll showcase how our partners are unlocking unprecedented value at pace with SDDI. Looking to learn more about SDDI? Download the new whitepaper.

title: Why Fast and Effective Data Integration is Essential for Supply Chain Resilience
description: See how England's most critical decision makers used Palantir to create a resilient vaccine supply chain during the COVID-19 pandemic.
author: Palantir
body: Supply Chain Palantirglobal Palantir Uk Palantir Palantir Foundry Why Fast and Effective Data Integration is Essential for Supply Chain Resilience Covid-19 has proven the immense impact that disrupted supply chains can have on all aspects of life, including the delivery of critical services Palantir 3 min read · Dec 10, 2021 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Over the past few months, society has viscerally and abruptly come to understand that robust, functioning supply chains are essential to our modern way of life. An ongoing and urgent challenge that supply chains face is that they often lack structural resilience, which is essential in the current environment of disruption. Through our work with several multinational organisations, we’ve seen a pattern indicative of a brittle supply chain: chiefly, a fractured and disconnected data landscape. We often find that procurement, purchasing, transportation and logistics, warehouse management, and production teams — along with many other stakeholders — are storing their data in siloed systems. A single organisation will typically have multiple enterprise resource planning systems, transport and warehouse management systems, Microsoft Excel files on individuals’ desktops, plus many other types of data spread across departments. This leads to making siloed decisions, without vital context. And that’s just the tip of the iceberg: the sheer interconnectedness and interdependence of modern supply chains goes way beyond the capacity of inflexible software written back in the 1990s. The more complex our supply chains grow, the more risks they generate, and the greater the chance of organisation-critical disruption. The old way of managing the supply chain no longer works, and the implications of getting it wrong can have severe, life-changing impacts. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Palantir Foundry addresses this fundamental challenge by building a digital twin of the entire supply chain — from the hand of the supplier to the hand of the customer. The digital twin is then directed at solving discrete supply chain challenges by connecting analytics and operations. This is exactly what we did with NHS England to secure the rapid, accurate, and effective delivery of the NHS’s largest-ever vaccination programme. S uddenly, the NHS’s mandate widened from patient care to an incredibly complex new mission of delivering tens of millions of vaccine doses against an aggressive timeframe. The NHS didn’t have the luxury of working within a greenfield project, instead having to incorporate hundreds of existing data sources in a matter of days. The work was taking place in an ever-changing landscape of urgency and uncertainty, with levels of vaccine supply, storage requirements, and availability of key resources like PPE in a constant state of flux. Using Foundry, the NHS integrated, cleaned and harmonised its disparate data sources across the supply chain to create a single, reliable set of information to inform decision-making. From there, they could track every aspect of the vaccination programme, including the number of vaccines being administered and the volume of vaccinations by site, geography and delivery model. This allowed the NHS to adjust their approach in real time and identify areas where more support was needed. The digital twin of the end-to-end supply chain allowed front-line services to deliver vaccines at record speed across the country. If you think your operations could benefit from data-powered decision making with Foundry, check out our supply chain offering . Or if you’d like to talk to some existing Foundry customers or a few of our engineers, just get in touch. Author Scott Adams, Engineering Lead, Palantir UK

title: From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part IV, Impact
description: From harmonizing 7 ERPs in just 5 days to reducing cloud costs for data preparation by ~80%, Palantir HyperAuto is accelerating time from data to value.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech Erp Software Data SaaS Software Development From Human-Defined to Software-Defined Data Integration — Part IV, Impact Palantir 3 min read · Dec 13, 2021 -- Listen Share Editor’s note: This is the finale of our four-part series exploring the origins, capabilities and impact of Palantir HyperAuto , powered by our Software-Defined Data Integration technology. Explore part one , part two and part three . Press enter or click to view image in full size A mistake common to commercial enterprises, government organizations, and SaaS providers alike is to value data as an end in itself , rather than as a means to an end. Data is valuable, of course — leveraging it effectively is one of the greatest challenges facing modern institutions. But, data is not intrinsically valuable. A distinction made in Kant’s ‘Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals’, an end in itself is pursued for its own sake, not as vehicle to achieve something else. Oppositely, a means to an end is valued for its utility in achieving something else; its worth is determined by the outcomes it can unlock. Time and again, we’ve seen organizations pour millions of dollars into collecting, cataloguing and holding as much data as possible — transactional system data, streaming data, sales data, etc. Their data lakes and warehouses swell with information pooled and pipelined across business units. However, the value of data is not in the having, but the using. Data is a means to business value, not an end in itself. Without a means of operationalizing this wealth of knowledge against pressing business problems, data becomes an inhibitor, rather than an accelerant. “You are still adrift while you still think that a means is an end.” ― Idries Shah Palantir’s Software-Defined Data Integration empowers our partners to do more with their data — to operationalize information at pace to inform smarter decisions. We’ve packaged the power of SDDI with the data discovery and integration components discussed in Part II and Part III of this series to create Palantir HyperAuto .
