For Palantir, digital sovereignty means that public and private institutions should be able to use today’s cutting-edge technology to process data to remain competitive tomorrow — all while retaining full control of their data and decisions. The autonomy to act Helping our customers be more autonomous has always been central to Palantir’s approach to building technology. Integrating and analyzing data in our platforms is not an end in itself, but helps our customers derive insights that can be translated into concrete solutions. Facilitating data-driven decision-making and thus radically accelerating our customer’s ability to act lies at the core of our business model and our success. Most importantly, Palantir is a software, not a data company. We don’t collect, analyze or sell customer data for our own purposes, nor are we involved in influencing customer decision-making. Our goal is to provide our customers with an operating system for lasting success. We provide the platforms they need to process their own data in accordance with their own rules and goals. Inbuilt privacy and security tooling enables them to not only trust, but also continuously verify that their data is secure, available, and reliable when they need it. A changing world From Brexit to Schrems II, our customers are confronted with a constant risk of sudden change. A fragmented political and regulatory landscape threatens our customers’ ability to act. Amidst this global uncertainty, it is crucial for our customers to retain localized control over their data to maintain their autonomy. To this end, Palantir has committed to enable our customers to process their data within their own borders — not only in the United States but also in the United Kingdom and the European Union. This is a significant technical and financial investment, one that was worthwhile for us to provide our customers with something priceless: the confidence that, when working together with us, they remain in full control over their data and decision-making at all times. Our customers thus retain full autonomy, regardless of any political, regulatory, and technical disruptions going forward. Authors Paula Cipierre, EU Privacy and Public Policy Lead Jan Hiesserich, Europe Strategy Lead

title: Designing for Deletion (Palantir Explained, #6)
description: Tactics for building an effective framework
author: Palantir
body: Designing for Deletion (Palantir Explained, #6) Tactics for building an effective framework Editor’s note: This is the sixth post in Palantir Explained, a series that explores a range of topics, including our approach to privacy, security, AI/ML safety, and more. Previous posts explored our business model, purpose-based access controls, anonymization, trust in data, and our unique approach to Privacy & Civil Liberties (PCL) engineering. As individuals become increasingly concerned with how, where, and for what purpose their personal data is stored, deletion has emerged as a central theme within the data protection discourse. Although privacy laws typically include provisions on necessity, purpose limitation, data minimization and, in the case of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the “right to be forgotten,” many organizations struggle to translate regulatory and normative expectations into practice. In this blog post, we explain what deletion is, why it matters, and what challenges it poses for organizations looking to define and construct a world-class framework for data protection. We offer recommendations based on Palantir’s work with some of the world’s most trusted institutions, as well as insights into how we help customers design and implement effective deletion processes. For more information about how we work with our partners to build deletion frameworks, read our full white paper, available here. What Deletion Means Deletion is the process of making data less accessible in a system over time. The term process is important here. Deletion typically happens in stages. First, front-end user access is removed. Then, as soon as an organization has verified which data is eligible, deletion of qualifying data can begin. The organization must then wait for the deletion process to complete, which can take time, depending on the deletion process chosen. At the same time, organizations must design a technical and organizational process able to accommodate human and machine error along the way. This requires organizations to ensure deletion remains reversible for a certain predefined period of time. “Hard deletion,” or making data irreversibly inaccessible, is the end goal of the process. As long as the deletion process can still reasonably be reversed, the data counts as “soft deleted” instead. Given that such accessibility requirements vary, there is no one-size-fits-all approach to deletion. How “deleted” data needs to be in practice depends on the context of processing, as well as the sensitivity at hand. Often, it is neither technically possible nor operationally feasible to hard delete data all at once. Understanding what data an organization holds, how it’s structured, and how it’s processed in accordance with specific regulatory requirements is a complex task. Ultimately, what matters most has less to do with the deletion process than ensuring the result: when data is deleted, it must no longer be possible to process it. Why Deletion Matters Deletion is an important aspect of data minimization and storage limitation, which are core principles in most data protection frameworks. Many data protection laws specifically outline the responsibility of controllers to limit the processing of personal data to that which is necessary and proportional to achieve a legitimate processing purpose. These laws also afford individuals, often referred to as “data subjects”, with certain deletion rights. A notable example of this kind of law is found in the GDPR, where data subjects have the right to request the erasure of personal data. Deletion also plays an important role in auditing and accountability. It’s in an organization’s best interest to be able to consistently monitor and report what needs to be deleted, by whom, and at what cadence. When working with our partners, we recommend they establish a clear understanding of what these expectations are as early as possible to ensure the deletion process is structured to meet these demands. Disjointed or incomplete deletion practices not only expose an organization to the risk of serious legal and financial consequences, but can also jeopardize trust with other businesses, stakeholders, and the general public. In certain cases, storing data longer than necessary can have lasting and devastating consequences for individuals, as the mere presence of someone’s data in a system can have significant legal effects. Questions to Ask When Creating or Evaluating Your Deletion Processes When considering how to structure or amend your own deletion processes, we recommend first working through the following regulatory, logistical, and technical questions to ensure a holistic evaluation. Regulatory considerations: What are the regulatory frameworks surrounding the data? Does deletion unilaterally apply to the entire datasource or solely certain properties thereof? Do different rules apply to data being processed in different jurisdictions? Could there be cases where ad-hoc entries could be exempt from deletion due to exceptions? Does some data need to be archived instead? How can we capture metadata about deletion and provide a proof of concept to demonstrate relevant regulatory requirements, e.g., data subject deletion requests, can be met? Logistical planning for deletion at ingestion: To minimize sensitive data handling and reduce risk exposure, what datasets need to be ingested to begin with? Is the data ingested incrementally or wholesale? How are the datasets structured? Are they joined with any other data sources? If so, what regulatory and data handling requirements apply to those data sources? Will ad hoc deletion requests affect the integrity of the core dataset? If so, how will subdataset level deletion be organized? How should downstream datasets be configured to take future deletions into consideration? Technical implementation: Does the deletion require manual user approval, or should it be automated based on a given propriety (e.g., temporal requirement for data retention based on ingestion date)? If the deletion is manual, which metadata needs to be captured to identify what (e.g., retention date) and who (e.g., ad hoc request) triggered the deletion, and if the deletion was successfully completed in practice? Often, this requires defining which teams/roles will be responsible for data deletion and how reporting ought to be conducted. Is the deletion purpose to prevent users from being able to access the information (soft delete) or does it need to be wiped from the source system entirely (hard delete)? What steps can be taken to make the process replicable and future proof? Case study — What Deletion Looks Like in (Hypothetical) Practice To illustrate the deletion process in action, let’s consider a notional example of a standard implementation project that Palantir could work on with a partner. Let’s assume that our partner here is a large European business in the financial industry. This customer needs to process personal data in accordance with the requirements of the GDPR, and therefore must be able to regularly delete personal data in both a streamlined and ad hoc fashion, to accommodate both normal deletion procedures as well as individual “right to be forgotten” (RTBF) requests. Note that the data not only needs to be removed from source systems, but deletion must also propagate to systems downstream. To ensure our partner can meet deletion requirements in practice, we agree to pursue a multi-stage approach building in both automation and human review strategies into the core workflow. The success of this approach relies on striking the right balance between the two: using automation contributes to ensuring the consistency and completeness of deletion, while human review and approvals adds appropriate checks and balances throughout. The stages are as follows: Triage RTBF requests with eligibility logic for each application. Deletion requests are processed based on rules and/or restrictions with handling data. For instance, some data may not be deleted due to a legal hold, or other account information could not be deleted if it was active. Locate and review impacted data for deletion. This step is critical for facilitating the review and data owner approval of all data that will be affected by the deletion process in their respective data systems. For complex pipelines, this means ensuring that the impact of deletion on any data upstream and/or downstream is analyzed and approved by the relevant subject matter experts before the data can be removed. Orchestrate the write-back to core source systems as soon as all the reviews are completed. Note that this requires connection to all the source systems with carefully tailored write permissions. Relevant scripts are then automated to sequentially conduct deletions throughout source systems and thus fully remove any artifacts still referencing the yet-to-be-deleted data. Enable continuous monitoring of existing data by conducting regular searches on the tables with data deleted to flag if any data re-enters the system. This may occur for many reasons, such as if the deletion was not successful, or if other source systems still contain the content that was supposed to be deleted. Document RTBF requests and subsequent deletion processes. This can then be used to provide regulators and auditors with the opportunity to review the effectiveness of deletion processes across the platform. Conclusion Defining and implementing the right deletion framework isn’t simple. For many organizations working across complex jurisdictions, deleting data consistently and completely often requires far more than a five stage process. However, defining and implementing a deletion framework enables organizations to reduce their overall risk exposure and to continuously review and improve upon existing procedures, thus ensuring any lessons learnt are fed back into the process by design. At Palantir, we’re dedicated to collaborating with our customers across industries to help define the right models for supporting thorough, compliant deletion processes. Whether working in Foundry or Gotham, Palantir is proud to provide our customers with cutting-edge tools that enable them to comply with applicable data protection obligations and become established privacy leaders in their industries. To learn more about how Palantir helps customers transform their business and meet their data protection requirements, please reach out to us at media@palantir.com. If you find these blog posts inspiring and would like to join us in solving the challenges described, have a look at the opportunities we have available — we’d love to hear from you. Authors Paula Cipierre, EU Privacy and Public Policy Lead Annabelle Larose, Technical Program Manager, Privacy & Civil Liberties Engineering, Palantir

title: A Day in the Life of a Palantir Deployment Strategist
description: As a Deployment Strategist at Palantir, you’ll have the freedom to define what you do and how you do it. Learn more in this blog post.
author: Palantir
body: A Day in the Life of a Palantir Deployment Strategist One of the most interesting, yet potentially confusing, roles at Palantir is the Deployment Strategist, known internally as “Echo.” At Palantir, we help companies leverage their data for a deep understanding of their business and build a digital twin of their operations. To solve our clients’ toughest problems, we often embed closely with them to design, configure and implement innovative workflows and applications. On a typical project, you’ll find a mix of Deployment Strategists and Forward-Deployed Engineers (commonly dubbed “Deltas”). Theoretically, Echos are more product-managers while Deltas are more technical, but in reality, both roles are a mix between product manager, software engineer and strategist and the lines between the two roles blur heavily quite often. In this post, we’ll focus on the unique role of the Deployment Strategist. Deployment Strategists run the gamut, from people who code all day, every day and rarely talk with clients to folks who never touch code but coordinate and mentor multiple projects internally and externally at the same time. In other words, it’s a pretty wide spectrum, and no two Deployment Strategists are the same. In a more traditional project setting, Deployment Strategists tend to focus on tasks like: Understanding the client’s operations and figuring out where Palantir software can have the biggest impact Designing and implementing user-centric workflows and applications around problems or gaps in the existing systems Iterating rapidly with users to make sure the solution is what they want and need Implementing and scaling developed solutions Managing client relationships Managing the project in terms of timelines and deliverables Representing Palantir with senior client leadership This list goes on… Daily life With so many priorities, you might be asking yourself: what does an actual day look like for a Deployment Strategist? Fortunately, dull moments are few and far between, because there’s so much variety in what you take on. Personally, I’m currently working on a pilot engagement for a large drugstore company in the US, even though I’m based in Europe. We’re working on co-creating a number of different workflows with the customer that are targeted at giving them more visibility into operations and automating certain processes, so they can focus on the challenges that really need their expertise. Here’s a look at a typical day for me, as well as for two of my colleagues. One of them leads a more established project and is becoming an industry expert in that space, while the other works at the intersection between embedded and internal development teams, bridging the gap between what our products can do already and what is needed in the field. And yes, we all have the same job title! Daily Life as a Pilot Lead (CO) 09:00 AM — Get my head in the game: recap the broader goals of my project, what the clients want and need, and where we are (frequently done during a run and/or accompanied by strong coffee) 10:00 AM — Daily stand-up: make sure everyone is on the same page, knows what to work on and why, and doesn’t have any blockers 10:15 AM — Continue working on a data pipeline to integrate the customer’s ERP system into an application that automatically resolves discrepancies in shipments 12:30 PM — Lunch — depending on which office you call home, head over to the canteen, venture outside, or order in, and find out what your colleagues are up to (the breadth of projects is wide and often there are interesting synergies) 01:30 PM — Iteration session with clients to show them the progress I’ve made since morning — understand their real-world problems, listen to their feedback, and nudge them to come up with new features they didn’t think were possible “just yet” 02:30 PM — Random Sync with someone else at Palantir to make sure I’m always meeting new people who work on different things than I do 02:50 PM — Moonlight on an initiative that excites me outside of my project world (I currently do outreach for Foundry for Builders, Palantir’s offering to start-ups, because I find it inspiring to see what our software can do in the hands of founders) 04:30 PM — Work on materials for an upcoming project milestone presentation to senior stakeholders, set up an internal dress rehearsal, and shoot off a quick progress update through Slack so my colleagues waking up on the other side of the world know what’s going on Daily Life as an Enterprise Lead 08:00 AM — Kick the day off with breakfast over emails 09:00 AM — Iterate on materials for a best practices session with the digital office of one of our major clients, focusing on supporting them to build organizational structures to increase ownership over value creation in Foundry 10:00 AM — Team up with an Industry Director to join a pre-sales meeting in which we are presenting Palantir’s offerings and discussing a potential partnership 11:00 AM — One-on-one meeting with one of my technical team members; discuss the past few weeks, their growth path, and fun weekend plans 11:30 AM — Meet with our Head of Commercial Business to discuss a partnership proposal with a large utilities company 12:15 PM — Lunch with one of my mentees who just started at Palantir; we talk about navigating the company and I get them in touch with a colleague from the London office for coffee. 01:00 PM — Weekly team meeting; reflect on the past week and plan the upcoming week 02:00 PM — Write a 1-page thesis to make the case for a feature that will be integrated into the core product by my colleagues in product development. 04:00 PM — Draft marketing material with one of the workstream leads on my team to increase Foundry adoption Daily Life as an Internal Echo 10:30 AM — Arrive at the office + have breakfast 11:00 AM — Catch up on emails/Slack and review pull requests (PRs) that came in overnight 11:30 AM — Working session prepping for a leadership meeting to come up with a business case for a new project initiative 01:00 PM — Learning Lunch: order in food and sit with my colleagues as we tune into the Q1 Foundry Roadshow for this year 01:30 PM — Get heads-down in my code to add functionality to Foundry that doesn’t exist yet in the core product but will help many project teams across the company 03:30 PM — Slack the Modeling Tech Lead a “Hey, quick question…” message, which inevitably launches me into a spontaneous learning session 04:00 PM — Go for a run in the English Garden/on the High Line/along the Seine/… 05:00 PM — Meet with a US sales team to identify potential use cases for Foundry to improve sales processes 05:30 PM — Meet with a client-facing team to give advice on a particular use case 06:00 PM — Daily team standup 06:15 PM — Sensor Data Pull Design Review with a select number of client-facing teams and the core product team Why this role Being a Deployment Strategist, or Echo, is like taking on a rainbow role. What I’ve found fascinating about this position is how you can shape it into almost anything you want. When I was looking for a job, a huge soft criterion was that I would still be able to learn new things that truly interest me and grow in areas that I deemed important. I wanted to improve my coding skills, even though I wasn’t very technical, and I made a point of writing code all day long until I felt somewhat satisfied with my knowledge. I also knew I wanted to become more skilled at project management and maximize the impact of my work. Palantir actively supported these goals of mine, even though from the company’s perspective, it would have made more sense to focus on my strengths and keep me far away from a code repository. As important as developing these skills was to me, I also enjoy being hands-on and building meaningful products that others find useful. Getting to work on Palantir Foundry has given me the opportunity to create things from scratch, and Foundry makes it easy to be iterative and rapidly build up, tear down, and adapt solutions. As an Echo, I have tangible output — I’m actually designing and implementing applications that will make clients’ jobs easier and more efficient — and I get to work side-by-side with the future users instead of working in a black box. As a project lead and mentor, it’s also part of my job to witness and support my team members’ growth paths both personally and professionally, which I’m constantly humbled by. I personally enjoy context-switching, so I’ve worked on a number of 4–12 week pilot engagements to see new industries and meet new colleagues, but there are many Echos that stick to one project for a long time and immerse themselves deep into the topic while building long-lasting client relationships. Why Palantir Data can be a blessing and a curse — it can spark invaluable insights if you know how to use it, but if you don’t, it can prove inadequate or even harmful. When reading about the world of data, I find it frightening how often data is misused and how little people question decisions that are “backed by data.” Helping private and public organizations leverage their data in ways that are logical, ethical, efficient, and transparent is something I find not only important, but also in alignment with my personal values — and that’s what I get to work on as a Deployment Strategist. On the outside, Palantir can seem like a black box. But on the inside, Palantir operates as a no-hierarchy company where the best idea wins, no matter your title or tenure. It’s still small (and resource-constrained) enough that you get a lot of responsibility early on. You’re constantly wearing three different hats — you’re usually responsible for running a project and building a product at the same time, while making sure all you learn flows back into Palantir’s software. You can text anyone for advice or context or examples, so you don’t have to constantly figure out tough things on your own. Palantir also does do a good job at pairing new folks with an experienced lead and mentor who can help you navigate this admittedly untraditional company and grow in the ways you want to grow. The most challenging aspect of working at Palantir As attractive as “no hierarchy” sounds at first, it does come with a very high assumed level of autonomy and responsibility. You frequently have to make confident decisions under uncertain conditions and set a course for an unknown future. Chances are, even though you don’t have a lot of context, it’s more than anyone else has. Constantly being under this sort of pressure can be exhausting. You will come out the other end with a strong muscle in dealing with ambiguity, but it’s still a process. Palantir’s flat hierarchy guarantees a steep learning curve. My advice for someone considering the Deployment Strategist role There are no defined paths to this role, no matching study backgrounds or industries, and no definitions of what it means to do well. You shape your own role as a Deployment Strategist. The more responsibility you take on, the more you get; the more opinions you form, the more people listen. Whether you want to write code all day, conduct user interviews, scale existing accounts or win over new ones, the stage is yours and you should apply your strengths and weaknesses to it in your unique way. Just as no day in our professional life is the same, no two Deployment Strategists are the same. We are a collection of people who don’t fit into a single role description, which is why we need to constantly define (and redefine) it. We go where we’re needed most and get inherently itchy when we see problems. We are the first ones in and the last ones out, have a get-shit-done mentality, constantly challenge the existing status quo, and value execution high. Deployment Strategists are strong at being reflective, self-driven, technical, and empathetic. You know best where your strengths and weaknesses are, and Palantir will ask you how it can get better as a company instead of molding you into a role. You see the roadblocks ahead and do what it takes to unblock yourself and your team, whether by teaching yourself a new coding language or by shouting at leadership. You truly care about understanding your users and their needs. In short, as a Deployment Strategist at Palantir, you strive to manage difficult situations and find unconventional solutions to data-centric challenges, and you do it your way — because you know best where you’re needed most. Sabine joined Palantir in December 2019 as a new grad hire. She is currently a pilot lead across various industrial sectors and involved in interviewing, outreach, and women in tech.

title: Internship Reflections: Working in Palantir’s D.C. hub
description: Read about the experiences of three college students who interned at Palantir’s Washington D.C. office in summer 2021.
author: Palantir
body: Internship Reflections: Working in Palantir’s D.C. hub The Interns Go to Washington In the summer of 2021, Palantir’s internship program operated in a hybrid model. Unlike in previous years, where interns were located across many office locations, interns had the option of either working remotely or working in-person from our London or Washington, D.C. offices. We invited interns who worked in the Washington, D.C. office to share their perspective on finding an in-person community at Palantir and talk about their experience in one of our busiest offices. What made your internship experience exciting? Miguel: Coming from an academic background — I did lab research, theoretical work, and research writing alongside my undergraduate courses — I was very new to the world of software engineering. Thanks to the help of everyone on my team, I was able to learn about software engineering, and not just from a technical perspective. My mentor handled technical questions, and my lead connected me with people across the company, so I learned more about different culture and growth opportunities. After the internship, I feel more attuned to how a company like Palantir works and how my code connects with the bigger picture. Saaniya: I definitely believe my confidence grew a lot during this internship, mainly due to the support I was given by my mentor and team lead to undertake projects that were out of my comfort zone but that they believed were well within my capabilities. I think just having those people in my corner — people who provided feedback on how to grow into the best version of yourself — gave me the comfort to truly explore uncharted technical territory. Michael: Not only was I able to learn new programming languages, cloud technologies, and tools, I was able to rapidly improve my debugging and code quality processes. This helped me to establish my own independence in a large codebase and drove my confidence and initiative to think beyond the scope of my project or explore my own curiosities. I was encouraged to present my newfound experience and ideas to many others in the company and became much more comfortable spreading my expertise to educate and help others. What was your support system like during the internship? Michael: My core intern team was comprised of a mentor, lead, and ally, but the mentorship I received expanded to my team, other interns, and everyone I reached out to for a 1:1 chat. My mentor and I collaborated every day on technical problems, explored D.C. during our outdoor 1:1 walks, and even did some rock climbing at the same gym. Fellow interns cheered for each others’ success and everyone I worked with tried their hardest to enable me to achieve the best result by the end of the summer. I really felt that everyone wanted the best outcome for everyone else. Saaniya: My support system during the internship was amazing and one of the big reasons why I am so excited to return in the fall. My mentor, team lead, and lead of the group I was a part of made sure to provide me with constructive feedback every week, which led me to both become a better engineer and also gain confidence in my abilities. What advice would you give someone considering an internship at Palantir? Miguel: Meet new people, as often as possible. There are some structured ways of doing this, including attending lunch talks and signing up for an (optional) “Random Sync,” which automatically matches you with another Palantirian. Also, be creative about how you meet new people. Ask mentors and leads to connect you with people you can learn from. Approach people at lunch or dinner, if it makes sense to do so. Hang out with the other interns, during and after work. The people at Palantir are so friendly and willing to impart their knowledge and experiences. Saaniya: I would tell someone who is considering an internship at Palantir that if they love the scrappy feeling of a startup while also having the support structure of a company, Palantir is the place for them. The Palantir mentality of “if something is broken, fix it, no matter your role” is something that I’ve found to be unique to Palantir, having worked at a couple of other internships Michael: The Palantir process was one of the most challenging I have ever completed, but it challenged all the right skills in the best way possible. The claims that Palantir makes around curating internship experiences that involve meaningful work could not be more true and easily outperform any company I’ve been a part of previously. They invest a lot of time and energy into understanding your skills and interests and match you with a problem/project and team that will flourish because of your presence. Washington, D.C. is also the cultural heart of our Gotham and United States Government work. Our work with the U.S. Government and Defense sector is not only how we started, but also a large part of the current landscape of Palantir. Here in Washington, D.C., our interns working on U.S. Government and Defense had a multitude of opportunities including close proximity to clients, ability to see the immediate impact of their work, and addressing some of the nation’s most important challenges. What was your favorite aspect of interning in Washington, D.C.? Miguel: The office is located in the Georgetown neighborhood, an incredibly vibrant place. During the summer, I visited the movie theater, the waterfront park, many restaurants featuring all sorts of cuisines, and the flea market on Sunday mornings. I highly recommend taking the weeknights and weekends to explore Georgetown, or any other part of D.C. That’s how I was able to decide that D.C. will be my new home after graduation! Saaniya: My favorite part of interning in Washington, D.C. was being able to experience a new city as a working adult. The last time I had been to DC was during my eighth grade school field trip, and being able to come back seven years later and immerse myself in the same culture and environment, but as a resident, was a very cool experience. Michael: All summer, the weather in D.C. was sunny and made walks to the office all the more enjoyable. The housing that Palantir provided proved to not only be the most fun location for ping pong, pool, swimming, karaoke, and movies but was also within walking distance of D.C.’s signature landmarks and museums. Since I worked on problems related to Palantir’s U.S. Government clientele, the D.C. area was that much cooler to me, as I was able to cross paths with so many others thinking about the same problems I was. I left D.C. with a richer appreciation of the history of the area as well as a strong affinity toward the important and necessary work being done to improve national security. What part of your work or internship made you the most proud? Miguel: Toward the end of my internship, I worked on a small feature with the guidance of my mentor. As it turned out, this feature became a significant point of discussion, even after I had finished building version 1.0 of it. In short, the presence of this feature inspired a larger conversation about the high-level architecture of our code, which resulted in long-term plans to change the architecture. My experience with this feature is proof that any intern at Palantir can do work that is not only productive, but also transformative beyond the code itself. Saaniya: The part of my internship that made me the most proud was taking a step back at the end of the internship and seeing just how much I grew in confidence and technical ability. It was amazing to me that by week eight of my internship, I was on calls with senior engineers at Palantir helping them debug their issues. I think this is a testament to just how much trust is given to interns because they’re all very capable of the work they’ve been given. Michael: Only a few weeks after I had completed my internship, it was announced that Palantir was selected for the Army’s Capability Drop 2 (CD-2) program to deliver the Army’s intelligence data fabric and analytics foundation. CD-2 had been a program and effort that I had heard about internally since the first week of my internship and was a big driver in the project I contributed to all summer. Both the importance of CD-2 to Palantir and the Army and the technicalities of Palantir’s deliverables were new problem spaces that I had never worked in before, but being able to work on these problems and see the contract awarded to Palantir was something I remain very proud of. Learn more about what our interns have worked on and meet some of our former interns here. Bios Miguel Opeña was an intern on Palantir Gotham, working in the Washington, D.C. office. He currently studies Computer Science at Princeton and will return to Palantir as a full-time Software Engineer after graduating. Saaniya Kapur was a Product Reliability Engineer intern in Washington, D.C. Currently, she studies Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Following graduation, Saaniya will return to Palantir as a Product Reliability Engineer. Michael Gutierrez interned on the Production Infrastructure team in Washington, D.C. He studies Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at Columbia University and will be a return intern next summer.

title: Engineering for Impact
description: Problem Solving with Purpose at Palantir
author: Palantir
body: Engineering for Impact Problem Solving with Purpose at Palantir Editor’s note: In this blog post, we sit down with UK Health Lead Joanna Peller, recipient of Data IQ’s 2022 100 award, to discuss what she’s learned leading Palantir’s UK Health work during the pandemic. Describe your path to Palantir. After growing up in Boston, Massachusetts, I moved to the UK to study Mathematics at UCL. I began my career as a software engineer working in Commodities at Goldman Sachs before joining Palantir as a Forward Deployed Strategist in 2016. I was drawn to Palantir because I wanted to be part of a business that would allow me to solve increasingly challenging problems. It was clear to me that I’d be working on projects that had real-world implications. In my early days at Palantir, I worked with a team focused on manufacturing and supply chain solutions. In March of 2020, this supply chain expertise became incredibly relevant, and I began working on the most complex problem of my career to date: helping the NHS deploy our software, Palantir Foundry, to form a single source of truth for the COVID-19 response. I now lead our Health work in the UK, which spans everything from vaccine supply chain optimisation to elective recovery and beyond. Data IQ just named you to their 2022 list of top 100 most influential people in data. Tell us a bit about what this award means to you. Being part of Data IQ’s 2022 list of most influential people in data was a really special privilege. Those of us that fall into the ‘data enabler’ category tend to be partners and service providers that, although not responsible for any data itself, are focused on building the right solutions and infrastructure to underpin it. So much of my own fulfilment in this role comes from witnessing our partners like the NHS realise value and make better use of their data with the help of Foundry. Having the opportunity to contribute, even in some small way, to the extraordinary work the NHS does every day has been the highlight of my career. Being recognised for that work is a real honour. How has Palantir’s health work changed in response to the Pandemic? In the UK, COVID-19 has not only changed the very nature of our work, but it has changed the significance of our outcomes as well. While the heart of our health work has always centred on improving patient lives, the pandemic gave this mission new meaning. Almost overnight, we were tasked with supporting the NHS in solving its largest peacetime logistical challenge as quickly as humanly possible. Local and national leadership needed to create the right data infrastructure that could allow them to see the true picture of infection spread and critical care capacity, and we were fortunate enough to be the partner they trusted to support them in tackling this problem. How would you describe the culture around problem solving at Palantir? How has it impacted your work? One of the mantras integral to Palantir’s culture is ‘the best idea wins.’ I’ve found that in order for the best idea to win, it needs to exist in an environment that encourages diversity of thought. It’s not something we can take for granted. I have a responsibility to my colleagues, and our partners, to identify opportunities to foster an inclusive approach to collaboration. Enabling this type of inclusive collaboration is an integral component of our external work as well. Often, companies like Palantir are seen as the “outsiders” that come into existing businesses to “consult.” I can understand in theory why that narrative exists — but that’s not how we work. Many of our healthcare partners have experienced staff that have spent years, if not decades, working with the problems we’re currently trying to help them solve. We never assume we have all the answers and we rely heavily on the expertise of our customers. When we can build an environment that’s rooted in mutual learning and collaboration, we all win. What’s one valuable piece of advice you were given earlier in your career that still resonates today? The importance of developing and nurturing a growth mindset. The concept of a growth mindset was developed by psychologist Carol Dweck, who describes it as an attitude towards intelligence as something that is never fixed, but continually developed. It considers trial and error to be an integral part of mastery. Underlying this mindset is a simple, but critical, motivation: an unwavering desire to learn new things, even when it is uncomfortable. Many of us are taught that embracing new challenges, learning from our mistakes, and thoughtfully considering the feedback we receive is what we ought to do, but to truly embrace a growth mindset, I have to decide every day that I want to learn and become better at what I do more than I want to have the right answer. I’m fortunate to be surrounded by, and constantly working with, lots of very smart people. They challenge my assumptions all the time. There isn’t a day that passes that I don’t learn something from (usually more than) one of them. I wouldn’t be where I am if I hadn’t embraced the cycle of trying, failing, and learning, and found a working culture that did the same. How is the work you do at Palantir different from other engineering roles? One of the things that sets my role apart is the actual solution I get to work with. Our Foundry platform is designed with an inherent flexibility that allows it to be adapted at speed, which in turn allows our clients to configure their tools and dashboards to accurately reflect needs on the ground. This means that I get to work on custom solutions that can provide major insights for our customer within a few days, and sometimes even within just a few hours. A compelling example of what this flexibility means for my work was the NHS COVID-19 Vaccination rollout. Over the course of just a few days, the NHS team was able to assemble the data infrastructure needed for the rollout, creating a full picture of all data sources and assets involved, down to individual vaccine doses. By tracking and integrating data from across the rapidly evolving supply chain, Foundry provided a consistent source of truth for thousands of NHS staff, who used these insights to make data-driven decisions every day. Being able to track and monitor everything from storage requirements to PPE availability allowed the NHS to create tooling that could anticipate future need, creating an end-to-end virtuous cycle that helped inform and build relevant planning models. The ability to work with partners to scale quickly and create immediate impact is a distinctive feature of this role, and operating in such an agile environment means that no two days are the same. What are your key areas of focus in 2022 and beyond? As we look ahead, our focus is simple: we want to continue to work with a broad range of healthcare and life science organisations to improve patient lives. It’s been a tremendous honour and privilege to work with partners like the NHS on projects that have been so critical to pandemic response. As the UK continues its pandemic response and begins to tackle its next set of challenges, we are focusing our efforts on partnerships with organisations that are at the forefront of innovating patient care. What keeps you up at night? Thinking about all the things that are left to build. Want to join Joanna in building the next generation of healthcare solutions? Find out more.

title: Palantir HyperAuto — Not Just An ETL
description: At first glance, you may think HyperAuto is just another ETL, but we’ve taken this foundation further to help accelerate your time to…
author: Palantir
body: Palantir HyperAuto — Not Just An ETL Having access to the right data at the right time to make the right decision is absolutely critical to modern enterprises. Data improves resilience to macro-shocks and can help businesses adjust with agility to changing market dynamics — to not only survive, but thrive in times of uncertainty. If organizations could unlock and operationalize this data, they could make better decisions, find opportunities for cost savings, save on resources, and in some cases, avoid massive waste in operational spending. Historically, the most accessible way of doing this was by employing an ETL (Extract, Transform and Load), such as Informatica or open-source on Apache Nifi. ETLs fit between raw data sources and an operational data warehouse, extracting data from these sources, performing routine, manual transformations and depositing the results into a repository — which, in turn, fed visualization tools like Power BI or Tableau. What’s an ETL? Extraction is the art of bringing data into a system. This can often be the most time-consuming step. The ETL must be manually programmed and reprogrammed to integrate data from hundreds of different legacy systems, file types and data structuring paradigms. Some organizations have millions of tables to extract. Transform involves cleansing the data, sorting the data, and combining it into a logical framework. This can be intensive for data engineers since they are tasked with custom-coding a lot of these transformations and applying unique rules to check for quality. Load is the final step where the ETL takes that transformed data and loads it into its end destination . Load can be completed in batches or all at once. The amount of information you are loading will determine how much time and compute this process takes. Common ETL Use-Cases Marketing and Sales Data Integration — pull web analytics or salesforce data into one place to better optimize persona-level marketing and understand granular audience analytics. Database Replication — for data resilience and redundancy, ETLs are often used to create a backup of key data in case something happens to the original Business Intelligence — pull data from across your systems to feed BI tools and workflows, including visualization and reporting. Ensure Data Quality- through data profiling and standardization, deduplication, data enhancement, data cleansing and verification, ETLs force organizations to take a hard look at the data living in legacy systems. Where can it feel limited? Extract — this step alone can take months, even years, with traditional ETLs, depending on how much data the ETL is processing. In some cases, this is millions of tables across 20–30 different systems. Transform — Because transformations must be often be custom-coded and validated by software engineers or developers, ETLs can introduce significant overhead and redundant, time-consuming work for your engineering team — whose talents are better spent analyzing and operationalizing data, rather than building custom pipelines. Load- the process ends here. You load the transformed data into an end system, but what comes next? How do you gain value from the data? An entirely separate process is needed to bring business value from the data you just ran through the ETL. That’s why we built HyperAuto. At first glance, you might think HyperAuto is just another ETL, but we’ve taken this foundation several steps further to help accelerate your time to value from months to days, even hours. HyperAuto already works out-of-the-box for many well-known ERP and CRM systems and can easily be extended to work for most other structured data sources of your choice. HyperAuto is able to extract data from source systems of your choice. However, our software-defined data integration technology, automates the transformation process as much as possible. With HyperAuto, your engineers no longer have to hard-code data pipelines and do the labor-intensive support work to maintain these transformations. Of course, teams still have the ability for customization, but this time-intensive process has been productized and automated. As part of these transformations, HyperAuto automatically generates an ‘ontology’ using the data, giving users readable objects that anyone in your business can interact with and understand. This ontology enables the business to start using your data to its fullest potential as quickly as possible. You can then load this mapping into the visualization tool of your choice. As mentioned previously, having data at your fingertips, while critical, is really just the first step. The most important part of data is what you do with it. With a traditional ETL you may load your data to the final destination, but now your original sources are out-of-date. HyperAuto includes state-of-the-art write-back to original systems, so all data is current. At Palantir we know the richest and most flexible downstream applications of data integration rely on starting from the most granular source data. We’ve automated as much as possible allowing the metadata to take charge — it can power dynamic data pipeline generation, slashing the overheads of manual data integration now and in the future. This can help you build a highly extensible knowledge framework and help close your organization’s operational loop.

title: How Palantir Foundry Powers bp’s Digital Transformation in Reliability
description: Reflections by bpSolutions Global Reliability Advisor Weimin Teng and Palantir Maintenance & Reliability Lead Daniel Herman
author: Palantir
body: How Palantir Foundry Powers bp’s Digital Transformation in Reliability An exploration of how Palantir’s platform improves bp’s production and operations reliability, with reflections and lessons learned by bpSolutions Global Reliability Advisor for Data, Systems and Tools Weimin Teng, and Palantir Maintenance & Reliability Lead Daniel Herman. Hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue can be unlocked with a reliable plant that is both safe and productive. Even a 1% improvement in overall operational availability can translate to a significant value. However, reliability in operating facilities can be impacted by many factors, including unforeseen environmental events, planned maintenance, plant turnarounds, and unplanned equipment failures. Timely analysis of such events is crucial to inform actionable plans that improve reliability. Millions of static and dynamic data points must be comprehensively analyzed to understand the potential impact of reliability-related vulnerabilities, risks, and bad actors. For bp, this includes the rapidly growing universe of engineering, transactional maintenance, and sensor data points generated every day across the globe. The potential to deliver business insights from these complex data assets is enormous. The Palantir Foundry platform makes it possible with quicker access to connected data, low-code data transformation technology, and easy to use data visualization solutions and operational applications — all in one environment. In this blog post, we explore how Palantir and bp — partners since 2014 — are embarking on a new undertaking to enable the transformation of bpSolutions’ reliability discipline. With operations in Europe, North and South America, Australasia, Asia, and Africa, bp is committed to delivering energy more safely, efficiently, and reliably — especially in times of disruption. Improving plant reliability is mission critical and even more challenging for one of the world’s largest integrated energy companies. Palantir’s Foundry platform brings data to end users across multiple regions in a coherent fashion. In collaboration with reliability subject matter experts, data is transformed, organized, and analyzed to support informed decision-making across different levels of the organization. How we started Given the global nature of the discipline, deciding where to begin is a challenge. To find our starting point, we first focused on understanding existing datasets and their value and relevance to reliability performance. By using the Foundry platform, we were able to connect existing data from disparate systems in a consistent manner, then organized the data to reveal bp production reliability and operational availability performance at regional, asset, choke, and systems levels. Displayed in a simple and easy to interpret format, this exercise yielded insights into where investments in digital transformation efforts could be beneficial to the business, and how to structure the underlying digital journey. From standalone to a connected data network to insights Eventually, every step of the business process becomes a coherent data point. While these individual points may produce limited meaning, when knitted together they create a story. Teams working on individual step(s) in the process have limited visibility into the big picture and are unable to track end-to-end execution effectively. By contrast, connecting data across disparate systems that support various reliability and availability analytics in a central, accessible location enables a common operating picture for the organization to assess the effectiveness of existing processes, identify pain points, and generate new insights. For bp, our initial transformation effort mapped how key datasets interact with each other in the reliability ecosystem. Through the connected data network, users have the visibility necessary to identify points of friction, touch points between different business process, and opportunities to engage in cross-team collaboration. Furthermore, this ground-up connectivity and data transparency improved alignment between leadership and front-line engineers and enabled a data-driven approach to delivering business results. Beyond intuition In order to make a difference to the business bottom line, intuition and business knowledge must be paired with data. Partnering with reliability subject matter experts and equipping them with data-driven tooling that sheds light on siloed data powers them in their day-to-day work and has many benefits. First, these experts are able to verify the accuracy, completeness, and relevance of the data. Second, examining insights surfaced by data can spark new ideas and thinking. For example, reviewing historic reliability and operational availability performance data and associated investigations, maintenance, turnaround activities and actions over several years, engineers can assess potential future impacts. Third, by automating trusted data preparation, engineers spend far less time collecting and manipulating data and more time on analytics. The benefits of bringing together reliability subject matter experts with Foundry to generate business-influencing insights are evident in our use case with bpSolutions’ reliability discipline. We brought together bp engineers from both the central and regional teams to ask them for their perspectives and data needs. Once we provided greater visibility into the data via the Foundry platform, they proposed unique solutions to improve their day-to-day analytics efforts and opportunities to improve data quality emerged. This connected data network was built to scale and to enable a multitude of use cases simultaneously. It has freed up engineers to get more involved in decision making, resulting in positive business impact. This is just the start of bp’s digital transformation journey. We are currently working to extend the model to enable more business processes — from tracking reliability investigations coverage to identifying bad actors that may lead to production losses. In summary, we hope this partnership reflection promotes understanding of where and how best to start a digital transformation journey in a complex global organization. It underscores our key takeaways: that data is a valuable asset and plays a key role in providing business insight across business processes. Palantir’s platform promotes cross-team collaboration. It enables a centralized and consistently built operational picture to bring leadership and front-line users closer to delivery of common goals and enhances day to day decision making. Additional information about the areas where Palantir and bp work together, including on strategic digitization and net zero efforts, can be found in this press release.

title: Broadening our Bug Bounty Program: Trust, Security, and Transparency
description: We’re expanding our public bug bounty program for Palantir’s software and infrastructure.
author: Palantir
body: Broadening our Bug Bounty Program: Trust, Security, and Transparency Security, privacy, transparency, and customer trust are pillars of our culture and business disposition. Continuing our investment in these values, we are excited to announce the expansion of our public bug bounty program for Palantir’s software and infrastructure. We are partnering with HackerOne to encourage security professionals around the world to help us maintain the highest standard of security and privacy for our users and their data. Effective today, our HackerOne bug bounty program will handle all reports for any security issue or defect on Palantir-operated infrastructure or applications. As the year progresses, we plan to invite members of the HackerOne platform to private programs that will grant them authenticated access to Palantir Foundry and Palantir Apollo for responsible security testing. We are adding new commitments to our disclosure policies and re-affirming others: Publicly disclosing and publishing common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) for all material security defects identified in our supported software products. We will endeavor to publicly disclose issues no more than 30 days after an issue has been identified, fixed, and communicated to our customers. Publicly disclosing all reported and resolved HackerOne security reports for our infrastructure or products. Maintaining the highest degree of transparency and communication regarding any material security issues or incidents that may adversely impact Palantir, our customers, or their data. Continuing our deep investment and innovation in security and privacy controls within our products, our organization, and partnership with the broader industry. During these times of heightened global turmoil and insecurity, our customers rely on our software products more than ever. We are up to the challenge. To learn about Palantir’s InfoSec team, visit our website or view our open positions.

title: Palantir et la Souveraineté Numérique en France
description: Préserver l’autonomie dans un monde en mutation
author: Palantir
body: Palantir et la Souveraineté Numérique en France Préserver l’autonomie dans un monde en mutation (Scroll down for English translation below) Les données sont l’un des moteurs sous-jacents de nos sociétés. Véritables réseaux interconnectés, nos vies privées et professionnelles sont de plus en plus innervées par la donnée et déterminées par des modèles économiques qui en tirent parti. L’évolution vers une société reposant plus sur le numérique a certes libéré l’innovation, mais également rendu le progrès indissociable d’un traitement rapide, efficace et responsable des données. Cette accélération nécessite plus que jamais un accès à des technologies numériques immédiatement déployables, sécurisées et fiables. Ce progrès technologique doit toutefois se réaliser avec un contrôle strict de la donnée. Palantir est au service de cette nécessité. Aux quatre coins du monde, des organisations parmi les plus sensibles et stratégiques, utilisent nos plateformes logicielles pour traiter leur données. Si ces organisations font confiance à Palantir, c’est parce que nos plateformes accélèrent les mécanismes de prise de décision de la façon la plus rapide et sécurisée qui soit. Dans ce post, nous partageons notre définition de la souveraineté numérique, et expliquons pourquoi ce sujet est au cœur de nos préoccupations. Nous détaillons également les investissements réalisés par Palantir pour permettre à nos clients de répondre aux nouvelles exigences réglementaires et aux défis d’un monde en mutation. La souveraineté numérique Depuis sa création, Palantir développe des solutions logicielles qui aident nos clients à relever certains des défis les plus importants de notre époque : de l’accélération d’une campagne de vaccination à la lutte contre la faim dans le monde, en passant par l’avenir des mobilités décarbonnées et la transformation numérique d’un des fleurons de l’industrie française. Ces défis, existentiels pour nos clients et leurs bénéficiaires, exigent la plus grande résilience en temps de crise. Ces acteurs publics et privés sont dépendants du traitement efficace et responsable de leurs données, et doivent parvenir à utiliser des outils numériques éprouvés tout en gardant le contrôle de leurs données et de leurs décisions. Notre mission en tant qu’éditeur de logiciels est précisément de leur fournir ces outils. C’est ici que la notion de souveraineté numérique est à prendre en compte. Bien que souvent utilisée dans le débat public, cette notion peut parfois rester vague. Certains pensent que souveraineté implique autarcie et que seules des technologies domestiques peuvent être utilisées pour traiter des données sensibles. Tenir une telle position est illusoire. Qu’elles soient numériques ou non, aujourd’hui les technologies s’inspirent ou dépendent de briques souvent développées ailleurs. Se priver d’innovations au motif qu’elles ne seraient pas purement hexagonales serait une erreur lorsqu’il s’agit de répondre à des défis comme ceux cités plus haut, parfois critiques pour nos clients et leurs bénéficiaires. En effet, la souveraineté est la capacité d’agir de façon autonome, et notre entreprise a été fondée sur la conviction que cette capacité est de plus en plus dépendante de l’aptitude à analyser et traiter des données à grande échelle. Toutefois, pour agir en autonomie dans un monde numérique, les entités souveraines doivent constamment garder le contrôle sur leurs données et les décisions prises sur la base de ces dernières. Ainsi, chez Palantir, nous pensons que la souveraineté numérique conduit à mettre en capacité des institutions publiques et privées dans l’utilisation des meilleures technologies disponibles aujourd’hui et ainsi rester performantes demain, tout en gardant le contrôle total sur leurs données et leurs décisions. L’autonomie d’action stratégique L’autonomie d’action de nos clients a toujours été au cœur de l’ADN de nos solutions technologiques. L’intégration et l’analyse des données dans nos plateformes ne sont pas pour nous une fin en soi, mais un moyen pour nos clients de tirer plus rapidement des enseignements de leurs données, puis de les traduire en solutions de problèmes objectifs. Faciliter la prise de décision de nos clients sur la base d’un paysage de données harmonisées et leur permettre ainsi d’agir plus rapidement est au cœur de notre modèle économique et de notre succès. Palantir ne collecte pas, n’analyse pas ni ne vend les données de ses clients pour son propre compte. De même nous n’exerçons aucune influence sur leurs décisions opérationnelles. Notre objectif est de fournir à nos clients un système d’exploitation dont ils ont la maitrise. En effet, contrairement à de nombreuses autres entreprises technologiques, Palantir ne fait pas concurrence à ses clients. Nous fournissons aux organisations les plateformes dont elles ont besoin pour traiter leurs propres données conformément à leurs propres règles et objectifs. Les outils de protection des données et de sécurité intégrés à nos logiciels permettent non seulement la mise en place d’un environnement de confiance, mais également de vérifier en permanence que leurs données sont sécurisées, disponibles et fiables au moment où ils en ont le plus besoin. Un monde en mutation Nous vivons une époque de changements constants. Du Brexit à Schrems II, nos clients sont confrontés à un risque de changement soudain. Le paysage politique et réglementaire de plus en plus fragmenté menace la capacité d’action de nos clients. C’est pourquoi, il est crucial face à un moment d’incertitude globale croissant, de préserver l’autonomie d’agir localement. Palantir, en tant qu’éditeur de logiciel-service (“SaaS”) permet à ses clients de traiter leurs données les plus sensibles à l’intérieur de leurs propres frontières, que cela soit aux États-Unis pour les clients américains, au Royaume-Uni pour les clients britanniques ou dans l’Union Européenne pour les européens. Ainsi, pour un client européen, cela signifie que toutes les données intégrées dans une plateforme Palantir seront strictement hébergées au sein de l’Union Européenne et ne subiront en aucun cas de transfert en dehors des frontières de l’UE. Garantir que les données ne quittent jamais l’UE a un coût financier — l’opération nécessite des investissements en matériel et en hébergement considérables — et technique — cela implique de faire travailler les équipes produits en continu pour assurer que la localisation intra-UE ne soit pas synonyme de compromis technologique. Cet important investissement de Palantir est nécessaire, car il permet d’offrir à nos clients la certitude qu’ils gardent, lorsqu’ils utilisent nos technologies, le contrôle total et intégral de leurs données et de leurs processus de prise de décisions. Ils conservent ainsi leur capacité à agir de manière indépendante, quelles que soient les perturbations politiques, réglementaires et techniques à venir. Encore une fois, Palantir ne collecte, ne distribue ni ne vend de données personnelles, sous quelque forme que ce soit. Notre objectif est de permettre à nos clients de mieux utiliser les données dont ils disposent et notre intérêt est qu’ils puissent continuer à utiliser nos solutions quelles que soient les évolutions du cadre juridique. En ce sens, Palantir confirme être l’anti-GAFA à l’heure où certaines entreprises technologiques font courir un risque à leurs clients et préfèrent exercer une pression sur le régulateur afin de continuer à transférer des données personnelles de citoyens européens vers les États-Unis. De la souveraineté numérique en France La stratégie nationale du numérique a connu un coup d’accélérateur sous l’impulsion présidentielle : La French Tech est en plein essor et les levées de fonds des startups françaises en 2021 devraient battre largement le niveau record atteint en 2020 ; l’excellence française en mathématiques garantit à la France une production locale des très stratégiques algorithmes ; un plan industriel de soutien à la filière Cloud française complète la stratégie nationale annoncée en mai 2021, etc. Combinées, ces actions permettent à la France de garantir sa souveraineté numérique sur les “briques les plus sensibles” : applications, algorithmes, infrastructures et protection cyber. C’est en associant ces briques les plus sensibles à des solutions technologiques éprouvées (étrangères lorsqu’elles n’ont pas d’équivalent hexagonal), labellisées aux exigences de souveraineté, et dont le traitement des données n’implique pas de transfert en dehors de l’UE, que la France pourra se doter rapidement des moyens nécessaires pour atteindre ses objectifs, voire les dépasser, notamment ceux de France 2030. Auteur Hugo Dobbelaere, Directeur Technique, Protection des Données et Éthique, Palantir France Palantir and Digital Sovereignty in France: Preserving Autonomy in an Ever-Changing World Data is the driving force of our society. True interconnected networks, our private and professional lives are increasingly dependent upon the ability to process data at scale. The move toward a more digital society has unleashed innovation, but also made progress inseparable from fast, efficient, and responsible data processing. This acceleration depends more than ever on access to immediately deployable, secure, and reliable digital technologies. Such technological progress requires strict data control. Palantir is committed to meeting this need. Around the world, some of the most sensitive and strategic organizations use our software to process their data. These organizations trust Palantir because our platforms accelerate decision making processes in the fastest and most secure way possible. In this blog post, we share our definition of digital sovereignty and explain why this subject is at the heart of what we do. We also highlight the investments Palantir is making to enable our customers to meet new regulatory requirements and the challenges of a changing world. Digital sovereignty Since its inception, Palantir has developed software solutions to help our customers meet some of the most important challenges of our time: from accelerating a vaccination campaign, to fighting world hunger, to working with one of France’s biggest aviation companies to shape the future of carbon-free mobility. These challenges require our customers to be resilient in times of crisis. These public and private actors depend on the efficient and responsible processing of their data, and must be able to use proven digital tools while maintaining control over their data and decisions. Our explicit mission as a software company is to provide them with these tools. It is here that the notion of digital sovereignty must be taken into account. Although often used in public debate, the notion of ‘digital sovereignty’ can be vague. Some believe that sovereignty implies autarky and that only domestic technologies can be used to process sensitive data. Holding such a position is illusory. Whether digital or not, today’s technology draws inspiration or even concrete components, from existing technologies developed elsewhere. To deprive ourselves of innovations on the grounds that they are not purely French would be a mistake when it comes to meeting the challenges mentioned above, which can be critical for our customers. Indeed, sovereignty is the ability to act autonomously, and our company was founded on the belief that this ability is increasingly dependent on the ability to analyze and process large-scale data. But in order to act autonomously in a digital world, sovereign entities must maintain constant control over their data and and decision making. At Palantir, we believe that digital sovereignty empowers public and private institutions to use today’s cutting-edge technology to process data to remain competitive tomorrow — all while retaining full control of their data and decisions. The autonomy to act strategically Helping our customers be more autonomous has always been central to Palantir’s approach to building technology. Integrating and analyzing data in our platforms is not an end in itself, but helps our customers derive insights that can be translated into concrete solutions. Facilitating our customers’ data-driven decision-making and thus enabling them to act more quickly is at the core of our business model and our success. Palantir does not collect, analyze or sell customer data for our own purposes. Nor are we involved in influencing customer decision-making. Our goal is to provide our customers with an operating system for lasting success. Indeed, unlike many other technology companies, Palantir does not compete with its customers. We provide the platforms they need to process their own data in accordance with their own rules and goals. Data protection and security tools integrated into our software enables them to not only trust, but also continuously verify that their data is secure, available, and reliable when they need it. A changing world We live in a time of constant change. From Brexit to Schrems II, our customers are confronted with a constant risk of sudden change. A fragmented political and regulatory landscape threatens our customers’ ability to act. This is why, in the midst of global uncertainty, it is crucial for our customers to retain localized control over their data to maintain their autonomy. Palantir, as a software as a service (SAAS) vendor, enables its customers to process their most sensitive data within their own borders, whether in the United States, the United Kingdom, or the European Union. This means that for all European customers, any data integrated in a Palantir platform (including metadata) will remain hosted within the EU and will never be transferred outside of the EU. Guaranteeing that data will never leave the EU has a big financial cost — it requires investments in hardware and hosting — and technical cost — it requires our product teams to have working hours spread around all timezones, to ensure that this decision doesn’t come at the expense of technological compromise. This significant investment by Palantir is necessary because it helps provide our customers with the certainty that they retain full and complete control over their data and decision making processes when using our technologies. Our customers thus retain full autonomy, regardless of future political, regulatory, and technical disruptions. Again, Palantir does not collect, distribute, or sell personal data in any form. Our goal is to enable our customers to make better use of the data they have so that they can continue to use our technology regardless of changes in the legal framework. Palantir is anti-GAFA at a time when some technology companies are putting their customers at risk and prefer to put pressure on the regulator to continue to transfer personal data of European citizens to the United States. Digital Sovereignty in France The current government has invested a lot in building a national digital strategy: French Tech is booming and fundraising by French startups in 2021 should should exceed the 2020 record; French excellence in mathematics guarantees a local production of highly strategic algorithms; an industrial plan to support the French Cloud sector completes the national strategy announced in May 2021. All combined, these actions allow France to secure its digital sovereignty on the “most sensitive bricks:” applications, algorithms, infrastructures, and cyber security. By combining these “most sensitive bricks” with proven technologies (foreign when there is no French equivalent), certified for use in sovereign domains, and whose data processing does not involve transfer outside of the EU, France will be able to quickly achieve, or even exceed, its ambitious digital goals, including those of France 2030. Author Hugo Dobbelaere, Privacy & Civil Liberties Engineering Lead, Palantir France

title: Palantir Edge AI in Space
description: Designing software for in-orbit data processing
author: Palantir
body: Palantir Edge AI in Space Designing software for in-orbit data processing Editor’s Note: In December 2022, we published an update about our on-orbit imagery processing efforts here. On April 1, 2022, Palantir and Satellogic launched our first Edge AI-enabled satellite into space as part of the SpaceX Transporter 4 mission. Incorporating Palantir’s Edge AI technology onboard Satellogic’s NewSat will allow us to begin processing imagery data on orbit, separating signal from noise in high-scale data to make the best use of limited bandwidth and enabling more opportunities for customers to gain near real-time data at scale. The April launch, part of Satellogic’s previously announced plans for 2022, expands its fleet to 22 satellites delivering high resolution data from space. Satellogic aims to launch a total of 34 commercial satellites to orbit by the first quarter of 2023, offering up to seven daily revisits of any point of interest, with the goal of orbiting more than 200 satellites by 2025. This will provide Satellogic with the capacity to remap the entire Earth daily. The new Edge AI-enabled NewSat is the culmination of a six-month project during which Satellogic adapted its hosted payload program and edge computing hardware to run Palantir’s Edge AI platform. Our joint project delivers new capabilities which will have broad applicability across mission sets in both government and the commercial sector. Overview Use Cases This launch introduces four major technical capabilities that lay a foundation for our larger strategy of Edge AI in space. Reduced Latency and Fast Insight Generation: The primary objective of moving our AI capabilities to the edge (onboard the satellite) is to help increase decision-making speed. Running processing on the ground — especially for high-resolution imagery — introduces latencies that Edge AI can eliminate. Edge AI starts processing data upon capture, delivering actionable insights faster than traditional ground processing. For example, we can inform future data collection onboard (closed loop) or selectively downlink pre-processed images based on their analytical value. Bandwidth Optimization: Traditionally, satellite sensors can capture higher volumes of data than they can currently send down. Edge AI allows us to make AI-driven decisions about which data will be the most valuable to our customers and to adapt to shifting priorities in near real-time. This means satellites can better utilize their sensor capacities to capture larger amounts of data that are most relevant to our customers for making time-sensitive decisions. Lightweight Model Update: A static algorithm on board a satellite can quickly become obsolete as mission requirements change and technologies improve. Enabling continuous algorithm update in-flight makes the asset adaptable to constantly changing priorities and operating environments. This is why our Edge AI-enabled NewSat has built-in mechanisms to update onboard models and software throughout the lifespan of the satellite. (See below for more on our upgrade infrastructure.) Third-Party Vendor Hot Swaps: We believe that the most capable Edge AI deployments need to manage and deploy algorithms from multiple vendors. On board the NewSat there are Palantir object and cloud detection models, a Xailient ship detector model, a MindFoundry image segmentation model, and a Pilot.ai multi-class detection model. We are able to hot-swap between models and chain capabilities, depending on mission requirements and terrain. For example, when the satellite passes over a port we can run the cloud detector, image segmentation, and ship detector models, and when passing over a town we can switch to vehicle and building detectors. Satellite Architecture Satellogic designs and builds every component of its satellites (i.e., cameras, onboard computers, power subsystem, sensors and actuators, optics, radios, and propulsion systems). Each spacecraft carries both a sub-meter multispectral camera and a 29-band hyperspectral camera, and includes an additional bay for proprietary or third-party payloads. This approach provides a massive cost advantage and enables shorter R&D cycles to scale and iterate more efficiently. For compute purposes, we optimized our software for NVIDIA’s Jetson Platform which runs within Satellogic’s payload system. Satellogic’s network of ground stations will be used for communication with the Satellite and the onboard Edge AI system. Fig. 1 Overview of the Satellogic hosted payload bay and edge computing hardware (from Satellogic) A Unique Deployment Environment Deploying Edge AI on Satellogic’s NewSat platform introduced a host of new challenges, including: Limited Compute and Random Restarts: It’s true: working in space is hard. In satellite operating environments, power is a scarce and finite resource. We carefully ration power between the Edge AI system and the satellite’s imaging and communications hardware. Practically speaking, the Edge AI system has only minutes of runtime on board the Jetson TX-2i. Changes to the satellite’s orbital trajectory and assigned capture tasks can further reduce this runtime, requiring our software to have increased fault tolerance. Novel Raw Imagery Input: The raw imagery presents a unique challenge for models. An image consists of four different types of data in a single channel: Near Infrared (NIR), Red, Green, and Blue light (Red, Green, and Blue light are collectively referred to as “RGB”). Most computer vision models for image processing are typically designed for three-channel RGB imagery. Model performance degrades severely when dealing with raw L0 data.
