The same hourly message will also be sent to the user’s email for redundancy. The user’s lead / supervisor will also receive the same hourly message. If / when a user changes their password, they’ll stop receiving notifications. If the user fails to change their password within 72 hours of the alert, their account will be locked. Following the full 72-hour lifecycle of a PhishCatch alert, a given user will need to have their account manually re-activated by Palantir’s support staff. Detecting Unusual Behavior Even if an alerting primitive doesn’t fall cleanly under a certain category of attack methods, we continue to author ad hoc alerting & detection strategies for any activity that could present risk to Palantir if performed by a party with malicious intent. To address such activity, the CIRT authors alerting & detection as follows: Attack Summary: The CIRT’s alerting & detection strategies have identified an ad hoc action that isn’t necessarily categorized as an explicit attack attempt, but is a suspicious or sensitive enough action that the user should be consulted regarding the activity. Detection Strategy: While the scope of the CIRT’s alerting & detection coverage is ever-growing, the following list represents a general picture of activity that we’d consider suspicious or sensitive enough to raise with a user: User enrolls a new device via mobile device management. User enrolls a new multi-factor authentication device. User logs in to high-risk infrastructure (e.g. VDI). User has account locked or marked as high-risk. Response: An InfoSecBot direct message notification is issued to the user whenever in-scope activity is detected. The alert payload presented includes: A summary of the activity itself. A timestamp of the activity. A brief description of why the activity could be concerning. In the event that the activity is unexpected or unusual, the user is given instructions on how to quickly surface it to the CIRT. Detecting Post-Exploitation While InfoSec teams should endeavor to never have an attacker reach the stage of post-exploitation, it’d be negligent to discount it as a possibility. A healthy alerting & detection posture should cover the entirety of the attack lifecycle, and consulting users regarding on-system activity can be a valuable tool in reconciling late-stage lifecycle alerting with its respective root cause. The following alerting & detecting strategies represent a sampling of Palantir’s user-centric alerting around post-exploitation activity. Detecting Post Exploitation: Data Movement or Staging To/From a Sensitive Destination Attack Summary: An attacker, who is already operating within the environment using a compromised account, uses the account to stage (i.e., archive, compress, or encrypt) or move/transfer data. Detection Strategy: In the event that an anomalous data movement, archiving, or encrypting operation occurs via a user account, endpoint logging telemetry will record the activity in question. The CIRT’s alerting logic will query the aforementioned logging telemetry to surface the activity in question. Response: When a user account is found to be interacting with data in a manner in-scope for the alert, the user will receive an InfoSecBot prompt containing the following: A timestamp of the activity. The system(s) on which the activity took place. A summary of the data interaction in question. The user in question must affirmatively respond to the InfoSecBot message prompt, and must additionally confirm an MFA prompt from InfoSecBot. If the user fails to complete the prompt / MFA, the alert will be escalated to the CIRT. Detecting Post Exploitation: Host-Based Reconnaissance or Scanning Attack Summary: An attacker operating on a given user’s endpoint, or operating on any endpoint using a given user’s account, may attempt to run discovery/reconnaissance commands in an effort to ascertain further details about our environment’s attack surface. Detection Strategy: The CIRT queries EDR logging telemetry for activity or commands that could be construed as reconnaissance, or for any commands consistent with discovery or port scanning (e.g., nmap). Response: When such activity is detected from a user’s account, or from a user’s workstation, that user will receive an InfoSecBot prompt detailing: The specific commands run from their account or workstation. A timestamp of the activity. The system(s) on which the activity took place. The user in question must affirmatively respond to the InfoSecBot message prompt, and must additionally confirm an MFA prompt from InfoSecBot. If the user fails to complete the prompt / MFA, the alert will be escalated to the CIRT. Crowdsourcing Appropriate Usage While the majority of InfoSecBot prompts are sent to a specific individual, there are some cases where it makes more sense to message a broader group. Consider the following factors: If an attacker has taken over an account, they could possibly take action to mute, delete, or otherwise conceal Slack messages sent to the taken-over account, which could obstruct the legitimate account owner from seeing the message. In an insider threat scenario, a given user would be well aware of their own actions; Slack messages to the user would provide no security benefit. Teams of coworkers, including the leader(s) of said teams, often have a general awareness of actions taken by team members. In recognition of the factors above, Palantir’s CIRT has found it prudent to target some InfoSecBot prompts towards Slack rooms, rather than individuals. Generally speaking, the target room is the dedicated / centralized channel for communications with a given team; consequently, all members of the team (including the leader(s)) are present in the channel. Additionally, channel membership is backed by group membership in Palantir’s IDP, and members will be automatically re-added to the channel in the event that they’re removed for any reason. For a crowdsourced alert, Palantir’s approach generally observes the follow practices: The alert will generally reflect privileged activities against sensitive, collective resources. e.g., SSHing to backend server using a breakglass credentials. The InfoSecBot notification will generally contain the full context of a user’s activity e.g., who took the action, what action they took, timestamp, etc. The alert will message the channel containing the entirety of the actor’s team. In the event that the activity is inconsistent with the actor’s work expectations, the actor’s team has instructions to escalate the matter to the CIRT. Other Miscellaneous Security Use Cases While InfoSecBot provides immense value in the context of security alerting & detection, there are other ad hoc cases in which InfoSecBot has been a valuable communication tool. For example: Software Compliance Palantir maintains a stringent list of approved & unapproved software for endpoint workstations. In cases where a user installs a product inconsistent with our security standards, InfoSecBot will notify them of the infraction, and they’ll be allowed a brief grace period to remove the offending content before a member of the InfoSec team intervenes. Additionally, Palantir also maintains an inventory of software versions on user workstations. In the event that a Palantir user’s workstation contains a software version with a known vulnerability, InfoSecBot will prompt that user to update their software. The user will have a brief grace period to update their software before the matter is escalated to Palantir’s InfoSec team. Emergency Patching In cases of high or critical severity CVEs which necessitate an immediate software patch or operating system update, Palantir’s security engineers have utilized InfoSecBot to notify users that their system may experience imminent downtime for updates. Users receive notifications through other means as well, but InfoSecBot provides an additional layer of communication redundancy to ensure that users aren’t caught by surprise for emergency patching. Further Reading and Acknowledgements Alerting and Detection Strategy Framework | by Palantir | Palantir Blog Distributed Security Alerting — Slack Engineering Meet Securitybot: Open Sourcing Automated Security at Scale — Dropbox

title: The Benefits of Remote Ephemeral Workspaces
description: Palantir's DevOps team explores how to best to combine the benefits of ephemeral infrastructure with the benefits of remote workspaces.
author: Palantir
body: Palantirtech DevOps Developers Remoteworkspaces Palantirengineering The Benefits of Remote Ephemeral Workspaces Palantir 9 min read · Jun 6, 2022 -- 2 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size As one of the DevOps teams at Palantir, we are always looking for new ways to improve the productivity of our developers. We recently decided to explore how remote workspaces — including AWS EC2 instances, AWS Cloud9, or dedicated machines — could be beneficial. There are lots of articles about the benefits of remote workspaces, like this one , this one , this one , this one , this one , or this one (and many more!). At Palantir, we took this paradigm one step further and used an ephemeral remote workspace model to improve local build times, make developers more productive, and reduce onboarding costs. And we did all this without breaking the bank! Complexities of an Enterprise Environment While the referenced articles emphasize the many benefits of remote development, we feel there are additional complexities of a large enterprise environment, particularly as they relate to performance efficiency, standardization, and optimizing for operational efficiency. Complexities to be considered include: Performance Efficiency Building large complex software products requires heavy compute resources (e.g., GPUs for ML training, increased RAM for tests and build), forcing developers to consider alternatives beyond laptops such as desktop towers, racked servers, or spawning a VM. Standardization Delivering development infrastructure to large organizations at scale without sacrificing development speed requires standardized offerings to help reduce operation and maintenance (O&M) burden. As development environment recommendations change, the configuration drift causes increased support burden, resulting in developers consistently running into the “works on my machine” syndrome. Providing environments that more closely represent how code is running on production, from system libraries (e.g., specific Python version) to deployment models (e.g., Docker containers). Optimization for Operational Efficiency Hiring and onboarding new people in a complex environment can be frustrating and requires time to initially configure. A given employee will be potentially going in and out of multiple development environments. They may need to work in different types of repos (front-end vs back-end) or have different competing requirements (i.e., different Java versions). This can contribute to significant overhead costs as they work through different requirements. You have to control your development costs. If your costs are growing faster than the benefits you’re providing, you’re probably not going to be a company for very long. Solving for Complexity At Palantir, we are big believers in ephemeral infrastructure and use this pattern in many of our production environments to address different challenges. (Check out this blog post on our Rubix platform or this one on Active Directory for how and why). For maximum impact and lower operational burden, we knew that if we could combine the benefits of ephemeral infrastructure with the benefits of remote workspaces, we could unlock a new level of productivity for the company. Some Options Before jumping all the way into our solution, let’s go over some potential options. Get people more capable laptops. This addresses the lack of compute but does not help organizations scale with cost. With so many working from home and recent supply chain issues, getting more capable laptops can also be logistically complicated. Have people provision their own VMs in the cloud. Palantir already has an internal service for people to self-service virtual machines (VMs) so this approach would allow us to leverage an existing capability. While some developers had already started using the remote development model on their own, this option requires a lot of configuration overhead per developer and can still lead to configuration issues and “works on my (other) machine” syndrome. Get people pre-configured VMs. While this option means developers would have to manage less, there would be a heavier burden on the infrastructure team (us) to make sure pre-configured VMs were patched, updated, and available when the developer needed them. This kind of overhead is something we were hoping to avoid and fortunately there are a few services in this space such as Amazon Workspaces and Google Virtual Desktops that provide a good starting point. Offload the management of some infrastructure. Offload portions of the infrastructure to a SaaS provider like GitHub Codespaces or something else to run on a container farm on Kubernetes. This lowers developer overhead while reducing the need for the infrastructure team (us again) to manage individuals. We wanted to avoid building our own product since we would have to worry about automating features like turning on a new workspaces, auto-updating containers, and SSH key management. After exploring all of the above options, we eventually settled on using Coder on top of Amazon’s Elastic Kubernetes Service ( EKS ) as it met the broader needs of our developers (at the time of writing this blog). What Excited Us About Coder Operational Wins: It works on top of Kubernetes for the compute layer. When combined with Amazon EKS we could minimize the overhead for our team. Standardization with Flexibility: Coder allows the user to have custom dotfiles and startup scripts. Developers have spent years optimizing their flow and this gives them the customization layer that they need to keep the environment feeling familiar. Developer Empowerment: Self service access for provisioning more resources. With a few clicks, developers can deploy new environments, request more resources, and get to work faster. Ecosystem Integration : It integrates natively with GitHub Enterprise. Users can easily clone repos and manage their own SSH setup. Coupled with self-service access features, such integrations eliminated a lot of the potential transactional support from our team. But Does It Really Work? After deploying the infrastructure, we knew our next most important goal was proving to developers that remote workspaces would greatly improve their lives. To do this, we partnered closely with our product development teams to ensure: Latency and user experience was seamless Development containers accurately represented the environment User guides were created for each code base Below are some of the benefits we got once we had deployed: Faster development cycles (including it here again because of how big of a deal this is). Developers can get more CPU/RAM with the push of a button. This sped up the entire develop → build → test process across the board. For example front-end build, build times improved 78%! Faster download times. Since the workspaces live right next to our code repository and artifact servers, download times and request latency are very low. For an example repository, this improved git clone times by 71%. While we expected faster development cycles in general, this was an unintended benefit. Reduced onboarding and support . The dedicated development infrastructure teams began advocating for users to switch to Coder. They were able to onboard new users faster and had to debug fewer issues on people’s local machines. This meant they could focus more time on optimizing the developer tooling. Increased external contributions. With an easier path to development environments, teams can easily contribute to each other’s codebases. This was especially useful for our engineers working directly with customers. The overhead for fixing small bugs was just requesting a workspace instead of downloading all of the product dependencies. Better local laptop experience. With many demanding parts of the developer workflows offloaded, people are seeing better performance on their local machine. No longer are we hearing “I can’t share my screen because my server is running!” Remote Docker environments . Some developers used the increased resources to create a hybrid environment. They did some of their development locally and ran docker and test servers remotely. We expected people to move all of their development over to their new workspace, but this showed that a hybrid approach was possible as well. Faster Development Cycles Deep Dive In this section, we offer some concrete examples of the improvements we saw. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in For context, in this test we used a Foundry repository to build the front-end. The repository uses a mono-repo concept and heavily uses git-lfs, is ~4.5 GB in size. Press enter or click to view image in full size These speed benefits speak for themselves. While smaller repositories saw improvements as well, this one highlights just how much faster things got. Research shows that it can take up to 20 minutes to get back into a state of flow , which is critical to staying productive. With hundreds of developers, that adds up to hundreds of hours of lost productivity every day. Whatever we can do to keep developers in the flow is a win for the whole organization. Cost Considerations Another important aspect to consider is cost. After all, giving developer’s infinite compute power would probably cost a lot of money. While we didn’t expect this project to reduce costs overall, we needed to make sure that we weren’t breaking the bank during our rollout. Let’s take a look at a quick cost breakdown. Macbooks. At Palantir, we replace a developer’s laptop roughly every two years. Most developers use a Macbook. For the standard developer today, we provide a 32GB M1 Macbook which costs roughly $2900. Spread that across two years, and that comes out to roughly $1500 per developer per year. EC2 Instances. For the a new world with remote ephemeral workspaces, the cost considerations are slightly different. Rather than buying a beefy Macbook, we would instead buy a standard M1 Macbook, which comes in at roughly $2000. This would bring the laptop cost per developer down to $1000 per year but we still need to account for the new EC2 costs. Most of our developers need more RAM, so we’ve decided to use r5.4xlarge instance types in Amazon. As of this writing, an r5.4xlarge costs $1.008 per hour. This comes out to $8830 per year. From here, we can make a few optimizations that most people won’t notice. Optimization 1 — On this instance type, we can very comfortably fit three developers. This takes advantage of the containerization architecture. Optimization 2 — We don’t need to have the instances on during the weekends. This means on average, we’re only paying for 5 out of 7 days. As long as we have automation that allows users to easily spin up during weekend hours, we’ll save good money here. Optimization 3 — We don’t need to have the instances on 24 hours a day. Most developers work in a 12-hour window relative to their region, so we can turn these machines off during off hours. We can use similar automation to above to make sure developers are never blocked. Press enter or click to view image in full size The differential is roughly a 41% increase in overall costs. However, there are other cost optimizations that could be considered: some developers will use smaller remote workspaces; some will not work a full 12 hours; and some developers don’t do development every day. For Palantir, this cost increase is more than offset by the productivity of our developers and better Operations & Maintenance (O&M) for us! Ultimately, it is up to your organization to decide if the cost trade off is worthwhile, but it certainly was for us. Where We’re Going We’re pretty excited about what we’ve been able to accomplish so far and we are seeing usage numbers increase as more developers find out about our new offering. Currently, we are seeing the most traction with our front-end repositories. These repositories are large and most developers are already using VSCode , which offers great support for remote development and has gotten good feedback from our developers. For our Java projects, we are testing other IDEs to ensure it provides a high quality experience for our developers. We continue to see improvements and hope to roll out ephemeral remote workspaces out more broadly soon. Conclusion Our experience reaffirmed remote developer environments as a great way to increase developer productivity. More importantly, applying ephemeral infrastructure paradigms is a sustainable and cost-effective way to manage these high-value investments. If you want to help us build this future and drive other important outcomes, please come join us! Author Ashir

title: Ein Tag im Leben eines Palantir Deployment Strategists
description: Im folgenden geben uns drei Deployment Strategists, die bei Palantir in Deutschland arbeiten, einen kurzen Einblick.
author: Palantir
body: Palantir Deutschland Palantir Palantirglobal Ein Tag im Leben eines Palantir Deployment Strategists Palantir 9 min read · Jun 9, 2022 -- Share Press enter or click to view image in full size (An English-language version of this post can be read here .) Eine der interessantesten, wenn auch potenziell verwirrendsten, Rollen bei Palantir ist die des Deployment Strategists, intern als “Echo” bezeichnet. Bei Palantir helfen wir Unternehmen, ihre Daten besser zu nutzen, um ein tiefes Verständnis für ihr Geschäft zu erlangen und einen digitalen Zwilling ihrer Abläufe aufzubauen. Wir entwerfen, konfigurieren und implementieren innovative Arbeitsabläufe und Anwendungen in enger Zusammenarbeit mit unseren Kunden, um deren schwierigste Probleme zu lösen. In einem typischen Kundenprojekt findet man sowohl Deployment Strategists als auch Forward-Deployed Engineers (allgemein als “Deltas” bezeichnet). Theoretisch haben Echos ihren Hintergrund eher im Produktmanagement und Deltas im Bereich Engineering, aber in der Realität beinhalten beide Rollen eine Mischung aus Produktmanagement, Software Engineering und Strategie, und die Grenzen sind im Allgemeinen fließend. In diesem Beitrag befassen wir uns mit der einzigartigen Rolle des Deployment Strategists. Die Palette der Deployment Strategists reicht von Palantirians, die den ganzen Tag programmieren und nur selten mit Kunden sprechen, bis hin zu Palantirians, die nie mit Code in Berührung kommen, dafür dann mehrere Projekte intern und extern gleichzeitig koordinieren und betreuen. Mit anderen Worten, es ist ein ziemlich breites Spektrum, und kein Deployment Strategist ist wie der oder die Andere. In einer eher traditionellen Projektumgebung konzentrieren sich Deployment Strategists auf Aufgaben wie: Verstehen der Arbeitsabläufe des Kunden und Herausfinden, wo Palantir-Software den größten Impact haben kann Entwerfen und Implementieren von benutzerorientierten Arbeitsabläufen und Anwendungen, um Probleme oder Lücken in bestehenden Systemen zu schließen Schnelles Iterieren mit den Nutzenden, um sicherzustellen, dass die Lösung ihren geschäftlichen Anforderungen gerecht wird und in ihre Arbeitsabläufe passt Implementierung und Skalierung der entwickelten Lösungen Pflege und weiterer Ausbau von Kundenbeziehungen Internes und externes Projektmanagement (z.B. mit Hinblick auf Ressourcen, Leistung, Zeitablauf,…) Vertretung von Palantir in der Führungsebene des Kunden Diese Liste geht noch weiter… Persönliche Einblicke Bei so vielen Prioritäten fragt man sich vielleicht: Wie sieht ein Tag im Leben unserer Deployment Strategists aus? Glücklicherweise gibt es nur wenige langweilige Momente, denn die Aufgaben sind sehr abwechslungsreich. Im folgenden geben uns drei Deployment Strategists, die bei Palantir in Deutschland arbeiten, einen kurzen Einblick. Der Alltag als Pilotprojekt-Leiterin Ich persönlich arbeite derzeit an einem Pilotprojekt für ein großes Drogerieunternehmen in den USA, obwohl ich in Deutschland wohne. Wir arbeiten gemeinsam mit dem Kunden an der Entwicklung verschiedener Arbeitsabläufe, die darauf abzielen, einen besseren Einblick in das bestehende Geschäft zu schaffen und bestimmte Prozesse zu automatisieren. Das Ziel ist, den Beschäftigten die Zeit, Informationsgrundlage und das Vertrauen zu verschaffen, sich auf die Herausforderungen konzentrieren zu können, die tatsächlich auch menschliche Expertise erfordern. Im Folgenden teile ich einige persönliche Einblicke in einen typischen Tag für mich und zwei meiner Kollegen. Einer von ihnen leitet ein etablierteres Projekt und entwickelt sich zu einem Branchenexperten in diesem Bereich, während die andere an der Schnittstelle zwischen eingebetteten und internen Entwicklungsteams arbeitet und die Lücke zwischen dem, was unsere Produkte bereits können, und dem, was im Feld benötigt wird, schließt. Und ja, wir haben alle die gleiche Berufsbezeichnung! Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in 09:00 Uhr — Ich bereite mich auf den Tag vor: Ich rekapituliere die allgemeinen Ziele meines Projekts, die Wünsche und Bedürfnisse des Kunden und den aktuellen Stand der Dinge und priorisiere die To-Dos des Tages für mein Team (dies geschieht häufig beim Joggen und/oder bei einer starken Tasse Kaffee) 10:00 Uhr — Tägliches Stand-up: Ich möchte sicherstellen, dass alle auf derselben Seite stehen, wissen, woran sie arbeiten und warum, und dass es keine Stolpersteine gibt 10:15 Uhr — Fortsetzung der Arbeit an einer Datenpipeline zur Integration des ERP-Kunden-Systems in eine Anwendung, die automatisch Unstimmigkeiten bei Sendungen auflöst 12:30 Uhr — Mittagessen — je nach Standort geht es in die Kantine, nach draußen oder wir lassen uns Essen ins Büro liefern, um uns über unsere jeweiligen Kundenprojekte auszutauschen (die Bandbreite der Arbeit ist groß und es gibt oft interessante Synergien) 13:30 Uhr — Iteration mit dem Kunden, um die morgendlichen Fortschritte zu zeigen. Ich erfahre mehr über momentane Herausforderungen, bekomme Feedback und rege das Experimentieren mit neuen Funktionen an, von denen kundenseitig bisher angenommen wurde, dass sie “noch nicht möglich” seien 14:30 Uhr — Ein sogenannter “Random Sync,” also ein zufällig generierter Termin mit jemandem bei Palantir, um sicherzustellen, dass ich immer neue Leute treffe, die an ähnlichen oder auch völlig anderen Dingen arbeiten als ich 14:50 Uhr — Ich arbeite an etwas, das mich außerhalb meiner Projektwelt begeistert (derzeit zum Beispiel Foundry for Builders, Palantirs Angebot für Start-ups, weil ich es inspirierend finde, zu sehen, was unsere Software in den Händen von Gründerinnen und Gründern bewirken kann) 17:30 Uhr — Vorbereitung von Materialien für eine bevorstehende Projektpräsentation an leitende Kundenkontakte in der Interessenvertretung, Festlegung einer internen Generalprobe und ein schnelles Update zum Stand der Dinge über Slack an Palantirians, die zwar am selben Projekt, aber am anderen Ende der Welt arbeiten und daher gerade erst aufwachen Der Alltag als Enterprise Projekt-Leiter 08:00 Uhr — Frühstück über Emails 09:00 Uhr — Ausarbeitung von Materialien für eine Best-Practice-Sitzung mit dem digitalen Büro eines unserer wichtigsten Kunden. Es geht darum, Organisationsstrukturen aufzubauen, die die Eigenverantwortung für die Wertschöpfung in Foundry erhöhen 10:00 Uhr — Teilnahme an einem Pre-Sales-Meeting mit einer Branchendirektorin, bei der wir die Angebote von Palantir vorstellen und eine mögliche Partnerschaft besprechen 11:00 Uhr — Meeting mit einem meiner technischen Teammitglieder; Besprechung der letzten Wochen, der Wachstumskurve und der Pläne fürs Wochenende 11:30 Uhr — Treffen mit unserem Leiter des kaufmännischen Bereichs, um ein Partnerschaftsangebot mit einem großen Versorgungsunternehmen zu besprechen 12:15 Uhr — Mittagessen mit einer meiner Mentees, die gerade bei Palantir angefangen hat. Wir sprechen darüber, wie man sich im Unternehmen zurechtfindet, und ich bringe sie mit einem Kollegen aus dem Londoner Büro auf einen Kaffee zusammen 13:00 Uhr — Debrief des Pre-Sales Meetings, Festlegung von Next Steps und Aufstellung eines Projektplans 14:00 Uhr — Wöchentliche Teambesprechung: Reflexion der vergangenen Woche und Planung der kommenden Woche 15:00 Uhr — Schreiben einer 1-seitigen These, um eine Funktion zu begründen, die seitens der Produktentwicklung in das Kernprodukt integriert werden soll 17:00 Uhr — Erstellung von Marketingmaterial mit einem der Workstream Leads in meinem Team, um die Akzeptanz von Foundry zu erhöhen Der Alltag als Echo für interne Projekte 10:00 Uhr — Ankunft im Büro und Frühstück 10:30 Uhr — E-Mails/Slack abrufen und Pull Requests (PRs) prüfen, die über Nacht eingegangen sind 11:30 Uhr — Arbeitssitzung zur Vorbereitung eines Führungstreffens zu einer neuen Projektinitiative 13:00 Uhr — Ein sogenanntes “Learning Lunch”: Essen bestellen und mit meinen Kollegen zusammensitzen, während wir uns auf die Q1 Foundry Roadshow für dieses Jahr einstimmen 13:30 Uhr — Arbeiten an meinem Code, um Foundry Funktionen zu schreiben, die im Kernprodukt noch nicht vorhanden sind, aber vielen Projektteams im gesamten Unternehmen helfen werden 15:30 Uhr — Slack-Nachricht an den Modeling Tech Lead. Eine Nachricht, die mit “Hey, kurze Frage…” anfängt, mich dann aber unweigerlich spontan in einen ausführlicheren Lernaustausch stürzt 16:00 Uhr — Joggen im Englischen Garten 17:00 Uhr — Treffen mit einem US-Verkaufsteam, um potenzielle Anwendungsfälle für Foundry zur Verbesserung der Verkaufsprozesse zu identifizieren 17:30 Uhr — Treffen mit einem Kundenteam, um Ratschläge zu einem bestimmten Anwendungsfall zu geben 18:30 Uhr — Tägliche Teambesprechung 18:45 Uhr — Überarbeitung des Sensordaten-Pull-Designs mit einer ausgewählten Anzahl von kundenorientierten Teams und dem Haupt-Produktteam Warum diese Rolle Deployment Strategist, oder Echo, zu sein, ist wie die Rolle eines Regenbogens zu übernehmen. Was mich an dieser Position fasziniert, ist die Tatsache, dass man daraus fast alles machen kann, was man will. Als ich nach dem Studium auf der Suche nach einem Job war, war ein wichtiges Kriterium, dass ich immer noch in der Lage sein würde, neue Dinge zu lernen, die mich wirklich interessieren, und in Bereichen zu wachsen, die ich für wichtig halte. Ich wollte meine Programmierkenntnisse verbessern, auch wenn ich nicht sehr technisch war, und ich nahm mir vor, immer weiter zu lernen, bis ich mit meinen Kenntnissen einigermaßen zufrieden war. Ich wusste auch, dass ich meine Fähigkeiten im Projektmanagement verbessern wollte um den Impact meiner Arbeit zu maximieren. Palantir hat das Erreichen dieser Ziele aktiv gefördert, auch wenn es aus Sicht des Unternehmens sinnvoller gewesen wäre, sich auf meine Stärken zu konzentrieren und mich weit weg von den Code-Repositories zu halten. So wichtig es für mich war, diese Fähigkeiten zu entwickeln, so sehr genieße ich es auch, selbst Hand anzulegen und sinnvolle Produkte zu entwickeln, die andere nützlich finden. Die Arbeit an Palantir Foundry hat mir die Möglichkeit gegeben, Dinge von Grund auf neu zu entwickeln, und Foundry macht es einfach, iterativ zu arbeiten und Lösungen schnell auf- und abzubauen und anzupassen. Als Echo habe ich einen greifbaren Output — ich entwerfe und implementiere tatsächlich Anwendungen, die die Arbeit der Kunden einfacher und effizienter machen — und ich arbeite Seite an Seite mit den zukünftig Nutzenden, anstatt in einer Blackbox. Als Projektleiterin und Mentorin bin ich auch dafür verantwortlich, die persönliche und berufliche Entwicklung meiner Teammitglieder zu beobachten und zu unterstützen, eine Aufgabe, die mir auch selbst immer unglaublich viel zurückgibt und lehrt. Da ich es persönlich auch mag regelmäßig die Perspektive zu wechseln, habe ich an einer Reihe von 4–12-wöchigen Pilotprojekten gearbeitet, um neue Branchen kennenzulernen und viele Palantirians aus der ganzen Welt zu treffen. Aber es gibt auch viele Echos, die lange an einem Projekt festhalten und immer tiefer in ein Thema eintauchen, genauso wie langfristig Kundenbeziehungen aufzubauen und zu pflegen. Warum Palantir Daten können sowohl Segen als auch ein Fluch sein — sie können unschätzbare Erkenntnisse liefern, wenn man weiß, wie man sie nutzt. Wenn ich über die Welt der Daten lese, finde ich es erschreckend, wie oft Daten missbraucht werden und wie wenig die Menschen Entscheidungen hinterfragen, die “durch Daten gestützt” sind. Ich finde es wichtig, privaten und öffentlichen Organisationen dabei zu helfen, ihre Daten auf logische, ethische, effiziente und transparente Weise zu nutzen. Das entspricht auch meinen persönlichen Überzeugungen- und genau das ist es, woran ich als Deployment Strategist arbeiten darf. Von außen betrachtet ist es sicherlich oft noch schwierig zu verstehen, was Palantir eigentlich macht. Aber intern arbeitet Palantir wie ein hierarchiefreies Unternehmen, in dem die beste Idee gewinnt, unabhängig von Titel oder Betriebszugehörigkeit. Die Firma ist immer noch klein genug, um es Beschäftigten zu ermöglichen, früh viel Verantwortung zu übernehmen. Manchmal zugegebenermaßen auch ressourcenbedingt, da wir nie genug Beschäftige haben, um all die spannenden Aufgaben zu bewältigen, die uns bei Palantir zuteil werden. Man trägt ständig mehrere verschiedene Hüte — in der Regel ist man sowohl für die Leitung eines Projekts als auch für die Entwicklung eines Produkts verantwortlich und sorgt gleichzeitig dafür, dass alles Gelernte in die Software von Palantir zurückfließt. Man kann hier jeden um Unterstützung, Kontext oder Beispiele bitten, so dass man nicht ständig das Rad alleine und neu erfinden muss. Palantir ist gut darin, erfahrene Führungs- und Mentorrollen für neu dazugestoßene Palantirians zu finden, die dabei helfen, sich in diesem zugegebenermaßen unkonventionellen Unternehmen zurechtzufinden und sich beruflich so weiterzuentwickeln, wie sie es möchten. Der herausforderndste Aspekt der Arbeit bei Palantir So verlockend “keine Hierarchie” im ersten Moment auch klingt, es geht mit einem außergewöhnlich hohen Maß an Autonomie und Verantwortung einher. Häufig muss man in einem unklaren Umfeld selbstbewusst Entscheidungen treffen und den Kurs für eine unbekannte Zukunft bestimmen. Die Chancen stehen gut, dass man selbst mehr Kontext hat als alle anderen, auch wenn man es in dem Moment vielleicht nicht so empfindet. Ständig unter diesen Umständen zu arbeiten kann mental anstrengend sein. Dadurch lernt man natürlich langfristig sehr gut mit Ambiguität umzugehen, aber das macht es im ersten Moment nicht einfacher. Die flache Hierarchie von Palantir garantiert auf jeden Fall eine steile Lernkurve. Mein Rat für jemanden, der die Rolle des Deployment Strategists in Betracht zieht Es gibt keine festgelegten Wege zu dieser Rolle, keine typischen Studiengänge oder Branchen, in denen Deployment Strategists “immer” arbeiten. Es gibt einfach kein festgelegtes und erprobtes Rezept, um in dieser Rolle erfolgreich zu sein. Dafür haben wir die Möglichkeit, sie immer wieder neu zu definieren und umzuschreiben. Je mehr Verantwortung ich übernehme, desto mehr bekomme ich auch zurück; je mehr Meinungen ich formuliere, desto mehr Leute hören mir zu. Ob man nun den ganzen Tag Code schreibt, Interviews führt, bestehende Kunden skaliert oder neue Kunden gewinnt, die Bühne gehört uns und wir sollten unsere Stärken und Schwächen auf unsere ganz eigene Art und Weise einsetzen. So wie kein Tag in unserem Berufsleben gleich ist, ist auch kein Deployment Strategist wie die oder der Andere. Wir sind eine Gruppe von Menschen, die nicht in eine einzige Rollenbeschreibung passen. Wir gehen dorthin, wo wir am meisten gebraucht werden, und es juckt uns von Natur in den Fingern, wenn wir Probleme sehen. Wir sind die Ersten vor Ort und die Letzten, die gehen. Wir haben eine Get-Shit-Done-Mentalität, stellen den bestehenden Status Quo ständig in Frage und legen großen Wert auf eine praxisorientierte Umsetzung. Deployment Strategists zeichnen sich durch Reflexionsfähigkeit, Eigeninitiative, technisches Verständnis und Einfühlungsvermögen aus. Wir wissen am besten, wo unsere Stärken und Schwächen liegen, und Palantir wird uns fragen, wie es als Unternehmen besser werden kann, anstatt uns in eine vorgefertigte Rolle zu zwingen. Wir sehen die Stolpersteine, die vor uns liegen, und tun alles, was nötig ist, um sie für uns und unser Team zu beseitigen, sei es, indem wir uns eine neue Programmiersprache beibringen oder indem wir hitzig mit unserer Führungsebene diskutieren. Es ist uns wirklich wichtig, die Bedürfnisse derjenigen zu verstehen, die Palantir Plattformen nutzen. Kurz gesagt, als Deployment Strategist bei Palantir ist es unsere Aufgabe, schwierige Situationen zu meistern und unkonventionelle Lösungen für datenbasierte Herausforderungen zu finden, und zwar auf unsere eigene Art und Weise — denn wir wissen am besten, wo wir individuell und als Team am meisten gebraucht werden.

title: La donnée n’est PAS notre fonds de commerce (Palantir Mode d’Emploi, No.1)
description: Palantir a bâti un logiciel permettant de baser ses opérations et prises de décision sur les données. Cette infostructure sert de trame sur laquelle l’organisation vient tisser ses données, ses capacités analytiques et l'exécution opérationnelle.
author: Palantir
body: Palantir France Palantir Palantirglobal France Technologie La donnée n’est PAS notre fonds de commerce (Palantir Mode d’Emploi, No.1) Palantir 4 min read · Jun 9, 2022 -- Share (An English-language version of this post can be read here .) Palantir a souvent été décrite comme une entreprise secrète. C’est en partie vrai car pendant de nombreuses années, Palantir a principalement servi les institutions œuvrant dans des domaines les plus sensibles comme la défense ou le renseignement, dont les attentes en matière de discrétion sont très strictes. Servant désormais des clients dans un grand nombre de secteurs, Palantir est plus transparent. C’est particulièrement vrai dans des domaines comme la supply chain, la décarbonation, et l’aéronautique. Notre capacité à fournir une technologie avec des règles strictes de gouvernance permet la mise en œuvre d’écosystèmes de confiance de la donnée entre acteurs pourtant très hétérogènes. La société civile doit pouvoir évaluer des technologies transparentes comme celle de Palantir et comment nos partenaires l’utilisent. Des idées fausses courent et avec elles la rumeur enfle : Palantir pourrait utiliser ou transférer les données de ses clients à ses propres fins, ou pourrait agréger puis vendre les données croisées de ses clients. C’est faux . La nature des activités de Palantir est détaillée dans cet article de blog ci-après. Ce billet consacré au “business model” de l’entreprise sera le premier d’une série intitulée “Palantir mode d’emploi”, explorant une série de sujets, notamment sur l’approche de la vie privée, la sécurité, les gardes-fous des algorithmes d’IA/ML, etc. Press enter or click to view image in full size Le modèle d’entreprise de Palantir Palantir n’est pas un “data broker”, un “courtier en données” ou un “agrégateur de données”. Contrairement à de nombreuses entreprises technologiques, le modèle commercial de Palantir n’est pas basé sur la monétisation des données personnelles. Palantir ne collecte, ne stocke, ni ne vend de données personnelles. Palantir n’utilise aucune donnée personnelle pour alimenter des modèles propriétaires d’IA ou de Machine Learning afin de les revendre à d’autres clients. Palantir n’a pas pour mission de permettre ou de faciliter la circulation des données entre ses clients, sauf lorsque ceux-ci ont conclu un accord spécifique entre eux. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Palantir édite des logiciels. Palantir a bâti un logiciel permettant de baser ses opérations et prises de décision sur les données. Cette infostructure sert de trame sur laquelle l’organisation vient tisser ses données, ses capacités analytiques et l’exécution opérationnelle. Les plateformes de Palantir relient en effet ces éléments entre eux, en apportant les données utiles aux personnes qui en ont besoin, leur permettant ainsi : de prendre des décisions fondées sur leurs données, de mener des analyses rapides ou très complexes , et d’affiner les opérations sur la base de l’évaluation des décisions prises Pour cela, Palantir concède des licences logicielles, permettant ainsi à ses clients d’exploiter des instances uniques, sécurisées et modulables, au sein desquelles elles effectuent leurs missions en toute indépendance et autonomie sur leurs propres données. Cette infostructure permet de rassembler les données les plus appropriées, au moment critique afin de répondre à des questions complexes et prendre des décisions pertinentes. Une nécessité alors que les systèmes existants sont trop souvent fragmentés, incapables de communiquer entre eux et les informations critiques isolées. Des institutions en charge de la santé publique ont, par exemple, utilisé le logiciel de Palantir pour relever de nombreux défis durant la crise sanitaire du COVID- 19, par exemple celui de la bonne répartition des équipements de protection individuelle (masque, blouse, gants, etc.) face à la constante fluctuation des stocks et besoins de milliers d’hôpitaux répartis sur des territoires entiers. Les plateformes logicielles de Palantir permettent aux organisations de mieux gérer les données dont elles disposent légalement. Les plateformes de Palantir sont utilisées dans certains des environnements les plus sensibles et les plus sécurisés au monde, qui nécessitent une protection et une gouvernance des données exemplaires. À ce titre, le bilan de Palantir en matière de sécurité de l’information est indiscutable. Chez nos clients, Palantir agit en tant que sous-traitant, tandis que ces derniers restent responsables du traitement des données. En effet, les organisations conservent la maîtrise de l’utilisation qu’elles veulent avoir des logiciels et services de Palantir: ce sont elles qui déterminent ce qui peut et ne peut pas être fait avec leurs données, elles contrôlent les actions réalisées avec les comptes Palantir. Tout ingénieur de Palantir qui les appuie dans ce travail suit scrupuleusement leurs instructions. Palantir ne réutilise ni ne transfère les données de ses partenaires pour ses propres besoins — et n’en a d’ailleurs pas la possibilité. Tenter de tirer profit des données de ses clients de cette manière serait non seulement illégal mais minerait durablement la confiance nécessaire pour travailler dans les environnements sensibles dans lesquels Palantir a construit sa réputation. Toutes les entreprises technologiques doivent être questionnées surtout lorsque leur technologie est utilisée par les gouvernements. C’est pourquoi, nous espérons que cette série d’articles de blog permettra aux lecteurs de mieux connaître notre activité et de mieux comprendre certaines des principales caractéristiques de notre technologie. N’hésitez pas à nous contacter .

title: Why Traditional Approaches to Continuous Deployment Don’t Work Today
description: Software is becoming more complex and linear pipelines are insufficient to keep pace with rapidly changing approaches to how software is developed and deployed. This is why we built Palantir Apollo.
author: Palantir
body: Continuous Delivery Continuous Deployment DevOps Kubernetes Palantir Apollo Why Traditional Approaches to Continuous Deployment Don’t Work Today Palantir 7 min read · Jun 15, 2022 -- 2 Listen Share Editor’s note: This blog post is the first in a series about Palantir Apollo, aimed at unpacking what Apollo is, the problems it solves, and how its novel approach to software deployment can provide a competitive advantage in an increasingly complex and fragmented software landscape. Press enter or click to view image in full size In this first post, we describe where traditional, linear approaches to continuous deployment (CD) fall short, and explain how Apollo rethinks the way software is deployed to truly solve the challenges arising from the new, complex realities of modern software development and deployment. The traditional approach: embracing automation through “linear pipelines” There have been amazing advances in CD over the past decade that have made it possible for changes to get from commit to production at an unprecedented speed. These advances helped software teams get new features to customers faster and more safely, while facilitating immediate feedback on how recent code changes actually work in production. However, under the hood, most traditional CD tooling still looks largely the same as it did ten years ago: linear pipelines. It was designed assuming that software was linearly flowing through a sequential process of testing, compilation, publishing, and deployment. Over time, more parts of the deployment process were automated with policy scripts layered on top of pipelines, and better UIs were created to provide a cleaner developer experience, but at its core, the approach that traditional CD takes has not changed significantly. The linear, “assembly line” model can only take us so far, however. The core challenge of linear pipelines today is that they fail to account for the astronomical rise in complexity with which software is both developed and where it is deployed. Specifically: The move away from monoliths to service-oriented architectures (SOA) means an individual update to a single service cannot be “linearly” deployed straight to a testing or production environment without first considering the implication its change has on potentially dozens of other dependencies . SOAs are valuable in that they enable development teams to ship features independently, enabling your software to evolve at the rate of the fastest movers and getting new features to customers faster. They also make your platform more modular, reusable, and resilient. However, more puzzle pieces can mean more complexity; managing large numbers of interrelated services is not trivial — and it is certainly not linear. It is now common practice for a single piece of software to be deployed to a number of different environments. In a growing push to meet customers where they are, it is now not uncommon for an organization to offer their software across multiple cloud providers and infrastructure types, each with varying levels of connectivity and access, as well as higher demands for compliance and data governance. This introduces a host of challenges that were not present when enterprise software sat in single on-premise data centers, or even in the dream single-cloud “SaaS” world that is quickly fizzling. The prospect of adding new, possibly heterogeneous environments as deployment targets, each with their own specific constraints/requirements, adds exponential complexity to deployment models. The overarching consequence of these major evolutions is more complexity, and linear pipelines, notwithstanding all their benefits, have proven insufficient in handling them. Where Traditional Methods Fall Short Managing Service Oriented Architecture Complexity It’s hard to safely manage deploying a platform made up of many distinct, possibly interrelated services, and the complexity scales exponentially with the number of services. Press enter or click to view image in full size A complex web of microservice dependencies Some challenges include: Cross-service dependencies , both for deployment and networking. In linear CD pipeline approaches, managing cross-service dependencies between pipelines is extremely difficult. At best, you string various pipelines together in a chain, which becomes very brittle and is not scalable. Handling rollbacks without breaking API compatibility becomes an extremely difficult exercise, especially if you aim to do it in an automated manner. Configuration at scale , especially when managing database URIs for dependent services across multiple environments. The number of configuration points that you need to set URIs for equates to the number of edges in your graph of services multiplied by the number of environments you have. Relying on humans to configure each of these by hand can make it very brittle and cumbersome. Another pain point is managing customer-specific configuration when you have more than one instance of each service across various deployment targets. Lack of standardization across pipelines. Many services means you have to have many pipelines. Pipeline skew quickly emerges as each pipeline evolves independently from the others. When teams create new pipelines, they usually clone a previous pipeline and then modify it to suit the needs of the new service or team. Additionally, linear pipelines tightly couple everything together — it’s difficult to create pieces that you can standardize, reuse or substitute. This can be problematic, because there is often no common knowledge across teams in terms of how their services get deployed; there are many different paths to production. Every time an engineer joins a new team, they have to spend time figuring out how the new team’s pipelines work. Debugging pipelines also becomes more challenging. This lack of standardization across pipelines creates more complexity and overhead, costing you time and money. Maintaining awareness of many moving parts — What exactly is deployed where, and what is its state? Who owns what and should be contacted to resolve issues? How long should teams have to maintain backwards API compatibility? Asset dependencies , such as static files used for the front end. Managing database schema version dependencies , among other challenges. Environment and Business Complexity Difficult to scale at pace of business need: Services and environments are coupled within pipelines. This is problematic when your deployment model requires you to deploy to many environments. Consider when your company needs to stand up a new environment. If you have a single pipeline, you tack on each new environment to the end of it. If you have many pipelines, then you have to add each new environment to each pipeline. This is neither efficient, nor scalable, and also means that your engineers are in the critical path of new business growth. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Challenge of deploying in various configurations: If you need to deploy your platform in different configurations, with different feature sets, pipelines are a nightmare. Oftentimes, different customers may require different parts of your platform and, with a linear pipeline based approach, it is difficult to deploy different subsets of your platform in a modular manner. Ballooning pipeline complexity: Pipelines get even more complicated when you add various compliance controls, security policies, approval steps, etc., causing pipelines to become humongous and often requiring teams to write automations scripts to manage them. Your teams are then left maintaining hundreds of pipelines and automation scripts. The linear nature of pipelines also makes them rigid — because they’re designed from left to right, it’s complicated to have a piece running in parallel that triggers something in the middle. Achieving this often requires more scripts on top of, or around, the pipeline. How Apollo Solves This At Palantir, we believe that software is only becoming more complex and demands of where it deploys is only going to increase, and therefore linear pipelines are insufficient. This is why we built Apollo. It was built on several key principles and components that help your business efficiently, resiliently, and securely deploy your software wherever it needs to go: Separation of concerns — Decouple software and environments. Apollo models the world in terms of software packages and environments. Developers know best how their software should be upgraded and how it should behave, so they define service specifications and constraints alongside their code. Operators know best what is important to their environments and customers, so they define environment specifications and constraints. Operators choose which services should be installed in the environment and Apollo will ensure they’re installed safely. Apollo will flag if constraints are not met, and often automatically resolve them. Everyone stays within their zone of subject matter expertise, and neither persona is reliant on the other. Hide complexity while maintaining flexibility — Release channels. Apollo’s concept of Release Channels is a way to strike the optimal balance between stability and velocity. Release channels give you a way of modeling risk, and using more risky channels as canaries. Environments are subscribed to a given release channel, defining at what point point they will get new product releases for each of their installed services. You can also subscribe to a different release channel per product. This allows an environment owner to take more risks on specific aspects of the platform, e.g., a customer that cares about specific features being on the cutting edge but is otherwise more risk averse. Automate wherever possible while retaining ultimate control — Guardrails. Security and compliance are first class concepts with Apollo; it ultimately aligns incentives between developers, operators, security, compliance, and quality teams. Apollo provides several gates into production so your teams can define the policies and workflows that must be abided by. Apollo aims to automate process wherever possible so a human is not required in the loop, while maintaining all necessary security and compliance controls (e.g., contextually aware change management features). It also provides several points for platform teams to set different types of golden paths, such as default release channels. The next Palantir Apollo series blog post provides a technical deep dive into how Apollo rethinks this entire problem space to achieve CD for modern software realities. title: Palantir and Google Cloud Announce Strategic Partnership
description: Palantir are collaborating with Google Cloud for better enterprise data management using scalable, trusted, and sustainable infrastructure.
author: Palantir
body: Google Cloud Palantir Cloud Partnerships Google Palantir and Google Cloud Announce Strategic Partnership Offering Commercial Customers Smarter Data-Driven Decision Making Palantir 4 min read · Jun 16, 2022 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Editor’s note: Read Google Cloud’s post and explore related content on their page . As the world continues to increase in complexity, business success hinges on an ability to effectively manage data, while translating analysis into better decisions and outcomes. To enable data-driven transformation for our clients, Palantir and Google Cloud are excited to partner in providing commercial customers with an end-to-end data solution, turbocharging Palantir Foundry’s operational decision making with Google Cloud’s capabilities in analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Our partnership with Google Cloud offers organizations a fast time-to-value bridge between technical experts, IT, and frontline business users, empowering them all to work with their data in more meaningful ways. We’re partnering with Google Cloud on three key fronts: Palantir is delivering its Foundry platform for enterprise data management on Google Cloud. Customers will be able to quickly and easily deploy Foundry and take advantage of its features, while also benefiting from Google Cloud’s global, scalable, trusted and sustainable infrastructure. They can also deploy Foundry directly from the Google Cloud Marketplace. Foundry will integrate with Google Cloud products to empower people throughout an organization to better work with data. Foundry users can bring together their data in Google BigQuery with a variety of other sources, and run Google analytics as well as AI/ML capabilities to help drive more effective decision-making and faster business value. Google Cloud and Palantir are going to market in order to help solve key industry challenges for our customers, starting with retail, supply chain, and the financial services industry. Bridging data and insights so you can achieve business value with speed By using pre-built Palantir Foundry workflows that connect with Google Cloud native and industry solutions, users can have a complete data foundation for enabling smarter Enterprise AI within weeks. Existing Google Cloud customers can quickly get data into BigQuery by directly connecting to source systems using HyperAuto powered by SDDI. They can then utilize Foundry’s operational application and decisions framework to leverage the capabilities of BigQuery and VertexAI. Palantir Foundry’s out-of-the-box workflow and rules solution delivers immediate business value and leverages Google’s AI/ML capabilities to help make our Foundry workflows even smarter when it comes to solving complex business problems. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in In taking away the technical backend complexities of data integration, we can empower frontline users to apply their own expertise and interact with their data more naturally, while activating it in real-time as they look to produce their best work. When problems do arise, using Foundry on Google Cloud enables organizations to collaborate dynamically — and again, in real time — in order to stay on top of their business by breaking down organizational silos that would otherwise prevent proper analysis. Solving key industry challenges To stay competitive in this new world of data, organizations should truly understand their end-customers. We’re not just excited about how this new partnership can improve knowledge of end-users, but also in their understanding of themselves, and where they reside within their wider industry landscape. Here are a few examples: Retailers can implement Palantir’s Inventory Management Workflows alongside Google Cloud’s Recommendations, Forecast, and Demand AIs to better predict when popular items will go out of stock, and also adapt to disruptions in their supply chains. Banks can better detect fraud and money laundering activities by collating transaction data, online activity, and fraud alert data in Foundry, while also deriving insights by bringing it into Google BigQuery and layering AI/ML models on the same data. Grocers can better address the persistent problem of operational shrink by bringing together data on sales, inventory, promotions, and products utilizing Palantir Foundry on Google Cloud, helping them better reduce food waste. By building use cases for common business challenges, Palantir and Google Cloud can accelerate digital transformation for customers and build the foundation they need to make mission critical decisions. Better together Organizational transformation rests on an ability to use data effectively for operational decision-making. This partnership will allow businesses to leverage Foundry’s capabilities in data-driven decision making and situational intelligence on Google Cloud’s trusted and secure infrastructure. title: Understanding ROI with Palantir Foundry
description: With Palantir Foundry, leaders can get a real-time view of their projects, and better measure ROI for more effective future strategy.
author: Palantir
body: SaaS Roi Financial Planning Business Palantir Understanding ROI with Palantir Foundry Palantir 5 min read · Jun 20, 2022 -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size These days, it’s nearly impossible to imagine a road trip without a mobile phone and navigation app. While printing out a guidance route or referring to a paper map seems so archaic to us today, we forget that these error-prone methods were the only options we had just a few years ago. How did we know when we’d get to our destination without knowing the traffic conditions lying ahead? What did we do when we took a wrong turn, or when the roads themselves had changed in the time since our map on hand was printed? In many ways, many companies today still use the equivalent of paper maps for navigating their financial and human resources. At Palantir, we’ve built the next-generation navigation platform for our finances, helping our people understand where they are today and see what lies ahead. For many leaders, the process of understanding where their companies are investing and how those investments are faring involves weeks of work from internal teams and outside consultants, due to siloed, sensitive data and fragmented organisational views. The data likely live in different systems altogether, and may include sensitive information that must be handled carefully or only for certain purpose. The best version of the resultant output is an accurate picture of a company’s state when the process started . The faster a company grows and the surrounding world changes, the more outdated the decisions made from this picture are. To avoid unpleasant surprises when it comes time to report, whether at the end of a quarter to shareholders or to ad-hoc investor meetings, many companies must resort to implementing hurdles designed to avoid spending outside of a rigid top-down structure. While this helps limit damage in some realms, it may inhibit organizations’ abilities to respond to change and even take advantage of investment opportunities. This is a technology problem. Why is getting a real-time view of your expenses and revenue hard? Let’s extend the metaphor just a little further. To help you traverse the physical world, your mobile phone’s navigation app needs to integrate data from a variety of sources ranging from GPS satellites orbiting earth to traffic information gathered from myriad databases. The task of compiling a real-time-view of your company’s operational picture and comprehensive ROI involves a similar set of challenges: Data is spread across databases that don’t talk to each other. From financial reporting tools, such as expense and billing management tools, to more task-specific tools like Google Ads or AWS billing, financial data and corresponding understanding of ROI are dispersed across systems. In order to understand a project’s performance, expenses must be married to other metrics, which likely live in different systems altogether: e.g. travel, payroll, and revenue data. The standard organisational view is fragmented. Each of the above-mentioned tools comes with its own, distinct data model, and sits at a unique vantage point within the organisation. The view from that vantage point does not often provide a holistic picture of how the overall organisation wants or needs to operate. This impedance mismatch can force the organisation to alter its structure towards one dictated by those tools, just so that the data provided will make sense. This can make it difficult to change organisational structures as needed, because the barrier to changing the corresponding external financial systems is too high. Financial data is often an organisation’s most sensitive data. Ensuring accuracy and appropriate access to financial data poses a delicate technological challenge where a mistake can have market-moving implications. The effort and complexity involved with disseminating this information can be a significant limiting factor to the organisation’s ability to diffuse decision-making across all areas of the business. This can lead to organisations centralising command, which is often counter-productive to business outcomes. Lack of coverage from existing tooling. Of course, the existing tooling and corresponding procedures were adopted for good reasons — they solve specific pain points for employees, finance, and increased management’s visibility into operations. And there are surely more opaque areas where the organisation would like tools that provide incremental visibility. Without a technological solution to those additional areas, decisions and transactions will be recorded in static form across spreadsheets and emails. How can Foundry provide a better solution? At Palantir, we faced all of the challenges described above — and more! But by wielding Palantir Foundry, we were able to tackle them directly and sustainably. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Foundry gives Palantir’s leaders across the business a real-time view of their projects’ ROI. Leaders are able to make independent and informed decisions based on a truly up-to-date view of the business. These decisions are then fed back via the common operating picture with minimal friction, enabling meaningful and relevant course-setting at all levels. When we kicked off these efforts, we had much of the necessary data in our internal Foundry instance, as it was used to drive other use cases. As our companywide operations evolved in size and complexity, Palantir incorporated new tools to meet the need. We then used Foundry’s out-of-the-box data connectors to connect these tools bidirectionally to Foundry. We integrated procurement and credit card data to get a real time view of expenses and added extra dimensions to this spend from other systems such as our recruiting platforms, marketing systems, and CRM software, giving us a comprehensive attribution to every dollar that is spent. With the benefit of an existing digital twin, we continued to expand this picture, integrating financial data into the way Palantir understands our business and enriching our existing structures and ontology with a financial dimension. This financial digital twin can be changed with little to no code, wherein the tools and dashboards built on this digital twin automatically update to reflect the evolving reality. We can rapidly test and adopt new tools, or even build our own with minimal investment when the market doesn’t quite have tools that meet our requirements. These real-time updates and ability to customise our solution enable Palantir to track and asses new organisational units and go-to-market strategies. In addition to the business advantage provided by Foundry’s digital twin, the platform’s data lineage and change management tools can help simplify auditing changes and monitoring data health. Multi-modal, granular security primitives make it possible to disseminate the right information only to the people who should be viewing that data. At Palantir, C-level leadership and on-the-ground project leads can use Foundry as the single pane of glass through which to view and assess financial and operational data, while appropriate access levels are enforced automatically. One of the most important advantages provided by business management in Foundry is that everyone can both see and agree on the validity of the data in front of them. This allows leaders to skip the step of validating and agreeing on numbers, and to instead focus on meaningful decision-making across the company. It also permits Palantir to practice distributive authority, as leaders at any level can see and understand the operational picture at a moment’s notice. By using Foundry as Palantir’s internal operating system we, not our tools, are in control of our organisational structures and operational future. To schedule a demo of these capabilities or simply learn more, get in touch . Authors MC Bousquette: Operational Lead Roi Nir : Technical Team Lead

title: Palantir Apollo Orchestration: Constraint-Based Continuous Deployment For Modern Architectures
description: By intelligently applying declared constraints, Palantir Apollo helps engineering organizations achieve stability and velocity.
author: Palantir
body: Continuous Delivery Continuous Deployment Kubernetes DevOps Palantir Apollo Palantir Apollo Orchestration: Constraint-Based Continuous Deployment For Modern Architectures Palantir 8 min read · Jun 23, 2022 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Editor’s note: This blog post is the second in a series about Palantir Apollo, following publication of Why Traditional Approaches to Continuous Deployment Don’t Work Today . Introduction Over the last 20 years, the software industry has focused on improving developer efficiency through various means: experimenting with different organizational designs (smaller, independent development teams, DevOps, platform engineering) adopting new project management approaches ( Agile ) adopting new software architectures (service-oriented, micro-service, and server-less) However, the rapid changes in how we build software and structure engineering teams has dramatically outpaced the tooling meant to facilitate these activities. While using platforms like Kubernetes may simplify deploying independent workloads, it does not help ensure those workloads are compatible with one another. As we move towards smaller, composable units, some popular continuous deployment platforms struggle to manage the complexities inherent in updating interdependent components in a distributed system when each component evolves independently. The inability of these continuous deployment platforms to manage inter-service dependencies means organizations can’t actually ship services independently. Instead, they “continuously deploy” a distributed monolith, not realizing any of the velocity gains afforded by modern software development techniques. We designed Apollo to address the unique complexities of modern architectures and enable efficient independent software development. A core element of Apollo’s approach to managing this complexity is the Apollo Orchestration Engine. This component enables deployment constraints to be encoded within software, as well as rules for when changes occur in the environment in which the software is running. It then ensures these constraints are satisfied when applying changes to managed software installations. This allows for true continuous deployment of the components of a distributed system, without sacrificing stability. In this post, we’ll discuss how the Apollo Orchestration Engine works, and how we solved some of the problems inherent in continuous deployment of service oriented architectures. The Apollo Orchestration Engine The Apollo orchestration engine is responsible for progressing an environment’s current state towards Apollo’s target state for the environment. This is similar to the Kubernetes operator design pattern which has become popular in recent years, with a crucial addition — the ability to recognize a distributed system’s interdependencies and constraints, and validate those constraints while performing work. Apollo applies this design pattern to manage the continuous deployment of many software installations spanning different environments, providing three inputs to its orchestration engine’s control loop: deployable software releases, sourced from the Apollo Catalog declared state for environments held in an Environment Configuration Store current (or “reported”) state provided by Apollo agents running within Apollo-managed environments Press enter or click to view image in full size Guaranteeing that the process of aligning current state with target state will not impact the availability of the software or violate the expectations of software or operators is critical. To that end, we designed Apollo’s orchestration engine to accept constraints defined by both software and environments, and only recommend steps towards the target state that satisfy all constraints. This design automates the process of solving within the provided constraints, ensuring the process is repeatable. Separately, developers and operators can leverage their domain expertise to define the appropriate constraints for the orchestration engine to apply. While Apollo also offers the ability to declare rules for when change occurs in environments, the rest of this post will focus solely on developers encoding constraints in their software, and the Apollo Orchestration Engine’s application of those constraints. Encoding Deployment Constraints in Software When building just one component of a larger architecture, developers make implicit assumptions about the surrounding pieces of the distributed system. Leaving these expectations as implicit requires humans to manually guarantee them at deployment time. Apollo enables these expectations to be explicitly encoded within software instead; this way, developers can encode these expectations once and leave the deployment process to Apollo, reclaiming time to focus on building product. When encoding software expectations, developers declare constraints alongside their code in a set of metadata known as a manifest. This manifest is provided to Apollo’s registry for deployable software, the Apollo Catalog, during product release registration. Once in the catalog, this information is available to the rest of the Apollo Hub — including its orchestration engine. The orchestration engine then applies these constraints when determining the safety of performing a given software update. Critically, Apollo reduces the need for humans to manually guarantee their software’s expectations . Below, we’ll walk through two types of constraints — how they’re declared, how Apollo honors them throughout the continuous deployment process, and the safety they provide software developers. Example: Service Dependency Constraints A modern software architecture’s functionality arises from communication between its components. In turn, this communication depends on API contracts between components. Handling the complexity of these interdependencies compelled us to build support for cross-service dependency constraints early in Apollo’s development. This investment has drastically reduced the human effort involved in feature rollout and deprecated API removal at Palantir. Get Palantir ’s stories in your inbox Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer. Subscribe Subscribe Remember me for faster sign in Imagine we are developing a new feature in service foo which depends on some new API in a separately developed service bar . Our feature will only work if it’s deployed alongside a version of bar which satisfies this new dependency. We recognize the need to declare this cross-service dependency when merging our feature, and include this constraint in our service’s manifest: service-dependencies: - product-name: bar minimum-version: 1.1.0 maximum-version: 1.x.x This service dependency is included in the manifest we publish to the Apollo Catalog upon tagging a new release (let’s say 1.1.0 ) of foo . Observing this new release, the Apollo orchestration engine considers upgrading an existing installation of foo in an environment with the following reported state: - service-name: foo version: 1.0.0 configuration-overrides: log-level: debug - service-name: bar version: 1.0.0 configuration-overrides: {} Apollo considers the feasibility of upgrading the reported installation of foo from 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 . Upon loading the foo 1.0.0 release’s declared constraints, however, it realizes that the current bar installation’s version violates the new foo release’s cross-service dependency constraint. In this case, Apollo will wait to recommend upgrading to our new release until bar has upgraded to a version which satisfies this constraint. Apollo applies service dependency constraints “both ways.” Imagine the owners of bar releasing a 2.0.0 version which removes support for endpoints deprecated in 1.x versions - Apollo would refuse to deploy this release without first upgrading to a release of foo which either (1) updates its service dependency’s accepted version range or (2) removes the dependency entirely. Without support for declaring cross-service dependency constraints, other continuous deployment solutions typically require human investment to ensure a new feature lands in the same monolithic release train as its dependencies. If an organization forgoes this manual effort, it can lead to production outages and time-intensive manual remediation. Apollo relieves developers of this manual coordination while also eliminating the human error inherent in such efforts. Example: Schema Migration Constraints Services responsible for reading and writing data to persistent stores adhere to database schemas when performing these reads and writes. Over time, feature work or performance improvement efforts may compel code owners to change a service’s schema. Getting a schema migration wrong poses significant risk, potentially causing irreversible data corruption and extended production outages. We recognized that, as components in a service-oriented architecture evolved over time, ensuring safe schema migrations in an automated manner would be critical. We thus determined to build Apollo support for schema migration constraints, and achieved this by introducing two points of interaction for developers: declaring supported schema versions in a release’s manifest at publish time serving the current and target schema versions of a service running in production, to be included in the service’s reported state Let’s imagine we want our service foo to complete a schema migration from V1 to V2 over multiple releases with different ranges of supported schema versions: Press enter or click to view image in full size 1.1.0 supports reading only the V1 schema version. 1.2.0 and 1.3.0 can read both V1 and V2. 1.3.0 additionally migrates all persisted data to V2. 1.4.0 drops support for the now-obsolete V1 schema. This approach’s correctness depends on the continuous deployment platform waiting to deploy the 1.4.0 release until the schema migration from V1 to V2 completes. We’ll declare these schema migration constraints by including the supported schema version range in our manifest for each release: # 1.2.0 manifest schema-migrations: [V1, V2] # 1.3.0 schema-migrations: [V1, V2] # 1.4.0 schema-migrations: [V2] Our additional responsibility as the developers of foo is to report the current schema version to Apollo agents upon request, which will include this information when reporting state to the Apollo Hub. Apollo expects a service’s current schema version to be incremented only upon successful completion of a migration - for us, this will happen when our 1.3.0 release has completed its schema migration to V2 . Apollo Orchestration Logic for Schema Migrations Let’s now consider Apollo’s use of this information when determining when to recommend foo service upgrades. Applying a schema migration constraint is the same as asking: Does the target release’s supported schema version range contain the current schema version reported for the foo installation? Critically, Apollo’s schema constraints result in two guarantees: foo is guaranteed to upgrade to a version capable of performing the migration ( 1.3.0 in this example) before it can upgrade further. Once upgraded to 1.3.0 , foo must report the migration has completed successfully before Apollo will consider upgrading foo to later versions.
